div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 219 • 18q2 k • NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- THE LAND QUESTION. CULTURE, Sze. in re est Rhondda ete I XVI. Great preparations are being made in Germany to export vices are suspended and the 0-, - • potatoes in large quantities to America. It is seen that in I The •ineo. •• New York potatoes cost fifteen marks per kilogramme; whereas in Germany they only fetch five marks. The " poor man's food" seems to grow better in the moist allu- vial soil of Germany than in its native land. The English competition will be great, and our authority, the Wiener Landwirthshaftliche Zeitung says that the large German seaports will have to exert all their energies in order to pre- vent Enaland getting the best part of the trade. . Some enterprising Hungarian agriculturists are trying to introduce the culture of rice in Hungary. Connoisseurs are to be instructed to examine the soil, and to report upon the likelihood of the climate being advantageous to the cultiva- tion of this plant, in order to avoid, if possible, all possi- bility of disappointment; but it would seem more practical to try and perfect the culture of the plants already culti- vated than to begin the cultivation of a new cereal, which, even if it succeeded, would probably not be more profitable than those now under cultivation. The Earl of Ellesmere has sold three Shire-bred stallions for exportation to Australia. They include Admiral (71), winner of the champion prize of the English Cart-horse Society's Show at the Agricultural Hall, 1880, and the first at the Royal Derby meeting; Emperor, tlfe two-year-old winner at the Royal Derby; and Sir Wilfrid Lawson, by Robin Hood (1874). Mr. G. M. Sexton has sent a Shire-bred stallion to Sweden. He :recently sold The Clipper, a two- year-old, bred by the Hon. Edward Coke, Longford, Derby, sire Matchless (1536), dam Candace, by Hercules (1022). The colt has been sent to the stables of the King of Sweden. LIE ADVERSE SEASONS AND AGRICULTURAL REFORMS. —lt is scarcely too mach to say that a succession of good seasons would gradually stifle the loud cries and complaints with which the air now resounds, andlull the British farmer once more to his normal condition of easy indifference to things political and social. Adversity has its uses, which have been called "sweet," and one of them seems to be to stir up people to renewed efforts te.; demand their rights, and to agitate for reformation: The agricaltural world is at present experiencing this frame of mind, the itnntediate, re- sult of a sort of hanger. Depletion has done its work, and the "restless giant,' who erst was content to enjoy his dinner and his siesta (?) is in the active mental condition which comes of constrained abstinence. We do not deny that the British farmer has many just causes of complaint, but it would be well for him to concentrate his aim upon thoroughly practical objects. A definite tenant-right which would give security of capital, not necessarily of tenure, is what he wants. There is much to be said in favour of the. idea of allowing tenants to erect buildings, and do other per- manent works, with power to claim compensation at the end of their tenure, within certain limits as to time. Surely common sense would restrain a tenant from laying out money in a useless manner, and the fact that the value of the work would eventually be decided by practical men would also act as a deterrent to extravagant or useless ex- penditure. After all it is the tenant and not the landlord who has the conduct of farming business, and it is he who suffers the inconvenience of insufficient accommodation or deficient apparatus. We wish to see the tenant freer in his action. We want to see a large number of possible improve- ments transferred from the schedule where a landlord's per- mission is required, to that in which the tenant may act without such permission. Asking for permission to put up a shed or a yard leads to discussion, to procrastination, to fresh proposals, and to eventual abandonment of the scheme, which had probably been better carried out at once by the tenant. If the bulk of landlords farmed their own land, we could not object strongly to the present state of the law ; but as the lands of this country are, and are likely to con- tinue, in the hands of tenant-farmers, it is necessary that these men (the actual tillers of the soil) should leave a greater amount of freedom than they are at present allowed. —Agricultural Gazette. GOOD AND BID GRASSES.—No notion is productive of more baneful results than that which supposes one grass is as good as another, the fact being that there are some grasses—and not a few, either—which are as devoid of value as forage pullets as the sedges themselves. And a most curious fact is this, that many grasses which present a very great number 04 characters in common, which are so simi- lar, indeed, that we cannot resist the conclusion that at some not far-distant period they must have diverged from a com- mon ancestor, are yet diametrically opposite to each other in their agricultural properties. Thus, the wheat plant so cicsely resembles couch-grass that botanists have felt com- pelled to include them both in the same genus, Tripticum ; yet the one is a most valuable cereal, while the other is the most abominable weed that makes land foul. AgainSamonget our earlier grasses there is none more excellent than the foxtail, Alopecurus pretends, the seeds of which are intro- duced into nearly all mixture.e, while another grass, a sort of first cousin to the foxtail, and known as Alopecurus agrestis, or black bent, is a pernicious pest, second only to the couch in the annoyarce it causes, and even in some dis- tricts out-rivalling the couch as a farmer's foe. Though grasses are so easily distinguished from all other plants, yet to discriminate between different grasses is, on the other hand, by no means an easy task, the distinctive characters being based on certain peculiarities in the construction of the inflorescence. It is, perhaps, on account of this diffi- culty—a difficulty not felt, however, by one who has a rudi- mentary acquaintance with botany—that amongst agricul- turists generally so little is known as to the different grasses, and it is probably for the same reason that all native gramineous herbs are still spoken of indifferently as "grass." Yet, with pastoral farming, and particularly dairy farming, steadily on the increase, it is becoming more than ever a matter of grave importance that a strict watch should be kept upon the quality of grass land, that is, on the charac- ters of the grasses which acquire a preponderance thereon. It is not too mach to expect-that any farmer should be able to go into his meadows in June of July, and point out or gather such good grasses as timothy, foxtail, cocksfoot, sweet vernal, dog's-tail, fescue, rye grass, and the true meadow grasses, or to detect and do his best to extirpate such usurping vagrants as false oat grass, soft grass, brome crass, hair grass, black bent, and many others. Lewes and Gil bert have shown that a judicious system of manuring is by far the best means of keeping up a healthy succession of good grasses, and at the same time of smothering their weed allies. AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION.—A very important paper appeared in The Times of Saturday from Mr. R. Giffen, of the Board of Trade, in which the extent of the deficient yield of late years in English agriculture is estimated upon the data afforded by the statistics of food importation, at two different periods, corrected by the increase of popula- tion during the interval. Food to the extent of £50,000,000 more had to be imported and was imported in 1877-79 than in 1867-69. But at £l2 per head per annum, at which the food consumption of a population is estimeted by Mr. Caird in this country, £38,000,000 more of food was required by ;the increase of population. Therefore £12,000,000 per annum less at the one period than at the other must have been provided by the home production. But this repre- sents, not difference of quantity, but difference of value. Applying the same prices at the one time as prevailed at the other, it will appear that the diminished yield in 1879, as compared with 1869, amounts to at least £18,000,000 per annum. This conclusion may, indeed, be explained, not only by bad years in the one case as compared with the other, but by a diminished individual consumption, or pos- sibly by a diminished area employed in the production. Both of these suggestions are considered by Mr. Giffen, and both of them, after consideration, are ttiemissed as unten- able, Besides, however, tbe Oirflinished annuAl proi..:Z9tion - whieh •-• • 1, • per acre resin& as thus attributed, there le,. ta; considering the position of the farmer, a largely diminished capital owing to diminished number and value of the live stock of the farm. This is put, after due consideration, at £5,000,000 per annum during the years of recent loss. Then, again, there is an increaee of rent in the ten years, and this also is put at £5,000,000 per annum. And there is a considerable increase in the cost of labour on the farm, and this, too, is put at £5,000,000 per annum. Adding all the particulars together, it appears that the Earner has been le eve off in average years of late by £38,000,000 per annnm, and in the years of maximum difference—i.e , when 1879 is compared, not with a comparatively poor year like 1869, but with the better years which preceded it—by at least £45,000,000. Taking £40,000,000 a year as a fair average, it appears that English agriculturists have in the last four years lost £160,000,000, of which £56,000,000 have been owing to deficient yield, and the rest to other causes. The loss to the country generally, however, is only the £18,000,000 spent in the increased importation of food, and this, being but 11 per cent. on the £1,200,000,000 repre- senting the whole annual income of the country. is but little felt by the whole nation, hoWever heavily it -falls on the agricultural interest by itself. The above short refer- ence explains to some extent the method of Mr. Giffen's argument, and the conclusions to which it leads. And the whole is a striking illustration of the light which one deer head, accustomed to the consideration of such subjects, is enabled by the statistical records of production and impor- tation to throw on the current situation. It illustrates at the same time the obvious weight and importance of the conclusions, based on a large body of facts, as compared with those conclusions to which single examples and special details might lead or mislead.

THE PURIFICATION OF Ant IN TUNNELS.—For talso- ground railways Dr. Neale has suggested to place beneath the railway carriages trays filled with slaked lime or caustic soda solutions, wlrch, combining chemically with the in- jurious gases, such as carbonic oxide, carbonic acid, and sulphurous acid, form harmless salts. For hospitals, Dr. Neale recommends a chemical punkah, whose fan being made of vegetable fibre, is saturated with caustic soda solution fed from a small tank above. TRACTIVE POWER ON TRAMWAYS.—It is satisfactory to know that horses employed upon tramways are not nearly so hardly worked as may appear to many ten-der-hearted persons at first sight. The truth of this assertion has just been proved by some experiments lately carried on at Salem, Massachu- setts, with a view of ascertaining the tractive force requisite to move street cars and vehicles on a macadamised road. The apparatus used consisted :of an inclined plane, at the upper end of which was an iron wheel over which passed a rope. A loaded box-car, weighing, with its contents,l2,B2olb., was drawn up the grade by a weight of 9701 b. suspended at the other end of the rope. the empty car, weighing4,B2olb., was drawn up the same grade by a weight of 2831 b. A smaller box-car, weighing, when empty, 2,7301 b., was occu- pied by fourteen persons, and drawn up by 3391 b., and, when unoccupied, by 1761 b. An ordinary load of sand on a mac- adamised road was started by 5141. b., and an empty hack, weighing 1,5501 b., by 1961 b. The same hack with four passengers inside required 2301 b. to move it. On a level road the load of sand was started by 2401 b., while the large box-car yielded to 561 b. These experiments were made by a horse-railway company, the object being to show that their work was not unusually severe for the horses, the result being declared altogether satisfactory.—lron. . THERE IS NOTHING LIRE LEATHER —From a series of tests 'of the tensile strength of different descriptions of driving-belts carried on by Herr J. Beuschinger, the well- known Munich professor, all doubt seems to have been re- moved as to which—cotton, indiarn.bber, or leather—is the , best material to be used. It appears from his experiments that, in making a graphic representation of the results, by setting the ieada per equaia. Ir. ele on a liatieentai line and erecting verticals corresponding to the elongaticns at the different loads, the curves thus obtained show considerable difference for leather, indiarubber, and cotton belts. All these materials stretch more at first, with light loads, than afterwards. The lines, therefore, are more curved at the beginning, and afterwards approach more to a straight line. But with leather belts the approximation to a straight line begins at once, and is more pronounced than with india- rubber or cotton belts, showing that they stretch from the beginning more in proportion to the load; and possess a high degree of elasticity. The conclusions drawn from the tests by Professor Bauschinger is that italiarubber and cotton ! belts are inferior to leather, not only as regards elasticity, but aloe as regards tensile strength, for the same section, 1 and only attain in strength that of medium or inferior sorts ' of leather. By cementing and sewing the ends, leather straps lose one-quarter to one-third of their strength, if the ' joints are made with great care. According to the experi- mentalist, therefore, the old saying must in future also be applied to driving-belts.—lron. ELECTRICITY AND HOME LABOUR —At the preliminary meeting, last week, of the Society for the Utilisation of Electric Force, M. Bontoux remarked :—" The really aristo- cratic machinery, still almost intact, the employer's real privilege in the working world, is motive power. The artisan, who needs a little motive power for his work, is forced to seek it in the employer's factory, while thousands of work- men and workwomen wear up their bodies and destroy their strength in impelling the sewing machine, the lathe, and the other motive powers of small industry. The division of electric energy is destined to effect an entire revolution in this sphere. The day will come, and sooner than is imagined, when the artisan tamily will see enter their dwelling by means of a magic wire the force which is now so costy to them, and this will be the dernocratisitien of force for the benefit of the working class." This last phrase is a striking one, and foreshadows the solution of a difficult social prob- lem. It. points to Abe enfranchisement of the artisan, wherever individual Can be substituted for cellective toil, from the dependence imposed on him by the absence of mo- tive power. Whenever the artisan, having motive power at home, can work surrounded by his family and training his sons, thus escaping from the contamination of the work- shop, from the influence of the wine shop, and from hurried and innutritiona meals; whenever his daughters can work at home instead of in wcmen's workrooms—far more de- moralising than men's workshops—a great step will have been taken towards the solution of the labour question. AFRICAN EXPLORATION.—AN IMPORTANT ADVANCE.—A lecture was given by Dr. Bayol, at Bordeaux, a few days ago, in the course of which he gave sundry interesting par- deniers of a new route by which it is hoped to open up the interior of Northern Africa. The country is completely un- known to Europeans, and the names of the various places visited .by the adventurous doctor will not be found on any accessible map. It must therefore suffice to say that a now watershed has been discovered, the river hitherto known as the Taneney, but which should be called the Konkednron, effecting a junction with another celled the Krikriman and draining a vast elevated plateau. On the opposite side of the chain of mountains, the-bigheet of which is the Londo Moli (7,600 feet), is a vast plain. It would be quite possible for Europeans to live on this plateau. The climate is temperate, snow is never seen, and there are very few inhabitants. The plain beyond, which is liable to inundation-during the rainy season, has for its capital the city of Timbo, and is most densely populated. All this part of the Fouta Djalon is rem arkably fer file—coffee, maize, rice, arachide, cotton, india-rubber, oily grains of every kind, particularly the Euphonic latkeiris, palm nuts, and sesame growing in pro- fusion. Dr. Bayol thinks that as in addition to those pro- ducts of nature, oranges, lemons, and bananas a,e found in great abundance, the swear cane might be cultivated with Metes& The country is also very rich fist minerals, there being an abundance of gold, copper, and iron. Politically, the State of Fouta Djalon is one of the most important of the Soudan with a population of 350,000, and a standing army of 25:000, all provided with firearms. The wealth of the people consists in their cattle—oxen, sheep, and goats— which propagate in an astonishing fashion. From Timbo the expedition returned down the Senegal, making treaties with the chiefs on the way, and opening up a vast expanse of new country, with literally unlimited possibilities of com- merce. The people of the Saud an appear to be generally friendly, though of course there were sometimes difficulties which needed some firmness and a Food deal of tact to over- come. Happily the party possessed a humorist as well as a geographer. M. Noirot, Dr. BAy ors ',companion, seems to have been jut the man for such an expedition—quick, sym- pathetic, and with a great sense of the droll side of life. His description of what he saw in Africa appears to have delighted the audience, and certainly affords a contrast to that of Dr. Bayol. The latter was hard, statistical, and pre- cise, confining himself chiefly to the economic aspects of the new district of Africa which French enterprise is about to . open up. M. Noirot told fanny stories, and amused his , audience with descriptions of the people which curiously re- call the tales in Mur.go Park's travels. He went, he says, expecting to find a mere race of dirty savages living in mud huts, and but little above the level of animal. Not the least important or urgent of the many phases and aspects of the Land Questien is the pre- sent and future position of the agricultural labourer, or, in other words, what is to be done for that section of the working class, who are dependent upon agri- culture for employment? Verily, it is a subject which calls aloud for an early solution. It is esti- mated that there are nearly 1,000,000 farm labourers in England, and Lord llartington tells us that under our present land system "the cultivators of the soil (the labourers) are never and can never hope to be- come its owners, and they have this one claim upon it, that in case of old age or absolute destitution they shoulel be supported without expense and almost Without labour on the land." Sir Charles Dilke has expressed the same views more concisely, as follows: —" The life of an agricultural labourer is a life of toil down hill, with the workhouse at the bottom." Were the writer to give his own views as to the social position of the agricultural labourers the result of personal observation in different parts Of the country, they might betaken to be overdrawn or too highly coloured, and he prefers, therefore, to give the evidence of witnesses who are not likely to be called in question. The Saturday Review is independent in politics, and its articles are written in a fearless and indepen- dent tone. It has stung Mr. Gladstone into a hot retort; but Lord Beaconsfield, in past years, felt the same lash, wielded in his case by the Marquis of Salisbury, who then increased by his pen the income of a younger son. Yet, an article in this paper tell us that when other subjects are quiet all sorts of odd persons and things have their share of public atten- tion, and even agricultural labourers are pitied and discussed, At other times V.lGy live on with no one much to tare for them—the firmer looking on them as his natural enemies, the parson's kindly soul get- ting weary of his long combat with their helpless, stolid ignorance, and the squire not knowing what he can do for them further than build two or three Elizabethan cottages, covered with honeysuckle, close to his gates. When foreigners come over and read of the condition of our agricultural labourers, they must be shocked, and "we are moved to a lan- guid shame and sadness by thinking how true the picture is, and what wretched, uncared for, untaught brutes the people are who raise the crops on which we live ;" and then the writer goes on to say, "The old feudalism of England—the state of things when there yet were serfs, and when the lords of the soil were almost a different order of beings—still colours the relations of the rich and the poor ;" and, further, "It is looked on as the duty and place of the poor man to stay in his native village for ever; to work hard for ten or twelve shillings a week, and bring up a large family respectably on the money; to go to church regularly, and to make out as much as he can of the service; to hate the public-house, and feel no longing for company and a bright fire or gossip, and to be guided towards heaven by the mirate and the young ladies. This is the poor man which modern feudalism actually produces, and who may be seen by any one who stands opposite the door of the village beershop on a Saturday evening." ' In the vicinity of the manufacturing districts of the North of England much of this has been modified, but it is still, unfor- tunately, accurate in many rural districts in the North of England and throughout the southern and midland counties, as was evidenced by the informa- tion contained in the report of the Royal Commission of 1809 as to the condition of women and children employed in agriculture. What are the homes of our agricultural labourers? The much respected Bishop of Manchester, who was one of the Commissioners, 'visited Norfolk, Essex, Gloucestershire, and Sussex, and described the cot- tages in one district as "miserable," in a second as "deplorable," in a third as "detestable," in a fourth. as "a disgrace to a Christian community." Ile fur- ther said that "even where adequate in quality, they are inadequate in quantity; and some rich land- owner, lord of all he surveys,' having exercised his lordship by evicting so much of his population as were an eyesore, or were likely to become a burthen to him—still employing their labour, but holding himself irresponsible for their domicile—has, by a most imperfect system of compensation, built a limited number of ornamental roomy cottages, which he fills with his own immediate dependents. Out of 300 parishes which I visited, I can only remember two where the cottage accommodation appeared to be both admirable in quality and sufficient in quan- tity. The majority of the cottages that exist in rural parishes are deficient in almost every requisite that should constitute a home for a Christian family in a civilised community. It is impossible to exaggerate the ill effects of such a state of things in every re- spect—physical, social,- economical, moral, intellec- tual. Physically, a ruinous, ill-drained cottage, cabin'd, cribbed, confined,' and overcrowded, gene rates any amount of disease—fevers of every type, catarrh, rheumatism,—as well as intensifies to the utmost that tendency to scrofula and phthisis which, from their frequent intermarriages and low diet, abounds so largely among the poor. Economically, the imperfect distribution of cottages deprives the farmer of a large proportion of his effective labour power; when he gets his mare he gets him more or less enfeebled by the distance he has to travel to his work. The moral consequences are fearful to con- template. Modesty must be an unknown virtue, decency an unimaginable thing, where in one small chamber, with the beds lying as thickly as they can be packed, father, mother, young men, lads, grown and growing-up girls, are herded promiscuously; where every operation of the toilet and of nature— dressings, nndressings, births,; deaths—is performed by each within the eight or hearing of all; where children of both sexes, to as high an age as twelve or fourteen, or more, occupy the same bed; where the whole atmosphere is sensual, and human nature is degraded into something below the level of the swine. It is a hideous picture, and the picture is drawn from the life." Such is the written opinion of the noble, outspoken Bishop of Manchester, and his fellow-commissioners in other counties report a similar ' state of things. The reason is that the labourer is not the landlord's workman, and he is not the farmer's tenant. It is no business of the farmer to look after his labourers' cottages, and the landlords are very many of them too poor to do so. As one of the Assistant-Commis- sioners asks, "What can the poor life-tenant, espe- cially if his estates he burthened, do towarN'provid- irrg good cottages for his labourers P Nine times out of ten he strives to do his duty, and suffers fully as much as the ill-housed labourers on his estates," while Mr. Portman said on the subject:—" I would venture to suggest for your consideration whether it is not expedient that legislation should take place in such a direction as to bring into the market those tracts of encumbered land, enabling those whe have capital to acquire such lands if they desire to do so, and conferring a boon on those who now possess them, by giving them money to spend on such an amount of territory as they wish to concentrate round their homes, while at the same time the curse of poverty and misery will be removed from those districts whence all the profit is drawn and to which none returns. Bad cottages would, I think, then be- come more rare; a portion at least of the profits would be spent on the spot, a more contented race of farmers and of labourers would be found, and the education of the people, now flagging for want of funds, would progress. Some may Fay that this question of the dwellings of the poor in agricultural districts is a passing question of the hour, and that it is not really so great an evil as represented. I would answer—Go into the country and see for yourself. What are the two great reasons for the sad pictures given by all the 'foregoing witnesses? Ist. The English peasantry—unlike that of any other country—is entirely divorced from the land; and 2nd. The agricultural labourers are divorced from political power. Is it any wonder that the effect of the above state ' of things operating upon generation after generation has been to render agricultural labourers thriftless, hopeless, aimless, impfovident, and immoral? What chance have they in life in those rural districts which do not adjoin great industrial centres? Even supposing a most deserving man rises to the position of foreman, and has a good cottage and garden at a moderate rent, with a number of perquisites, he must not venture to hold a contrary opinion or do a single thing distasteful to the squire or the parson. For in- stance, it is not advisable in ninny districts for such a man to have pictures of Bright or Cobden hung up in his cottage, or to take a prominent part at a Dis- senting chapel or a political meeting called for the purpose of advocating the improvement of the posi- tion of the labourers. No, such a man is always "subject to the powers that be ;" he is not an inde- pendent free agent; or, if he does think for himself, he must not let it be known. Even those -who get the best positions are not able always to provide for old age, and if they live long enough become more or less paupers, notwithstanding a life of toil and sobriety. The least worthy look forward to parish relief as a natural thing, and form no small propor- tion of the immense total for England and Wales, viz. :—for 1881, 803,120 paupers, the estimated cost of relief for the year being £7,682,009. The most enterprising labourers either migrate to the manufacturing districts or leave the country altogether. When the labourer lands in the United

But while it is a fact, and the most competent authorities, like Lord Darby and others, tell us that it is a fact, that the soil of this country might produce double the amount of food which it now does, we do not want the agricultural population either to migrate in such great numbers to large towns or to take their muscle and sinew to foreign lands to swell the tide of foreign competition. There is work for them in their own districts to increase the produce UD to Lord Derby's standard, and they must be enabled to find it their interest to stay there by being secured the fruit of their labour. How must this be done?: Ist. Give them the fran- chise, and, as they become alive and educated to their opportunities, in case their moral claim to some part or lot in the soil they cultivate is not granted, they will be in a position by means of their votes to send such men to Parliament as will pass the neces- sary legislation which shall render the honest ac- quirement of Some, Portion, however small, of the land of this country feasible to the industrious and thrifty farm labourer. The great barrier which separates the labourers from the farmers, and still further from the landlords, must be bridged. Give them some hope and some chance of acquiring land, either absolutely or for a long term' or for ever, at a fixed, moderate rent. A tenant ata quit rent is to all intents and purposes a proprietor. But, as Mr. Mechi has said, "We grasp and grudge the indus- trious labourer's patch of ground, but, inconsistently enough, pay cheerfully heavy gaol, police, and pauper rates to restrain or punish crimes consequent on his poverty and demoralisation. A man with his cow, pig, and an acre of ground has a stake in the soil," &c. _

met on Monday, and —decided to raise a fund of £50,000 to• wards the building fund and scholarships. New subscrip- tions amounting to over £3OO were stated to be promised, bringing the total amount to about £B,OOO. At the Burnley Police Court, on Saturday, two members of a working-men's club were summoned for illegally selling intoxicating drinks, and fifteen others for aiding and abet- ting. On Christmas Eve the police entered the club, and found five non-members drinking, and two men drunk, One of the defendants was fined 1:,9!", and the other cases were adjourned for a month, to allow the club to be clesed, FATAL COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN SOUTH WALES.—The Risca Colliery in South Wales has been the scene of another explosion, resulting, it is supposed, in the loss of four lives. The last disaster at the colliery, about eighteen months ago, was of a much more terrible character. Monday's accident was caused, it is said, by the firing of a shot, a pretty sure way to bring about a disaster when the pit is a dangerous one, and the coal is fiery. DEATH OF SIR R. MALINS.—Sir Richard Malins, whose life had been despaired of for several days, died at half-past ten o'clock on Sunday evening, at his residence, 57, Lowndes- square. Sir,Richard, who was 77 years of age, was educated at Caius College, Cambridge, where he was fifth junior op• time in 1827, was called to the bar at the inner temple in 1830, appointed a Queen's counsel in 1849, and a Vice- chancellor in 1866. On retiring last year he was created a Privy Councillor. From July, 1852, to July, 1865, he re- presented Wallingford in the -Conservative interest. MR. BRIGHT AND THE REPRESENTATION OF IRELAND.— Replying to a correspondent who had controverted some of _ _ _ . _

the statements in his Birmingham speech on representation, Mr. Bright says the statements in his speech were accurate. " Our representative arrangements," he says, " require re- vision and amendment, but the fact remains that the popu- lation of Ireland have as many votes in Parliament as double its number have in London, Lancashire, and Yorkshire." THE LAND QUESTION IN ENGLAND.—A conference was held at Westminster, on Monday, under the auspices of the Land Nationalisation Society. Mr. A. Russell Wallace pre- sided. The speakers were numerous, and included Miss Helen Taylor. Several resolutions were passed protesting against the monopoly of private property in land, as leading to bad cultivation, diminishing production, and checking permanent improvement; while by depriving labourers of their rights in the soil it was one of the chief causes of pauperism, demoralisation and crime. The conference was adjourned until Tuesday fortnight. THE BISHOP OT DURHAM AND THE DRINK TRAFFIC.— The Bishop of Durham, speaking at a meeting of the United Kingdom Alliance at Newcastle on Monday, said that in dealing with the drink question all should sink minor differ- ences, and do their utmost. As to local option, he should -speak cautiously until he saw the form the measure would take. He approved of the main objects and aims of the Alliance. The blame of intemperance rested as much with the consumers as the vendors. He himself had experienced much benefit from teetotalism ; and; he advised all, especi- ally young men, to give up the use of alcohol. - A warrant was on Saturday granted at the Bow-street .Police Court, London, again Hadj Ben Ig:thorned, the pro- prietor of the Beni Zoug Zoug troupe of acrobats, under the child-stealing section of the Act 24 and 25 Vic. The applica- tion for the warrant was based on the information of Mrs. Ads, who stated that in 1873 she apprenticed her son, then aged eight, to Hadj Ben Mahomed, on the distinct under- standing and agreement that the boy should not be taken out of England. In 1878 she heard that her son had. been taken to Spain and for three years she had heard nothing of him, and could not ascertain whether he was alive or dead. THE FIRST CASE UNDER THE NEW NEWSPAPER LIBEL ACT was heard at Newcastle Assizes on Monday. Two nurses at the Gateshead Workhouse sued the proprietors of the Northern Echo for damages for publishing a report of a public Meeting in that journal, in which a speaker at the meeting made an unfounded charge against the plaintiffs of drinking the liquors supplied for the paupers. The Guar- dians of the Gateshead Union vindicated their officers, and the editor of the Echo published a statement acquitting them of the charge, but observing that "it had been hawked about." Mr. Justice Matthew held that the report of the original meeting was privileged, aud that the subsequent , comment was not libellous. The jury entered a verdict for the defendants. THE REPORTED BOROUGHS.—As soon as the Government has got rid of the question of procedure, it will have to deal with the cities and boroughs in which the existence of cor- ruption was reported by the Rayal Commissions specially appointed to investigate the subject. The issue of the writs for these places was suspended by an Act passed last year until seven days after the next meeting of Parliament. .Prompt action is therefore necessary. I believe that the Government will propose by disfranchisement very materi- ally to reduce the Parliamentary power of these boroughs. Some will be disfranchised altogether, others will lose one member, and probably some seven or eight seats will thus be gained. These, in addition to the four already t obe dis- posed of by the disfranchisement of Beverley and Bridge• water, afford a very solid basis for a schema of redistribu- tion.-Lonclon Cor. Some eight and twenty years ngo, a man named Vince left his wife and three children, and went to Australia, and from that time nothing was beard of him, and his family supposed him dead.. About three years ago he returned to Yarmouth, and opened a shoe shop under the name of Barnard, and here he has been living unrecognised by his family, who are all living, until a day or two ago, Although his sons frequent- ly passed the shop, and must have often spoken to him.- The other day, however, his wife went into the shop to make a purchase, and her husband's features seeming familiar to her, on investigation was made, which resulted in the dis- covery that Mr. Barnard was her lost husband, be having assumed his Christian name. The family, however, now refuse to receive back the husband and father who has 90 lcng deserted them. SERIOUS SALVATION ARMY DISTURBANCE AT SHEFFIELD. —Serious disturbances in connection with the Salvation Army proceedings occurred at Sheffield on Monday. A coancil of war is being held, and a series of meetings and triumphal marches have taken place, attracting great crowds. On Saturday, Lieutenant Emerson Davison, better known as "The Converted Wrestler," was struck in the mouth with a stone. On Monday the crowd was again very great, and the Army, which was announced to bombard Satan's kingdom, was subjected to continuous assaults in the march from Thomas-street Barracks through the principal streets to Albert Hall. The persons walking in the procession included General Booth, Mrs. Booth, Col. Colville, and captains of divisions, with brass bands and female trumpeters, headed by "the Converted Wrestler," in scarlet uniform and brass helmet, and mounted on a white horse. There were 700 rank and file. Stones and mud were thrown, Major Cadman was hurt by a stone, and " the Converted Wrestler " sus- tained concussion of the brain. Another disturbance took place at the hall, where bricks were freely thrown. Many tradesmen hurriedly closed their places of business. SUSPENSION OF 8,000 FORESTERS.—The executive coun- cil of the Ancient Order of Foresters, acting upon the deci- sion of the Northampton high court meeting, has expelled from the order 14 districts, comprising GO courts, with 8,315 members, in consequence of their having failed to register under the Friendly Societies Act as legal branches of the order. The executive state that this was the only course open to them,as any further delay would have brought the general law, and the High Court which passed it, into contempt. They add that already courts with nearly 2,000 members have applied to know what steps they can take to become registered and then to be reinstated in the order. The districts thus suspended are Altrincham, 7 courts, and 1,628 members; Bacup, 2 courts, 102 benefit members; Bolingbroke (Lincolnshire), 9 courts, 1,263 members; Dunstable, 2 courts, 257 members; Headingley (Yorkshire), 4 courts, 365 mem- bers; Holland (Lincolnshire), 2 courts, 477 members; Knnts- ford (Cheshire), 10 courts, 2,352 members ; Newton-on-Ouse (Yorkshire), 3 courts, 298 members; Pateley Bridge (York- shire), 4 courts, 363 members; Ropsley kLincelnshire), 3 courts, 245 members; Swadlingcote (Derbyshire), 4 courts, 408 members; Swineshead (Lincolnshire), 2 courts, 204 members; and Wakefield (new district), 2 courts, and 41 members. On the other hand, during the last quarter 19 new courts have been opened, 15 in England, two in Scot- land, and one each in Wales and Tasmania.

The experiment of small cottage holdings has been tried in this country with success, as the following letter from the Bishop of Ely will show : Palace, Ely, November 10th, 1877.—My dear sir,—l beg to acknowleoge your letter relating to the letting of glebe land in allotments to cottagers. I have no hesitation in expres9ing my hearty approval of the plan. When I held a country living in Gloucestershire I was in the habit of
No. Hereditary b Who would

letting 7-2 acres-of glebe in allotments, ranging in quantity from a quarter of an acre to two acres, those who managed the small quantities well being gradually promoted to larger holdings as vacancies occurred. This scheme worked ad- mirably in every way. It greatly improved the habits as well as condition of the cottao•ersf and I believe that in the course of thirteen years I did not lose £5 from default of payment of rent.-1- remain, yours very faithfully, J. R. ELY. —John Todd, Esq. Similar evidence is given of the same system on the Duke of Rutland's estate, and there is no doubt that were the plan generally adopted of labourers holding a piece of land or small farm, either abso- lutely or in fee simple, or on a long lease, or in per- petuity at a fixed moderate rent, they would in time be noted. for self-help, thrift, energy, intelligence, and morality, instead of their present dependence, im- providence, apathy, ignorance, and immorality. It has had that effect in those countries where the Land Laws have been reformed, and some form of the system of Peasant Proprietorship on the Conti- nent, noticed in the next article, might-with great I advantage be introduced into this country.

This is the fourth occ ision on which the right hon. gentleman has treated his tenants in this liberal fashion. THE PREMIER'S RENT AUDIT.—At Mr. Gladstone's rent audit at Hawarden, Captain Vickers, the agent, announced that the right hon. gentleman had again decided to remit 10 per cent. on the rentals, and that the Rev. Stephen Glad- stone, rector of Ha warden, would alsa remit 10 per cent. on their tithes. AN EGYPTIAN GEITTLEMAN.—Egyptian men of all ranks shaved their heads and their entire faces, except sometimes a portion of their chin, from which a short square beard was allowed to depend. The barber was in attendance on the great lord every morning, to remove any hair that had grown, and trim his beard if he wore one. The lord's wig was also under his superintendence. This consisted of numerous small curls together, sometimes with lochs and plaits, fastened carefully to a reticulated groundwork, which allowed the heat of the head free escape. The dress, even of the highest class, was simple. It consisted, primarily, of the shenti or kilt, a short garment, folded or fluted, which was worn round the loins, and fastened in front with a girdle. The material might be linen or woollen, according to the state of the weather, or the wearer's inclination. Over this the great lord invariably wore an ample robe of fine linen, reaching from the shoulders to the ankles, and provided with full sleeves, which descended nearly, if not quite, to the elbows. A second girdle, which may have been of leather, confined the outer dress about the waist. Tha arms and lower parts of the legs were left bare; and in the earliest times the feet were also hare, sandals being un- known; but they came into fashion at the beginning of the filth dynasty, and thenceforward were ordinarily wore by the rich, whether men or women. -They were either of leather lined with cloth, or a sort of basketwork composed of palm leaves or the stalks of the papyrus. The shape varied at different periods. Having dressed himself with the assistance of his valet, the Egyptian lord put on his ornaments, which consisted commonly of a collar of beads or a chain of gold round the neck; armlets and brace- lets of gold, inlaid with lapis lazuli and torquoise, round the arms; anklets of the same character round the ankles; and rings upon the fingers of both hands. Thus attired, the lord took his baton or stick, and, quitting his dressing-room, made his appearance in the salon or eating department.

IRELAND. Fair and sweet as the morning air, Bath nature formed thy face ; And nouitht but trust, and praise, and prayer should intercept thy place ! With bounding hope, - A power to cope With ought in fortune's race ! Glad meadow, and gay verdant hill, Grand grove, and mighty stream; Thy locks that aye with wonder fill The mind as in fair dream, Are all thine own, Through ages gone, Are not now what they seem ! Thy children stout and stalwart born, Thy people shrewd and great ; Thy sons have from their c.,untry shorn Its beauty and its fate! Its high aspire, With calm desire, By murder rudelz torn! Once there was honour on thy nrlme, Once there was virtue thine ; Once—ere the turbulert demon came— Thine honest brow did shine With wonted pride; But now abide Thy country's vise and shame. Shake off thy trammels that now bind, The enemy's deep snare; as thou wert, so calm and kind, And mind thy work and prayer! Heed not the tongue That leads thce wrong, Be peacelul as you were! Then shall the sun of Erin rise, More glorious to behnld, To smile is cloudless, fairer s'sies, O'er industry ai-pcl gold Religion then, hai comfort men And knit them in ane fold!

"BUT THE GREATEST OF THESE IS CHARITY." Tell me will the wild rose bloom, When wintry winds are sighing? Say will echo find a voice To silence dull replying? No, ah! no. Some vvice must echo waken, The fragile rose unshaken, By cruel winds must blow. The thorns around us growing Too oft are our own sowing, 'SG bile Love's wild rose, nipped by unkind winds, dieth, And Love's sweet echo, in unbroken slumber, lieth In many a friendless heart. Play thou a nobler part, Waken Love's echo, which from kindly deeds is born, And for thy guerdon reap Love's rose without its thorn. Gledhow. MARY Avis (MADDOCK.

DOING. Oh, friend whoe'er thou art, who dost rejoice, In the sweet tones of thy melodious voice; Which to thy fancy are so rich and clear, Falling like music, on the list'ning ear, Of thee I ask, What bast thou done of that thou bast to do? Art silent? Then I say, Until thy deeds are many let thy words be few. Oh, man, whoe'er thou art, within whose breast The glowing thoughts disdain ignoble rest; Whose soul is labouring with a monstrous birth Of winged words, to scatter through the earth, Of thee I ask, What hast thou done of that thou hast to do? Art silent? Then I say, Until thy deeds are many let thy words be few. Oh, brother mine, who would'at reform mankind, Purging the dross, and leaving all refined; Preaching of sinless love, sobriety, Of goodness, endless peace, and charity, Of thee I ask, What hast thou done of that thou hast to do? Art silent? Then I say, Until thy deeds are many let thy words be few. Speech without action is a moral dearth, And to advance the world is little worth: Let us think much, say little, and much do, If to ourselyes and God we will be true; And ask within, What have I done of that I have to do? Is conscience silent—say, Oh : let my deeds be many and my words be few. J. G. L. BULLEID.

A fashionable lady, in boasting of her new "palatial re- sidence," said the windows were all of stained glass. "That's too bad !" exclaimed her old-fashioned grandmother, "bat won't soap and turpentine take the stains out ?" A fine young gent, in turning swiftly on his heel, ran his head against a young lady. He put himself in a position to apologise. "Not a word," said the quick-witted beauty; "it isn't hard enough to hurt anybody." The coxcomb frowned, and the young lady smiled and curtsied as grace- fully as an angel. Some person whom Quin had offended one day met him in the street and stopped him. "Mr. Quin," said he," l— I—I understand you have been taking away my name." "What have I said, sir ?" " You—you--yen called me a scoundrel, sir." "Oh, then keep your name, sir," replied Quin, and walked on. An Irishman, being annoyed by a howling dog in the night, jumped out of bed to dislodge the offender. It was in the month of January, when the snow was three feet dup. He not returning, his wife ran out to see what was the mat- ter. There she found her husband in his night suit, his teeth chattering, and his whole body almost paralysed with cold, holding the struggling dog by the tail. " Arrah, Pat," said she, "what seud ye be after doin'?" "Hush," said he, "Don't ye see? I'm thrying to haze the baste " ROSA BolixErrit.—Rosa Bonheur is below the average height of her sex, but she is robustly and broadly built, and she carries her head with an air of freedom, and, when a younger woman, almost of defiance. The carnation has not yet left her cheek, and her comely face speaks of health and vigour. Her hair, however, is fast turning gray, and she still wears it cat and parted like a man's. When in her studio and at home, her attire also follows that of the sterner sex; but, as a clever =temporary remarks, "her face re- stores a perfect womanliness to the whole figure—small regular features, soft hazel eyes, and a dignified benignity of expression. The manner matches the face. She has a low, pleasant voice, and a direct sincerity of speech most agreeably free from the artifices of compliment." When she goes to Paris she dresses in the uniform of her own sex; but she never assumes petticoats without deprecating the custom, and complaining of their interfering with the freedom of the limbs, and thereby impeding the power of locomotion. ITALIAN COMITSIIIP.—Coartsbip and marriage go on, of course, in remote Italian villages as elsewhere; and it has been incumbent on me to assist at many weddings, and to listen to many confidences as to how it all came about, the efforts made to get settled and the difficulties enccuotered being told on both sides with engaging candour. The pros and cons are discussed openly; friends and acquaintances are asked if they will kindly look out fora young lady with a handsome dot for Antonio, or if they will just men tion all the excellent nuelities ef Merle te the perente of le eligible young neati: on both mats haggle and bargain until each side thinks that it has "dote" the other pretty completely. When all the preliminaries are settled, but on no account before, the young couple are introduced to one another and told to fall in love. A young lady of my ac- quaintance came to me for nay congratulations on her ap- proaching marriage. I gave them heartily' as he had pre- viously confided to me that, having spared no pains with her trousseau, and having it all complete and tied up with blue ribbons, it was annoying that the sposo should alone be wanting, eseeeially as her younger sister was always having offers which she could not accept; for the father was a methodical man, and would on no account have a daughter married out of her turn. Having offered the proper felici- tations, " Well, and what is his name ?" I inquired. " Oh.! I don't know. Papa has net yet told me that," answered the bride-elect. The necessity of giving wedding presents is imposed only upon the near relations of the bride. Odes are cheaper, and many a poet unknown to fame will rhyme. industriously when any young lady of his acquaintance gets married. He will thee have his effusions printed on ornamental paper, and on the wedding day the tables are strewn with original poems, some sentimental, others facetious, and many what we English are disposed to think " sholting " (always without the c), and which are indeed calculated to startle one brought up accord- ing to our ideas of decorum. These improprieties are especially observable in the odes written by priests. It is thought correct to endow the bride in these compo- sitions with every virtue and grace, but more emphatically that particular virtue or grace in which she is moat deficient. Thus an ugly girl will be extolled for her amazing beauty a stupid one for her extraordinary taints, and an tempered one for her angelic meekness of disposition. The mother and sisters of the bridegroom do not go to the wedding—they sit at home to receive the pair, who do not immediately start on their honeymoon, but betake them- selves first to the bride's new home, where some relations of her own will perhaps accompany her and stay until the next morning. A young man is but little consulted about the choice of his partner in life, and a girl is seldom allowed any voice at all in the matter. A father who said that he would not marry his daughter without her own consent created quite a sensation by the declaratiogno.Thedaa. Per.nghter in question exclaimed, "Now, isn't that ca of p„ip haps it is because mama poveretta had never seen him till she married, and at first she didn't like him at all." The peasants have a freer choice in marriage: A pretty peasant girl will change her betrothal a good many times before she finds one to her mind. "Well, and when are you going to marry Pasquale ?" one inquires of Asstmta, who replies, "Oh ! I have got tired of Pasquale; he beat me the other day, so I have broken with him, and now I am going to see how Giacomo will suit me." By the time she does marry, neither Pasquale nor Giacomo, but Arigo, she will be very proud Of the number of pairs of earings of which she has despoiled her discarded suitors. She, too, has been working at her corredo from an early age, and will have an oaken chest full of linen for the house and for herself. She returns home after the marriage ceremony, and remains with her parents for two or three days; the bridegroom then comes . to fetch her home, and it is at his house that the fcsta takes place.—Cornhillingazine. The following statistics with regard to the leading reli- gious bodies, stated to be compiled from trustworthy sources, will be read with interest, as showing the relative postions of the denominations mentioned:- THE ESTABLISHED CHURCH OF ENGLAND.-TWO arch' bishops, 29 bishops, 3 suffragan bishops, 17 retired colonial bishops, whose services are availaele upon emergencies 30 deans, 82 archdeacons, 613 rural deans, and 23,000 clergy of all classes-probably one-fifth of these are without parochial charge, being engaged in works of education,. dm. Fixed, incomes, derived from endowed Church property, manage" by Ecclesiastical Commissioners, are paid to the prelates. The Archbishop of Canterbury receives £15,000 per annual, the Archbishop of York, £10,000; whilst the incomes of the Bishops vary from £lO,OOO to the Bishops of London to £2,400 to the Bishop of Sodor and Man. Twelve bishopS receive £5,000 and upwards. The two archbishops and all the bishops, save five, are entitled to sit as Peers ea the House of Lords. According to" Whitaker," the gross income of the Established Church, including tithe, glebe, pew reel, and moneys from other sources, is nearly £8,000,000. The church population is estimated, on trustwarthy data, at ov 13,000,000, and about 6,200,000 church sittings areer provided for their accommodation. According to a recent Parliamene tary return, 6,700 benefices have been permanently aug- mented and endowed by the Ecclesiastical CommissionerS during the past 40years, yielding an annual value of £620,000. The total number of benefices is about 13,500. In the Cite' of London there are 108 parislies and 62 churches. The diocese of Rochester contains 1,800,000 souls. In Ireland there are two archbishops, 10 bishops, 1,260 deane, arcladem cons, and incumbents, 360 curates, and 180 other oflicialSo in all 1,800. Number of benefices, 1,240. Foreign missionary income, £32,536. Total church incoeae, £383,000. Sunday school teachers 6,829, scholsro 61,e25. Foreign missionary income, £12,090; Jewish Mls' sionary income, £1,149. Total for all church purposeS, £205,630. div.p: ILLITSTRIOU IRISH I EN.

• No. lII.—II ENRY FLOC D. Hereditary bondsmen! know ye not Who would be free, themselves must strike the blow ! Byron. Before we introduce Henry Flood to our readers, there is another "Illustrious Irishman" whose name we must not fad to mention. We refer to Charles Luca.. This champion Of the rights of Ireland was originally a Dublin apothecary • little of very moderate means and position, and of very a e education, but courageous, pertinacious, industrious, nd vituperative. In 1741 he detected and exposed some serious !, encroachments that had been made in the electoral rights of ,the Dublin citizens. Rising from petty Corporation politics to the height of the great argument of national indepen- dence, he inflamed the patriotic spirit by his writings, be- evale the most popular writer in the Dublin Press, advocated • I.5Le principles of Molyneux and Swift, and urged the neces- rof shortening the duration of Parliament. The Irish . °use of Commons, however, was not yet prepared for the reception of such bold doctrines, and in 17-19, at the instiga- tion of the Government, voted him an "enemy to his country," le. ailed a proclamation for the seizure of his per. 'itOri, and thus compelled him to go for some years into exile. e ev fled to England, where he practised with some success— theactnpilonatohfyt.he Government making him a special ohict Very yf sy. "Let the man," wrote Dr. Samuel Johnson, "thus driven into exile for having been the friend of his country be re- • Feived in every other place as the confessor of liberty, and !et the tools of power be taught in time that they may rob oat cannot impoverish." When in 1760 he returned to his tca.tive land, he became for a time the most popular man in e kingdom, and though he did not achieve any great sue- , Me such as crowned the labours of Grattan or of O'Connell, Yet the original steps which led to the Octennial Bill passed ll' 1768—a bill which in its turn gradually led to Ireland's ehortlived independence—was due, in the opinion of the • celebrated Lord Chatlemont, to the influence of Lucas. As Tie Well said, "He raised his voice, when all around was • uesolation and silence—he began with a Corporation, and he Vded with a kingdom." No promises or offers could seduce m from untainiedpatr.iotism, and when he died in 1772 the , citizens of Dublin ded well to erect in their Exchange a Statue to the memory of this " Illuetrious Irishman," Dr. • Charles Lucas. Henry Flood, whose name stands at the head of this article, entered Parliament at the same time as Charles Lucas— that is in 1760, the first _pier of George 111., " England's tecond hope." Lucas sprang from the ranks of the people, at Flood was an aristocrat—a son of the Chief Justice of the King's Bench in Ireland. Both, however, had views in common on the subject of Ireland's Independence' and both pok their seats on the Oppoeition benches of the Irish Par- lament—Charles Lucas as member for Dublin, Henry Flood as member for Kilkenny. Tnere was much in the Irish Parliament at this period to 4wa'e•en indignation and shame in the breasts of all true Patriots. It was by no means a representative assembly. The Roman Catholics, who composed the vast majority of eee neople, were excluded from all representation, both Qtrect and indirect. Out of the three hundred members Who Composed the Parliament, two hundred and sixteen were returned for boroughs or manors. Of these borough members two hundred were elected by one hundred indi- vlduals, and nearly fifty by ten. Lord Shannon returned to less thaa sixteen members, the Ponsonby family tatterned fourteen, Lord Hillsborough nine, and the Doke , Leinster seven. Besides forty-four Placemen, the °use of Commons in 1784 contained eighty-six mem- bers who represented constituencies which were let out to the Government in consideration of titles, offices, or pen- Lclifs• Fit ty-three Peers are said to hwe nominated one tundred and twenty-three members of the Lower House. alPng the Irish nobility absenteeism was so common that • ft assures us that in his time the Bishops usually consti- luted half of the working members of the House of Com- trioe ' 8. At the same time the House of Commons was ' entirely free from popular controlefor unless dissolved by th • a Will of the Government, it lasted for the whole reign. e'eue the Podia 'cent of George 11. in this manner continued Years. It was this Parliament that Swift satirised as the "Legion Club." Not a bowshot from the College, Half the world from sense and knowledge; Always firm in its vocation To the Court against the nation. • 411 ce Was the condition of things when Henry Flood, in co .lempany with Dr. Lucas and other patriots, took his Beet the Irish Parliament. This small band, with Flood as _Reit leader, carried on a desultory w-rfare for several years, ctir though they often embarrassed the Minister and some- . males carried a -division, yet their measures were always ul- comately rejected, either by the Parliament or by the Privy tO,ncil. When, however, Lord Townsend became Viceroy, ° ratriots began to think that they had not laboured in •he'll or spent their strength for nought. His Lordship had e'en sent over by the English Government for the express rhurPose of effecting great changes in the system of govern- •bl Ireland, and the better to accomplish these he made a for the sympathy and support of Mood and his fol- a;Wers• One of the objects which the Patriots sought to e • he-mnaplish was the shortening of the duration of Parlia- ' :eat. Dr. Lucas had made several ineffectual attempts to Zocure a Bill for limiting the duration of Parliament. But le' the Viceroy actually sanctioned with his countenance oTsupport this favourite object of the wishes and attempts , p Patriots. A Septennial Bill was transmitted to the glaii.sh Parliament, and was retureed with an alteration in e„lnt of time, having been changed into an Octennial one. :lila Irish Commons accepted the Bill in its altered form, reedeevot!d a respectful and grateful address to the throne. tching his Majesty "to accept their unfeigned and ratef •na n 1 acknowledgment for the condeecension so signally , rilphifested to his subjects of that kingdom in returning the •„nu. !or limiting the duration of Parliament, which they •17.nsidered not only as a gracious mark of paternal benevo- . th're, but as a wise result of royal deliberation." Flood w' as offered by the Viceroy the office of the'reacsuree, which office though characterised by him as oPpoeluge for tried incapacity," he accepted. At once his teon to the Government ceased. e teeny ,`"oneeit„... seven years he remained silent on those great 'el y '"donal questions which in former years he had cease- :and eloquently expounded. He defended the Govern- teubitlgnatliotsn conduct of the American War, regarding the VuDire, the Colonists as of vital importance to the r qua}, "of Destruction," he said, "will come upon the 't ere,e'mOire like the coldness of death. It will creep upon thott.2._ the extreme parts." He designated the four cae4: Irish troops which were sent to fight the Ameri- L'Y th rnaed Negotiators"—an unfortunate exprdsion, to least of it, and one to which Henry Grattan alluded kribbdTking of Flood in his famous invective ; he de- ll" a brihini as standing "with a metaphor in his mouth, _e in his pocket, a champion against the rights of

America, the only hope of Ireland, and the only refuge of the liberties of mankind." But in accepting office under Government Henry Flood might not have been influenced by selfish motives. His temptition was not strong in the direction of money. He had an ample fortune with his wife, and no children. It is quite certain that the times were not 'very favourable to aggressive action, and it is possible that Flood accepted office under the impression that in this way he could best serve his country. Anyhow it was a great blunder. After this his character was not, like Caesar's wife, above suspic on, and he lost that which was his chief element of power, the conficlence of the people. In the days of 'B2 we again find him in the Patriot ranks. He had thrown up his office and rejoined his old friends. But in vain did he seek to regain hie forfeited position. A more brilliant genius had appeared upon the scene, and his seven years' silence had alienated his friends. When in 17W Yelverton brought forward a Bill for the Repeal of Povning's Law, Flood, while supporting the measure, com- plained bitterly that after a service of twenty years in the study of this question he had been superseded. " The honourable gentleman," said he, "is erecting a Temple of Liberty. I hope that at least I shall be allowed a niche in the fane." Yelvertan retorted by reminding him that by the civil law if a man should separate from his wife desert and abandon her for seven years, another might then take her and give her his protection. We shall for the present pass over the events that imme- diately followed the triumph of Irish Independence, and the unfortunate quarrel between himself and the illustrious Henry Grattan, as they belong more especially to the life of Grattan, and will come before us again. Much of Flood's conduct during the exciting scenes of that glorious time de- serves the highest praise, but much, too, is at least qu,estion- able, and certainly his narrowness, not to say downright intolerance, with regard to the claims of the Catholic portion of his countrymen deserves the severest condemnation. No Parliamentary Reform that did not establish the newly-won irdependence of the country on the broad basis of the uni- versal Irish nation could be, from the nature of things, per- manent or beneficial in its character and issues. That pitriotism was certainly defective in its aims which sought to make half a million people hold down and coerce over two millions of disarmed and disfranchised people. Nation- ality, in Ireland could not be other than delusive and evan- escent

So long as Ireland did pretend, Like sugar loaf turned upside down, To stand upon its smaller end. After several abortive attempts to obtain a .reform of the Irish Parliament, Henry Flood sought and obtained a seat in the British House of Commons. Strange to say, the maiden speech of this celebrated orator proved a failure. "He was," said Grattan, "an oak of the forest too great and too old to be transplanted at fifty." Mortified at this failure, he scarcely spoke again in the House. But in 1790 he broke the silence which is said to be golden, and accord- ing to Berke, no mean judge, "retrieved his reputation." In bringing forward a Reform Bill his genius shone forth with something of its old brilliancy, as the san occasionally bursts forth in all its glory at the close of a cloudy and stormy day. He died the year following. Conscious of the approach of death, he requested his attendant to retire, and thus atone this "Illustrious Irishman" passed over to the "great majority." In taking leave of Henry Flood we shall do wisely in re- membering "the greatest of these three," and to "put on charity." With all the drawbacks we have mentioned he was one of Ireland's greatest patriots. It was his lot to sow seed, the fruit of which others have reaped. According to his lights he worked nobly for Ireland, and if he sinks lower than Grattan on the roll of the Patriot party of that period it is because he remained to the last an enemy of Catholic Emancipation, and persisted in favouring that vicious and petty policy for confining the nation with all its powers and rights to one-fifth of the inhabitants. According to one of the most faithful of Irish historians, we may say of Henry Flood as Grattan said of Kirwan :—" The curse of Swift was upon him to have been born an Irishman and a man of genius, and to have used his talents for his country's good."
