div.p: FOREIGN INT ELLIGENCE.

- - EGYPT. Intelligence received at Alexandria reports the assassina- tion of the Greek Consul at INlantalout, in Upper Egypt. A Times Alexandria telegram of Wednesday says :—The President of the Egyptian Parliament yesterday presented to the Ministers an elaborate project of Parliamentary organi- sathan, claiming Ministerial responsibility for the Chamber, the right to discuss and vote the Budget, and that the initia- tive of all laws should emanate from the Parliament. Cherif Pasha has determined to refuse these demands. The Con- trollers are equally decided not to admit the right to vote the Budget.

div.head: HOLLAND.
div.p: HOLLAND.
An official journal at the Hague contradicts the assertion of the Berlin Taybiatt that the relations between Germany and Holland had become gradually less cordial.
FRANCE.

M. Gambetta, in the Chamber of Deputies on Saturday, read the Bill for the Revision of the Constitution. It deals with the election of senators, the principle of scrutin de liste, and the powers of the Senate with reference to financial matters. It also provides that the system of offering public prayers at the opening of the sessions of the Legisla- ture is to be abolished. There is a Ministerial crisis in France. The bureaux of the Chamber of Deputies have elected a committee to examine the Government bill for the revision of the Con- stitution. It appears that a large majority of those chosen as members of the committee spoke in the bureaux in op- position to the Ministerial measure, the voting against which was, it is said, in the proportion of ten to one against the Government. M. Garnbetta having made the adoption of the bill a Cabinet question, a serious crisis is expected, and the Prime Minister's resignation is already spoken of as probable. This totally unexpected Ministerial reverse created a great panic on the Paris Bourse on Thursday, and the news spread through the provinces like wildfire, creating everywhere intensa excitement. TURKEY. According to a despatch from Constantinople, the Sultan considers that the Collective Note ie intended to pave the way for the introduction of a Protectorate of the Western Powers over Egypt, which would entirely paralyse the Sul- tan's power in that country. Owing to the displeasure thus created Lord Dufferin, it is said, has again had great diffi- culty in obtaining an audience of the Sultan. It is stated to be not improbable that Germany, Austria, Russia, and Italy will address a Note to the French and English Cabinets formally expressing their regret at their having interfered in the internal affairs of Turkey without first consulting the Government of that country. PRUSSIA. The Prussian Diet was opened on Saturday. the Speech from the Throne being read by the Vice-President of the Ministry. It was pointed out that the state of the finances continued to show a progressive improvement. In addition to the Budget, bills would be submitted for improving the position of the deceased functionaries having held direct appointments from the State, and for effecting more favour- able arrangements for the benefit of officials retiring after having been employed many years in the public service. A measure would be. submitted with the object of furthering the peaceful arrangements of politico-enclesiastical affairs, the way for which had already been paved in the interest of the Catholic population. CHILI AND PERU. Despatches from Buenos Ayres and Lima announce the conclusion of a treaty of peace between Chili and Bolivia, and the "permanent occupation" of the Peruvian capital by the Chilians. It is asserted not only has Senor Cal- deron's Government been broken up and Calderon taken prisoner to Chili, but Pierola, the former president, has fled the country, and the Chilians have assumed even the muni- cipal government in Lima and elsewhere, deposing the Peruvian officials. They have also taken possession of the Post-office, and supervise correspondence and telegrams. Montero has assumed by nrochtmation the presidency of Peru, but it is nominal and unsupported, and he is a refugee in the mountains. THE UNITED STATES.

A destructive fire has occurred at Galveston, in Texas. A private telegram from New York states that the ship- ments of wheat and flour from Atlantic ports during the season of 1881 show a decrease of 28,653,000 bushels over the previous year, but the shipments from the Pacific ports show an increase of 10,516,000 bushels. The exports of corn are about half what they were in 1880. The total falling off in wheat and corn is 33,497,000 bushels. New York telegrams report that a terrible accident has happened on the Hudson River Railway. The train con- veying the members of the State Legislature from Albany to New York was run into by a train at Spuyen Byvii Creek. The engine of the local train crashed into two Wagner palace cars, which were completely telescoped and instantly caught fire. Nine persons lost their lives, and twelve were injured.

TUNIS. It is reported that the cold is so intense on the Sahara frontier that in one day the Louis column lost 400 camels. Many soldiers are dead, and more are ill. The Delabecque column has nearly succumbed to famine. Many men are said to have perished in the snow. Considerable excitement has been caused in Tunis by the arrest of Taib Bey, second brother of the reigning Bey. At a late hour on Monday the Minister of War, with a number of native cavalry, surrounded his palace, and he was in- formed that he was a prisoner, and was required to proceed to the Bardo. He protested that he had done nothing to warrant his arrest, but the Minister of War said that this was M. Roustan's doing, and that if Taib Bey did not submit French soldiers would be immediately despatched to seize him. He submitted, and was conveyed to the Bardo on Tuesday. It is said that his ethissaries had been traversing the country promising persons good posts on his accession to power.

There is nothing more nourishing and warming in cold weather than a cup of really good Cocoa, but the difficulty has been to obtain it pure. This may be secured at a cost of one halfpenny for a large breakfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocoa Essence, which goes three times as far as the adulterated and starchy compounds ordinarily sold, the smallest packet making folrteen breakfast cups of strong Cocos.—. Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 21,1;1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 21,1;1882.

( PUBLIC MEN ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS. • Mr. Bradlauzh addressed a meeting at Exeter on Monday, held under the 'auspices of the Working Men's Radical Association, on the subject of perpetual pensions. He was very favourably received. The meeting approved a motion for appointing a commission of inquiry. Dr. Lyon 'Playfair,- speaking at a Liberal meeting in Edinburgh, on Wednesday, expressed his belief that the Conservatives in the House of Commons would not inter- pose any serious obstacle to the carrying out of needful alterations in the rules of parliamentary procedure. Mr. Childers, the Secretary of State for War, delivered an address to his constituents at Pontefract, on Thursday, on army reform. He gave some highly interesting information with regard to the working of the short-service system, the increase of the reserve, the assimilation of the militia with the line, and the " localisation" of regiments. Mr. Illineworth, M.P., speaking at the annual meeting of the Bradford Chamber of Commerce on Monday, expressed the opinion that the depression of trade in the district was attributable to the changes of fashion. Alluding to the French treaty negotiations, he felt confident that the Govern- ment would enter into no treaty of a retrogressive character. Mr. F. S. Powell also spoke. The Right Hon. W. E. Forster, M.P., has written to the Bradford Liberal Electoral Association, thanking them for a resolution of confidence passed on the 12th instant, and stating that there are very few members of Parliament who have had such generous support from their constituents as be has had from Bradford in the fulfilment of a difficult duty. He also expressed a hope that be and his colleague might have the opportunity of meeting their constituents early in the session. Speaking at Oldham on Monday, Mr. Stanley, M.P., said it was with a spirit of hearty congratulation that those living in that part of I.ancashire congratulated Liverpool on the educational effort it was now making, and on the very liberal sums subscribed. They all hoped the new University of Liverpool would go band in hand with Owens College, Manchester, and do much for education in this county. It was stated that the Royal Commission on Technical Instruc- tion would shortly visit Oldham. Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P. states, in a letter which was read on Wednesday at a meeting in Leicester, that the mode of the administration of coercion by the Irish Excutive loudly calls for protest. Mr. Forster seems to him to be " delivered into the hands of 'Dublin Castle,' an institution which is a survival of the time of the penal laws," and the policy adopted is in Mr. Calling's opinion, calculi ed to destroy the grace, and prevent the working, of the Land Act. He has such faith in the Land Act that he believes, even now, "if the prison doors were thrown open, and the sus- pects either tried or released ; if the shameful police circu- lars were cancelled ; if words of conciliation and trust were addressed to the Irish people ; and, further, just reforms indicated, order would be speedily restored in Ireland, and much done towards the conciliation of the Irish people." Sir R. A. Cross, M.P. opened a new Conservative Club at Tyldesley, on Wednesday. Speaking at a dinner which followed the opening ceremony, he referred to various matters which are likely to engage the attention of Parlia- ment during the next session. He expressed his intention of again opposing the admission of Mr. Bradlaugh to the House. On the subject of Parliamentary procedure, he acknowledged the evil of obstruction, and gave the assurance that if the Government sought only to prevent wanton abuse of the forms of the House of Commons, or to place a check on an unintentional abuse, they would be supported by the Conservative party generally. As for the cloture, be was of opinion that its introduction would absolutely destroy the independence of Parliament, and anything that tended to do that was greatly to be deprecated.

f INAUGURATION OF LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY COLLEGE. On Saturday afternoon a public meeting to inaugurate the college was held in St George's Hall, Liverpool, which was crowded. Lord Derby took the chair; and amongst those present were Lady Derby, the Bishop of Liverpool, Mr. Wm. Rathbone, M.P., Col. A. H. Brown, M.P., Sir James Picton, Mr. Chris. Bushell, Mr. Robt. Gladstone, and Professor Roscoe. Lord Derby, who was received with applause, said: Ladies and gentlemen,—lt is perhaps unnecessary to say that I am not here for the purpose of delivering an inaugural address at the opening of our new college. That duty, happily, is in more appropriate and more capable bands. I rise only for the purpose of asking you to listen to what I know will be the wise and well-considered utterances of onr principle, Professor Rendall. (Applause.) He has under- taken a grave responsibility. He has accepted an honour- able but an arduous offiO, and I am sure that he will be supported, as he ought t 5 be, not oely by his assistants in the teaching work, but by the parents of those who will frequent this college, and by the whole educated class of Liverpool. (Applause.) I need not remind you that this college is established on an absolutely neutral and unsec- tarian ',principle. (Applause.) That is now so much accepted as a matter of course in regard to an institution of this kind, that I should have probably passed it over without notice only that it is curious to look back and to observe the change that has taken place in our habits of thought even within the last 40 or 50 years. Forty or 50 years ago it would probably have been impossible to establish a college npon such a basis, without giving rise to eager and possibly to emuittered controversy; and it is equally superfluous to tell you, or the majority of you, that from the first inception of the design, the college has enjoyed the equal and the cordial support of both, or perhaps I should say all, political parties. (Applause.) It is intended for the community as a whole, and not for any section of the community. (Hear, hear.) We have never been indifferent in Liverpool to the claims of higher estucation. Not to go back to distant dates, we have had in existence during the last 40 years two ex- cellent institutions in friendly rivalry with one another— one, which, te avoid confusion,l may call by its old name, the Collegiate Institution, in Shaw-street; the other, the Liver- pool Institute, which I believe preceded it in point of time. Twenty years ago Sir Wm. Brown, whose name will always be honoured, as it should be, in Liverpool, gave us that Free Library which has perpetuated his name. (Applause.) It was the first gift of the kind upon so large a scale; and be- sides the actual good done it has set an example which has been and which will be largely followed in other places. Sir Andrew Walker followed suit with the Art Gallery— (applause)—and I may claim for a predecessor of mine— (applause)—some share in the creation of that museum which is the accompaniment and the supplement of thus, two kindred institutions. We have, in addition, the School of Science, which is doing useful work in an unostentatious way; and I don't know that if we had left matters these we should have been much behind our rivals in other towns. But we wished for something. more. We thought that if Manchester had Owens College we ought not to do less on our side of the county; and accordingly three years ago the movement was started of which you now see the earliest results. I may remind you in half a dozen words of what has been done so far. Including trust funds a sum of £lOO,OOO has been raised. I believe by the latest reports a little more, but I speak of the figures as they stood a week or two ago. Six chairs or professorships hese been founded with an endowment of £lO,OOO each, and within the last few hours I have heard that the endowment fund is. completed for a seventh chair—the Roscoe Professorship of Art. A building has been obtained, temporarily indeed, and which probably we shall not be satisfied always to go on with, but quite enough to meet our present requirements. We are, as you know, in connection with the new Univer- sity of the North which has its centre at Manchester, and we begin our work to-day, not indeed wholly equipped, not indeed supplied with all the funds which we shall require, but having done well so far, being clear of debt and confi- dent from our experience of the past that we shall find help and support in the future. (Applause.) Perhaps I may mention as`a proof that we have not yet come to the end of 'our resources, or rather the resources of our friends, that since I took my seat at this table I have had a list handed to me. Mr. Muspratt gives £l,ooo,—(applause)—Mesers. Gamble and Co. £l,ooo—(applause)—Messrs. Gaskill £l,OOO —(applause)—Mr. Clifton Brown £l,ooo—(applause)—Mr. Sandbach £l,OO0—(applause)—and, as I mentioned just now in more general terms, a lady has agreed to complete the endowment fund for the Roscoe chair. (Applause.) Now, I don't want to utilise this occasion for begging purposes, but I will just remind you that if any man or if any woman wishes to do good service to this town without distinction of party or sect—(hear, hear)—and if at the same time they wish, which to my mind is a very honourable and reasonable object of ambition, to keep their names in remembrance in the place in which they have lived and worked, an endowment there of a Professorship or of an exhibition, or even, if no more could be done, of a simple prize, is about the easiest and the surest way of accomplishing both those results. (Hear, hear.) We live in changing times, but Democracy appreciates education— (cheers)—and especially appreciates science—(hear, bear)— and I think a scientific foundation is pretty sure not to be diseedowed, whatever happens. (Laughter, and bear, hear.) Let me add only this: Over and above its special educational work, our college, we hope, will do two things. It will be a centre of local patriotism, a means by which local public spirit may well display itself; and it will give fresh evidence, if evidence is needed, that commerce and culture, so far from being antagonistic, are natural allies (Applause.) They were so in Athens; they were so in Alexandria; they were so in the Italian republics of the middle ages; and I don't think that a probably busier existence and a certainly smokier atmos- phere—(laughter)—constitute acy reason why they should not be so here likewise. (Hear, hear.) It is some- times contended that the cheapening of Oxford and Cam- bridge, the increased facilities which are given now for the sons of comparatively poor persons to be edueated at the older universities, render local colleges of this kind super- fluous. I think that is a mistake, (Hear, hear,). In the first place, the number capable of being admitted at Oxford or Cambridge is limited by the necessities of the case. In the next place, it must always be more costly to send a youth, under however careful arrangements, to live at a dis- tance from home rather than to keep him in his own family, (Hear, hear.) And, apart from the question of expense, there are many persons who doubt whether entire separation from domestic influences, and whether the comparative absence of personal supervision which exists, and must exist, at the older universities, is always the safest and wisest course in dealing with a young man at the most critical period of his life. (Applause.) But that is a wide question, and Ido not propose to enter upon it. Fer our purpose it is enough that the experience of other towns and the observation of popular feeling show us that there is a large and certain demand for the kind of education which this college will supply—(applause) ;—and it is our duty, and it will be our aim, to see that that demand is very fairly met. Professor RENDALL, afterwards delivered the inaugural address, in the course of which be said :—lt was time that English artisans became less mechanical than the machines which, by rule of thumb, they manage; time that they made their own the funda- mental conceptions of work and energy. It was time that simpler thermo-dynamics or the theory of indicator diagrams were not untraversed mysteries to skilled mechinists ; time, too, that our mechanical engineers should have readier op- portunity of mastering the laws of electricity, which seemed likely so soon to divert into new channels the direction of so much labour. These things were taught in German Poly- technica and Real schools- but where is the School of Chemistry that Widnes and Runcorn had a right to look for in the second city of the kingdom ? Or where the School of Navigation, at which future mates and captains from the largest merchant shipping port in the world could learn enough of nautical astronom-v and spherical trigonometry to understand the processes which underlie their daily observa- tions, or obtain at least some general acquaintance with that subtle force which ruled the compass and determined its correction? (Applause.) So far they had viewed science from the utilitarian side alone. But there remained the vaster and more honoured field of science pure and abstract; science that sought no better reward than attainment and advance of truth. Indeed, one service that these multiply- ing colleges would render was to make knowledge held more dear, and examination tests more cheap, and to revive in an age of 'competition a keener relish for the thing and not the ELOPEMENT OF A CLERGYMAN WITH A FARMER'S name. ST. ELPHIN'S JUNIORS V. WIDNES RECHEA.TION.—A m itCh between the above clubs was played on Saturday last, on the ground of the former, with the following result :—St. Elphin's Juniors: Oue try and nine touchdowns. Widnes Recreation, one touchdown. ,

WARRINGTON FREE WANDERERS V. WIDNES TRUE BLUES. —This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday last and resulted in a victory for the home team. The score was as follows: Free Wanderers, one goal, one touchdown and a touch in goal to True Blues, six minor points. The teams were as follow :—Free Wanderers: Full back, Crank; three-quarter backs, Boardman, Waywell ; half backs, Matthews, Helsby ; forwards, Proctor, Potts, Speak- man, Foster, Fogg, Hill, Whit&ld, Wilcock and Wright. True Blues: Full back, Prot three-quarter backs, Wilkin- son (captain), Bingham, and Jackson; half-backs, Stirrup and Whittle; forwards, Jackson, Hague, Laws, Riddle, Pountain, Upward, Barton, Robinson, and Spencer. NEvrroN (THIRTEEN) V. LATCHFORD (SIXTEEN).—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and after an hour's play ended in a victory for the visitors by one try (disputed) four touchdowns to one touchdown. The first half of the game was very well contested, each side scoring a touchdown. After changing ends it was thought the home team would show to advantage, but such was not the case, for the Newton team playing up with great vigour the ball was scarcely ever out of the Latchford quarters. Hobson. Liptrott, Boardman, Hewitt, and Massey played very well for the visitors, the latter's splendid screw kicking being greatly admired by the spectators; while Burgess, Leigh, and Slater were most conspicuous for the home team. Newton team :—A. G. Hobson, back; T. Massey, S. Hewitt, G. McCormick, three-quarter backs; G. Wood and T. T. HELENS RECREATION V. RIINCORN.—PIayed On the St. Helens ground on Saturday. Runcorn elected to play with the wind, which was blowing hard, but they were unable to get near their opponents' goal, which was held safely by the excellent back play of Pennington and J. Taylor. Green made a good run in for St. Helens (dis- puted), but the place kick Nvs a failure owing to the wind. On the change of ends the Recreation made it hot during the remainder of the game, Green securing another try, but the kick just missed. Cunliffe had also been playing with great dash throughout, and was at last rewarded with 'a try, neatly kicked over by Foster. Atkinson gained a try from a maul (disputed), and at the call of no side Runcorn were nilled, the score being a goal, three tries •(two disputed), and a dead ball for St. Helens. H. Hughes and Larkin played in excellent style for Runcorn, and Roberts was lively in addition to those named. The game was pleasantly conducted. Players :—Recreation: T. Pennington and A. Tickle, backs; J. Taylor (captain) and R. Valentine, three- quarter hacks; C. Cunliffe and A. Atkinson, half-backs; T. Green, P. Roberts, W. Cook, S. Forster, J. Petty, H. Adam- son, J. Harkinson, F. div.head: STATE oF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE oF IRELAND.

Several arrests were made under the Coercion Act on Tuesday, the apprehensions including two brothers named Clune, who were taken into custody at Clare, and conveyed to Naas Gaol. A Boyle telegram announces the arrest of Mrs. Highland, at Ballantore, county Leitrim, for participating in Ladies' Land League meetings. She was brought before the resident magistrate and remanded. On Tuesday, the depositions were taken of Walter Smyth, of Caherfiinsker, who was fired at on the 12th inst. Smith stated that a man fired two shots, and be believed this man to be John Kennedy, of Cahererin, who is now in custody. While a party of people were having a wake in a Dublin tenement room on Monday night, some young men entered, and, being unwelcome visitors, were attacked. A terrible fight then took place where the dead body lay, oaths, screams, and curses making the scene a shocking one. The young men, ' who were arrested, were badly injured. The Dublin Freeman of Tuesday states. that a circular ' has been issued inviting loyal people to form a rifle club in Dublin, to become proficient in the use and practice of fire- arms, in order that, should occasion arise, they would be able to render effective aid to the authorities in the execution of their duties. The services of the club would be placed at the Government's disposal. A Land League hunt was held near Woodford, Roughles, on Tuesday. Several thousand persons assembled, and two hundred police, under the command Captain Mansfield, were present. Seventeen persons were arrested, and as they were being taken into Woodford by the police, the latter were pelted with stones by the mob which followed. The prisoners were taken before the magistrates and remanded for eight days. Refusing to give bail, they were taken to prison. It is said to be the intention of the followers of Mr. Par- nell in the House of Commons to move separate motions relating to the suspects immediately Parliament re-assem- bles. The first motion will be as follows: "That this House disapproves the arrest and imprisonment of Charles S. Par- nell, and censures t!se Government for the policy of the Irish Executive." As there are between 400 and 500 suspects, the Irish members will, if they carry out their present in- tention, occupy a considerable portion of the time of the session. The Commissioners under the Land Act, sitting in Belfast, on Monday, gave their first judgment as a Court of Appeal. The case was one in which the sub-commissioners had made a reduction of rent from £36 7s. 6d. and £3O 15s. with costs against the landlord. Mr. Justice O'Hagan and Mr. Litton upheld the reduction of rent appealed against, but on the qeestion of costs decided in the landlord's favour. Mr. Vernon the third commissioner, dissented from the judgment, which, he said, laid down principles never con- templated by the Legislature. The result of the appeal case has been awaited with great interest throughout the country. The judgment clearly shows that the much- abused sub-commissioners have been acting quite in accor- dance with the principles of law and justice in their reduc- tions of rent, while, on the other hand, the tenants are likely to feel it a great hardship if they are to be saddled with costs where they come into court for the purpose of showing that their landlords are forcing from them—and may have been doing so for years—an unjust and extor- tionate rent. In other respects the judgment is satisfactory from the tenants' point of view, and shows that the too obvious efforts of the landed interest to averawe and intimi- date the Land Court have happily failed.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

BARROW-IN-FITANESS, MONDAY.—The demand for Besse- mer pig iron is very strong, although the business done is still quiet, owing to the large tonnage of sales which have taken place for forward delivery. The aspect of the iron market is, however, more cheerful and it seems likely that a good business will be done at better prices. Stocks of iron are small when the stocks accumulated for shipment are taken into consideration. Prices are firm at the rates quoted last week, 635. being an average quotation for marked parcels of Bessemer iron at market. The steel trade is steadily em- ployed, and there is a full demand for all the classes of metal produced here. Iron ore is in brisk demand at from 16s. to 18s. 6d. per ton. Shipbuilders are especially well off for , orders.

LANCASHIRE, WEDNESDAY.—The coal trad eof this district continues extremely dull so far as the demand for all classes of fuel for house-fire consumption is concerned. The bulk of the Lancashire collieries are not being kept going more than four or five days a week, and in the neighbourhood of Manchester, where the pits are running full time, heavy stocks are accumulating rapidly. Apart from the house-fire coal trade, which has naturally been depressed by the ex- ceptionally mild weather, there is generally a good demand for iron making and other trade purposes, but this is not sufficient to take off the surplus supplies of coal thrown upon the market by the very limited requirements for house.- fire consumption, and common round coals for steam and forge purposes are consequently also plentiful in the market. The advance on wages conceded to the men at the close of last year has naturally necessitated a strong effort on the part of colliery proprietors to maintain their prices awl so far as list rates are concerned there has been no very material change as yet, but where orders have been competed for in the open market ceiling prices are easier. The better sorts of engine fuel move off without difficulty at late rates, and good qualities of slack are scarce, but of inferior descriptions supplies are plentiful. The average prices at the pit mouth are about as under: Best coal, Os. Gd.; seconds, 7s. to 7s, Gd; common house coals, ss. 9d. to 6s. 3d.; steam and forge coals, ss. to ss. Gd.; good burgy, 55.; good slack, 4a.; with . inferior descriptions offered at 63. to is. per ton less. The continuance of stormy weather is still effecting the shipping trade, and there are large quantities of coal lying at Liver- pool which sellers have been unable to move in consequence. Prices have shown a downward tendency to the extent of Gd. per ton in some cases. In the iron trade business has been quiet during the week. There is, in fact, very little iron actually wanted for present requirements, owing to con- sumers being mostly so well bought, and the inquiries com- ing into the market are chiefly for deferred deliveries, which makers show very little disposition to entertain. Notwith- standing the downward tendency reported in Scotch and north-county iron, makers here are exceedingly firm, and are not influenced by the fluctuations of outside speculative markets. Local brands of pig iron have even shown an up- ward tendency, Lancashire makers during the week having advanced their list rates is. 6d. per ton, and for delivery equal to Manchester their quotations are now 225. Gd., less 21-, for both forge and foundry qualities. District brands, such as Derbyshire and Lincolnshire, are without material change. In the finished-iron trade although the same pressure of orders as a short time back, there is a good, steady demand for home requirements with considerable in- quiries for the ensuing spring shipments. Lancashire bars are very firm, at £7 to £7 2s. 6d., with some makers quoting £7 ss. per ton for delivery into the Manchester district.

div.head: LYNN,
div.p: LYNN,

BEGGING AT LYADL—At the Lymm Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. Dewhurst, two men, named John and Edward Ellis, were brought up on a charge of begging at Lymm.—Sergeant Foden said that he found the prisoners begging in Higher-lane, and Sergeant Harrington stated that numerous complaints had been made to the effect that such cases were becoming a source of great annoyance to people. —The prisoners were each sentenced to seven days' im- prisonment with hard labour. LYINIM CONGREGATIONAL CHURCFL—The annual tea meet- ing in connection with this church was held in the school- room, on Tuesday evening. About 180 persons sat down to tea, the tables being presided over by the following ladies: —Mesdames Bedell, Rowson, Dyson, Bowen, Merchant, Nightingale, and Poole; Misses Forrest, Bedell, and Vicker-• man. 'The pastor of the church, the Rev. J. Bedell, pre- sided at the meeting held afterwards, and was supported by the Rev. W. T. Pinn, M.A. (Stockport). Rev. S. Stafford (Primitive Methodist), Messrs. S. Jackson, %V. Milne, Wood- ward, &c.—The Chairman, after wishing those present a happy new year, expressed his sympathy with those who were in bereavement, and went on to say they were met together, he supposed, in part to review the year that had gene, and in part to take a forecast of and look forward to the work that they might and ought to do during the year upon which they had now entered. If they asked him what they had been doing during the past year, lie thought it might be said they had not been doing as much as they ought to have done, and that they had very much to look back upon with regret, and wish it had been better. Still, they had cause to thank God and to take courage. For nine months they had been trying the weekly offering system instead of letting the pews, and the result had been very satisfactory. The finan- cial committee, in presenting their first quarterly report, stated that they " had :nuch pleasure to state the income derived from the new system amounted to £lB 83. 2d. more than by the old method in the corresponding quarter of last year." In the next quarter the committee reported that the income amounted to £52 17s. Id , which, although not so good as in the previous quarter, in comparison with the cor- responding quarter of last year showed an increase of £l2 3s. Td. in favour of the new system. In the last quarter the committee reported the amount of offerings received was £5B is. Id., which was £l3 15s. 3d. better than the corres- ponding quarter of last year under the old system. During the three quarters of the year that the new system had been in operation, the increase had been £44 7s. (Ap- plause.) The report of the Sunday school secretary showed that the number of scholars on the books was—boys 100, girls 93, infants 56, total 249. The average attendance in the morning was 45, and in the afternoon 160, the largest attendance being 205. The clothing club numbered 71 members; the amount paid in 1881 was £l9 6s. 3d., an in- crease on the preceding year of £l3 123. Bd. The amount collected by the scholars by missionary cards was XI 14s. 44. In the library they had some 400 volumes. Respecting the coming year, they must go forward, and try to do better than they had done with the single desire to glorify God. —The Rev. WT. Pinn expressed the pleasure he had in meeting them that night, and said he was very glad to see that they were making progress. He congratulated them upon the very pleasing report that had been read, and , remarked that in regard to finances they had everything to encourage them. He was very glad to find they had such a , large number of scholars in the Sunday school, and hoped next year the morning attendance would be larger than it was. There was one subject which he thought ought to be brought before the churches this year. In 1881 they had had censuses taken. They had had a census of the population, and since that they had had a census of the numbers attending the places , of worship. The result of the latter census had been such as to make the Christian churches consider whether they were doing their duty. There was a great number outside the places of worsh:p who wanted bringing in, and he thought that was what the Christian churches ought to lay. at heart. He did not think it was a matter for the deacons and ministers only. It was a matter for the Christian churches, for every member of the Christian churches. What the ministers had to do was to stir up the people so that they might feel the necessity was laid upon them to take some steps towards bringing within the sound of the Gospel those who did not attend any place of worship. It seemed to him one duty of the members of the churches was to shine, and to hold out a light to their fellowmen, and so draw them to the Gospel and to Christ.—Addresses were also delivered by Mr. S. Jackson, Rev. S. Stafford, Mr. W. Milne, and Mr. Woodward, and the meeting closed with the usual vote of thanks.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.

PRESTON. A number of the workingmen Conservative electors of Preston, on Thursday, declared their determin.tion to assert their independence as free electors and return Mr. Tomlinson as member for the borough, in spite of the small clique in Guildhall-street and the Conservative wire-pullers. The Liverpool Executive at Preston decided, on Saturday, not to contest the seat vacant by the elevation of Sir John Holger to the bench. This decision has not been well re- ceived by a large section of the electors, who are particu- larly anxious that Mr. Raikes shall not be allowed a walk over. On Wednesday morning the Liberal deputations had a final interview with the Right. Hon. A. S. Ayrton, who had l:;een invited to the town by a number of working men. Afterwards the following official report was issued :—" The working men of the Liberal party having invited the Right Hon. A. S. Ayrtonto come to Preston, that gentleman held a conference with them to-day and with a deputation of the executive of the local Liberal Association. After carefully con- sidering all the circumstances under which the ensuing elec- tion would take place, they unanimously arrived at the con- clusion that it would be most expedientto defer entering into a contest until a future opportunity." Mr. Tomlinson is expected to fight. The canvassers on behalf of Mr. Tom- linson who were out on Tuesday report highly favourable results. They are arranging for a demonstration. There is strong sympathy for Mr. Tomlinson among all classes of voters. On Wednesday a resolution was passed by the Con- servative Working Men's Club condemning the action taken by a portion of its members in endeavouring to bring out Mr. Tomlinson as a candidate, after Mr. Raikes bad been chosen by the meetings connected with both clubs.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND MR. RAIKES.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND MR. RAIKES.

The President of the Board of Trade, writing to a corres- pondent who had sent him one of Mr. Raikes' election speeches at Preston, says :—"I suppose we must not look too closely into the statements which are made during the heat of an election, especially by a Tory candidate; but Mr. Raikes has rather exceeded the usual license when he at- tributes to me an admission that the Government did not exert itself lo restore law and order, because they were afraid they mig!)t choke off the agitation which would enable them to carry their Idli. Of course, I never said anything of the kind; but this fact will not prevent Mr. Raikes and others of his party from continuing to make the assertion as ion ias thzy think it will promote their political interests."

div.head: FORTSMOUTH.
div.p: FORTSMOUTH.

The annual demonstration of the Portsmouth Liberal Association was held on Wedaesday. It was stated that at the next general election Mr. J. D. Lewis and Mr. Deverell, both Hampshire gentlemen, would contest the southern divi- sion of the county; and that Mr. John Bonham Carter, resident in Portsmouth, would contest the borough. Resolu- tions were adopted in support of the policy of the Govern- ment. Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., expressed his determination to support the Ministerial policy. He,deprecated the introduction of Protection, and expressed a hope that obstruction would be effectually put down in the ensuing session.

div.head: NORTH RIDING OF YORKSHIRE.
div.p: NORTH RIDING OF YORKSHIRE.

The nomination of candidates for the vacancy in the representation of the North Riding took place at York, on Thursday. The candidates nominated were Mr. Rowland- son (L) and the Hon. G. C. Dawnay (C). The polling takes place on Tuesday next.

div.head: SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.

Henry Thompson, 1G years of age, who lived in a back house off Morton Bank-road, and for a short time worked at the Laffak-Garswood Colliery, committed suicide about half-past two o'clock on Thursday afternoon. Deceased overslept himself, and did not go to work. He played about until dinner time, when he and his master had a few words about a bammer which deceased had left on the floor, and which a child haa thrown at another. He appeared to be all right both before and after this, but shortly afterwards went upstairs. Mrs. Thompson went upstairs in about 10 minutes, and found deceased had tied a strap round his neck and hooked in on the pin in the top of the tall wooden bed- post. He had then pushed his legs away, so that the weight of his body, being bent, fell on his neck. His face was covered with an apron. Mrs. Thompson screamed, and a neighbour came in and lifted the strap from the pin, but de- ceased was dead. Although Mrs. Thompson sat on the bottom stair, and the bedroom door was open, she says she heard no sound.

BEDROOM VENTILATION.—IS it necessary to state that the sickening odours so perceptible at the first of the morn- ing in any ill-ventilated sleeping apartment arise from the fact that a considerable volume of carbonic acid, with the vapour of perspiration and other animal exhalations, are mingled with the atmosphere of the chamber. Science proveslthat all these products are deadly poisons. Nature , expels them from the system because they poison the I system. Yet we insist on enclosing them within four walls. We shut up doors, windows, and even chimney-places, that not a particle may escape. Nay, we surround oar beds with close-drawn curtains for the express parposa, it would seem, of preventing ventilation, and for the express purpose of hugging close the poisonous atmosphere of our own bodies, and so re-absorbing into our systems the very atoms which, by the laws of God, have been cast out because they are detrimental. That we do re-absorb these poisons needs no ! proof. The same act of breathing which renders them per- ceptible to the sense of smell causes them to visit every air-cell, to permeate every blood-vessel of the lungs, and come into positive contact with all the countless myriads of streams which are traversing the one hundred and sixty-six square yards of respiratory surface. "MORE CRY THAN WOOL."—Some time ago I sat listen- ing to Mr. Spurgeon, as he preached in a favourite and fashionable watering place in Wales. A well-dressed and apparently well-to-do man sat next to me on the platform; indeed he seemed such an important person that I made way for him, gave him my chair, and betook myself to a form close by. I don't think I ever saw a man evince more in- terest, more delight, more strong and varied feeling while hearing a discourse. All through the service he was deeply irterested. He joined in the singing with great enthusiam ; Mr. Spurgeon's well-known running comment which he gives as he reads the Scripture so delighted him that he knocked the platform vigorously with his walking-stick,l and several times cried out "Hear, hear !" Daring prayer I was much disturbed by my neighbour's pious ejaculations. Then came the sermon, and a good sermon it was, as Mr. Spurgeon's generally are. My neighbour was a great study to me. I fear that I was more observant of him than mindful of the discourse. The preacher was humorous, my neighbour laughed tight heartily; the preacher was pa- thetic, my neighbour drew out his handkerchief and ap- plied it again and again to his streaming eyes; the preacher was eloquent, my neighbour looked and listened in an ecstacy of wonder' admiration, and joy; and when it was over he blessed God and three times cried "Amen !" Mr. Spurgeon, in his discourse, said some excellent things about liberality, which appeared in an especially manner to ap- prove themselves to my neighbour, who repeatedly looked round towards me, remarking, "Good, good !—that's good! very, very good !" In all that Mr. Spurgeon said about meanness, selfishness, niggardliness (and he did say some scathing, scalpin things), my neighbour seemed fully and g entirely to sympathise. Well, the sermon over, then came the collection. I watched my neighbour. It was an un- mannerly thing to do, but I did it; and my apology is this —that, partly at my request, Mr. Spurgeon had travelled far to preach for a charity in which I was much interested. So I watched my demonstrative, enthusiastic neighbour. I did not expect much, for I thought of the proverb " More cry than wool." Still, I thought this man, who had been so enchanted by the discourse, and who had very distinctly declared, in my hearing and in the hearing of many others, that—were the whole realm of nature his it would be a present far too small—l thought he might be good for half- a-crown; especially as he had wept profusely when Mr. Spurgeon, in feeling terms, referred to the object for which he pleaded. I saw my neighbour pick from a handful of silver and gold a shilling, which he put upon the plate. I said to myself," 'Well, this is a hypocritical humbug." But I further saw that when my neighbour had put down his shilling he picked up off the plate a sixpence and five pen- nies, one by one, which he put into his pocket. I hope he did not take more; but for the elevenpence out. of the twelve I can vouch; and then the mean wretch had the cheek to roar out another "Bless the Lord" and another "Amen" at the benediction.—Rev. Hugh Stowell Brown in " Plain Truth."

CONSTITUENTS.
DISORDERLY MEETING.

One of the stormiest meetings held iri—ManchesfeTin recent years took place on Monday, on the occasion of the annual meeting with their constituents of the Liberal mem- bers of Jacob Bright and Mr. John Slagg. Mr. Robert Leaks, M.P , presided, and a resolution approv- ing of the policy of the Government and expressive of confluence in the members was moved and seconded. Mr. Thomas Wright, a Radical, who has latterly taken a pro- minent part in the association with the Irish party in the borough, came forward to move an amendment protesting against coercion in Ireland and the barbarous practices of the Chief Secretary and his satellites, which were attributable entirely to her Majesty's Government ;and also condemning in the strongest possible manner the conduct of Mr. Slagg in supporting the coercion measures of the Government. For a long time Mr. Wright was unable to obtain a hearing, in spite of several appeals by the chairman, and ultimately he was compelled to give up the effort.—Dr. Dickson, who seconded the amendment, was received with continued groans, and was unable to make himself beard even by the reporters.—The amendment was rejected by an overwhelm- ing majority.—Mr. Jacob Bright, in responding to the resolu,tion, entered in some detail into a defence of his con- duct in opposing the Coercion Bill, and was subject to several interruptions, but they were not of a serious character. —Mr. Slagg, who followed, was, however, received with an evident determination on the part of a section of the audience that he should not IoE. heard, and for over half an hour the ball was in a state of general uproar, fighting taking place in several parts of the building. .For some time Mr. Slagg spoke only to the reporters, and it was not until large num- bers of the people had been expelled that anything like order was restored.

div.head: ANNOYING MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: ANNOYING MR. GLADSTONE.

The man wlao is in custody at Hawarden on a charge of breaking the peace, he having sent an insulting letter to Mr. Gladstone and attempted to impede his departure from the Hawarden rent audit dinner, at first refused to give his name, but it has now transpired that he is a Henry William Wilson, who was formerly employed as a grocer's assistant lat Reddish, near Worcester. There he was discharged from his employment. This seems to have preyed upon nis mind, and be took to drinking. According to his own account, be I has been a constant correspondent to Mr. Gladstone, and sent that gentleman sometime ago a cepy of the New Testament in shorthand. On the day before the rent audit dinner he wrote to Mr. Gladstone from Birmingham informing him that unless he received a telegram before 10 o'clock the next day he should "take French leave and pay him a visit." At half-past two on the following day he made his appearance in the vicinity of Hawarden, and after ordering some drink at a public-house he left without paying, and walking towards Hawarden Park depesited his portmanteau at the lower lodge with the intimation that he was paying Mr. Gladstone a visit. He then made his way to the Glynne Arms Hotel, at Hawarden, where the dinner was being held. There were several constables about the hotel, and in answer to one of them who asked him his busines he said that he had a letter for Mr. Gladstone, who was expecting him, and was accordingly allowed to pass. He took his seat far not from the Premier and helped himself freely to wine and dessert, and as be was mistaken for a clerk no one interfered with him. It now appears clear that he is partially demented. Asked why he had sent such a letter to Mr. Gladstone, he said he was determined to be attended to; he was a poor young man out of employment and without friends; this was called a Christian country; Mr. Gladstone was a Christian and ought therefore to assist him. Prisoner has been taken before a magistrate and remanded.

div.head: NESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: NESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held on Monday evening, at the clerk's offices, Derby- street, Mr. W. L. Evans, J P., presiding. There were also present—Messrs. J. J. Brown, J. Wycherley, W. Golds- weirth, and T. P. Hewitt; with Mr. Henry Cross (clerk).
APPOINTMENT OP AN ASSISTANT MASTER.

The CLERK read the proceedings of a special meeting held on the 4th instant to consider applications and select candi- dates for the assistant mastership in the boys' school. There were 36 applications in all, and after the testimonials of each had been examined, Mr. John Birtics was selected as the most suitable person for the post.—He was accordingly appointed at a salary of £55 per annum, on the motion of Mr. JoitN WYCEIERLEY, seconded by Mr. GOLDSWORTFL

div.head: ATTENDANCE AT TILE SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE ATTENDANCE AT TILE SCHOOLS.

Miss DUKE, mistress of the girls' school, said there were 66 present at the opening of the school that morning, and 76 in the afternoon.—Miss MCGILEGOR, mistress of the infant school, reported tha4t, the average attendance at her school for the week preceding the holidays was 61, an compared with 109 in the corresponding week of last year.—Mr. LIGHT- FOOT, head master, stated that the average attendance at the boys' school for the month preceding the holidays was 173, as against 172 in the corresponding month of last year. There were 212 on the roll, but only 125 put in an appear- ance when the school opened that morning; but this number increased to 140 in the afternoon. Mr. Birtles, the newly- appointed assistant master, commenced his duties that morning. '
THE AIIDIT OF THE ACCOUNTS.-THE MASTER SURCHARGED.

A discussion took place respecting the report of the assis- tant auditor (Mr. Knott), who had lately audited the Board's accounts, with regard to the schools' fee book. The report was as follows :—" Fee Book.—The weekly entries in this book are not kept separate for each quarter, and the columns are not cast up at the foot of each quarter's account. In Mr. Lightfoot's and Miss McGreg,or's fee books the amount of fees excused appeared to be deducted by them twice over. They were not present at the audit, and no explanation of this apparent discrepancy could be given." The auditor surcharged Mr. Lightfoot to the extent of £8 is. Bd. • Mr. Lightfoot now explained the matter to the satisfaction of the Board, and said that the auditor had deviated from the course adopted by his predecessors.—lt was resolved that Mr. Lightfoot put his explanation in writing, and that the same be forwarded through the clerk to the auditor.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

In reply to the Chairman's inquiry, the CLERK stated that Mr. Lloyd, the attendance officer, had informed him that he had nothing to report except that the two persons against whom he was ordered to take out summonses at the last meeting for not complying with the Education Act bad been convicted, and fined 55., including costs.—The CLERK stated that the amount"still outstanding on the call made in July was £l5O. Cheques were drawn to the amount of £27 ss. From the financial statement of the Board for the year ended the 29th day of September, 1.881, a copy ef which was placed before each member, it appeared that the receipts from all sources amounted to £1,003 13s. 2id., and the ex- penditure to £B2O 2s. 8.43., leaving a balance in hand of £243 10s. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 21, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 21, 1882.

good prospect of a nice lawyer's bill to pay, in times when trade is anything but lively. Under these circumstances, it may have been quite right that the opposition should not know the arguments which the Commissioners are pre- pared to advance in support of entering a gentleman's pre- mises by search warrant, but it is just as important to the ratepayers, who will have to pay the piper, that they should know a little•about the tune that is being played. There was not the slightest necessity that anything likely to injure •the matter whilst it is sub judice should have gone forth to the world, but on a question of such monetary importance the people who have the rates to pay ought surely to be en- lightened as to what the possible res Ult may be of contesting the action. It may be said by some that the affair, if pro- ceeded with, will be tried at Chester or Liverpool Nisi Prins Court, but the appellant, I believe, has the power of choice, so that it may be heard in London, where the jury would be far away from the reach of any local influence. If this statement be correct—and I have reason to believe it is— and all the Commissioners, as defendants, have to make a journey up to the metropolis, the length of the bill which will have to be paid will rather astonish the ratepayers. Of course, it is quite within the bounds of possibility that the Local Government Board auditor may raise some objections to sanctioning the payment of a large amount of money on this head, in which case, I suppose, the individual Commis- sioners concerned would have the pleasure of paying it. Counsel will have to be employed, and London agents will, of course, be already at work entering in their daily journals such lively items as " To perusing draft of "case in Re Beasley, and long consultation thereon, £3 35." "To drawing brief for counsel "—heaven only knows what the amount of this item will be! FLACCUS.

VISIT OE MR: HARRY LISTON TO WIDNES.—Mr. Harry Liston, the well-known vocalist and ventriloquist, is announced in our advertising columns to give his popular entertainment, "Merry Moments," in the Drill Hall, Widnes, on Wednesday evening next. Mr. Lislon will be accompahiect by Master Zandre, "the lightning limner," who will paint in oil groups of flowers and landscapes in minutes and we have no doubt those of our readers who visit the hall will find the entertainment to be of the usual enjoyable character. ENTERTAINMENT AT FARNWORTILA miscellaneous entertainment was given in the girls' schoolroom, Farnworth, on Monday evening, maid of the parochial funds. The chief artistes were the Misses Bond, who have already won for themselves a reputation among local vocalists, and who sang with their accustomed ability and taste; Mr. E. Sansom, who is well known in Widnes for his histrionic abilities, and Mr. J. Lea. The above vocalists were assisted by the Farn- worth Glee Party, who gave several favourite pieces in their usual succebsful style. The second part consisted of selections by the Farnworth Negro Troupe' who rendered the various songs which they undertook in a highly creditable style. CIIIIRCII -OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE MEETING AIT WIDNES.—A • meeting in connection with the Church of England Temperance Society, took place in the National schoolroom, Waterloo-road, on Thursday evening. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams occupied the chair, and there was a crowded attendance, especially of children for whom indeed the entertainment was principally intended. The Chairman, having delivered an opening address in which he pointed out the necessity of temperance work ambng all classes, and its special importance to the young, the programme commenced with a pianoforte duet from Masters J. and Lewis Kilcross, which the youthful pianists gave in a praiseworthy style. Recitations, dialogues, and songs followed, which were all creditably rendered.

THE ODDFELLOWs' ANNUAL , TEA .PARTY AND BALL AT RUNCORN.—On Thursday evening the sixth annual tea party and batl in connection with the Loyal Wright's Pride ,Past Grand Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, M.1.T., was held in the Public Hall, which had been tastefully decorated. At half-past six the members and friends of this • Order, numbering about 250, hdd tea, which was provided by Mrs. Waterworth, of the Anchor Inn, Brunswick-street. The following are the names of the ladies who presided at the tables :—Mrs Robert Gorst, Mrs. Wright, Mrs. Briscoe, Mrs James- Price, Mrs. Molyneaux, Mrs. Weedal I, Mrs. Yates, Mrs. Ramsdom, Mrs. Faulkner, Mrs. Saunders, Mrs. Dykes, Mrs. Holt, Mrs. Dutten, and Mrs. Able. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Canon Barclay, and the following gentle- men accompanied _him on the platform :—Messrs. F. Salkeld, C, Cooke, Prov.C.S. ; R. Wright, P.P.G.M.; Geo. Riley, ; John Barrow, P.P.G.M.; Thomas Cook, P.P.G.M. Geo. Crate, P.P.G.M.; Rich%rd Bowles, P.P.G.M.; R. W. Cringle, Prov.G.M. ; Geo. Burrows, secretary;Roberts, HP ..GB. ; Toone, P.G. ;J. Pritchard, P.G., dm Mr. F. S.Alkeld moved a vote of thanks to the Rev. Canon Barclay, which was seconded by Mr. J. Pritchard and carried unanimously.—The quadrille band for dancing, was provided by Mr. T. Woods. OLD WOMEN'S SUPPER AT HALTON.—The" Old women's supper," an -institution mainly dependent on voluntary sup- port, took place On the 'night of the 12th inst., at Halton, when 44 elderly, females partook,of the best cheer that Mrs.- Ormson, of the Norton Arms Hotel, could provide. The table was filled with roast turkeys and sausages, roast beef und mutton, boiled beef and mutton, rabbit pies' &c., and. with a plentiful supply of plum cake and other delicacies. The wants of all having been appeased, the chair was taken by Mr. Thomas Wright, and the vice-chair by Mr. Stokes, ably supported by Mr. J. Haddock and Mr. William Nixon. The loyal toasts having been duly honoured, the chairman called upon the company to drink the health of Mrs. Orm- son and Mrs, Haddock who, he remarked, had been instru- mental in.providing the supper. • He then went on to speak of the annual supper of the old men, which had had to be postponed in consequence of a death they all regretted, that of Mr. Carruthers, so that the old women's supper took pre- cedence. They owed much to the disinterested and willing efforts of Mrs. Ormsonl and 'Mrs. Haddock, who went to much trouble to make Their, proceedings enjoyable. Mr. Haddock, on behalf of his wife and Mrs. Orrnson, responded, and in doing so said both ladies laboured, far a. motive of love and had their reward in the amount of pleasure and satisfaction they gave to the old .people. The next toast was "The donors of the feast," and this was enthusiastically received. The toast list was interspersed with singing, which greatly enlivened the proceedings. Mr: John Ravens- croft was at the piano, and some of the old people present, with limbs no doubt affe6ted by the " rheumatiz," heartily joinedin-the merry rustic dance.. Mr. Haddock, Mr. Fryer, and Mr. Matthews also gave songs; and at half-past nine, with a liberal supply of fruits and cakes, the old people dispersed with every manifestation of pleasure. WYCLIPIE CHURCH, WARRINGTON.—The Rev. J. Yonge preached his monthly sermon to young men, in Wycliffe Church, on Sunday evening. Taking as his text the 17th, 18th, and 19th verses of the 7th chapter, second book of Kings, the rev, gentleman dwelt at length upon the siege of Samaria by the Syrian army; of the distress felt by the besieged, and of the King's inability to give successful battle, owing to the numerical superiority of the Syrians. He related the incident of the doubt entertained by one of servants of the Syrian king, that food should be sold on the following day within the city for a trifling sum ; and ' of Elisha's promise to the servant that, although he should see the food being sold, he should not partake. Mr. Yonge spoke of the doubt and scepticism so prevalent amongst young people; and said he would give the apostle Paul's advice, to "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." WYCLIFFE INFANT SUNDAY SCHOOL ENTERTAINMENT. —On Tuesday evening, the children of the Wycliffe Infant Sunday School had their annual tea meeting, at which there were present about 200. After tea a successful entertain- ment was held under the presidency of the Rev. John Yonge. I The children unitedly sang a number of hymns very pleasantly, and Arthur Picktonjecited "God made the little bird to sing • " Clara Weir, " lam a little pilgrim;" Jessie Shaw, " God can see me ; " James Helsby, "Little Jack Homer; Louisa Edwards, "121st psalm ; " Cissie Hackney,. " The heart's desire ; " Alfred Podmore, " Pussy's doctor ; " Beatrice Helsby, "The little shroud ; " Herbert Bawling, "Lubin, a tale ; " Ellen Halt, "The Bible says we may Annie Travis, "The stray lamb;" Thomas Jordan, "23rd psalm ; " Annie Bawling, "The song of Christmas ; " Annie Howard, "The day is past and over;" Arthur Brayshaw, " May ;" Samuel Phillips, "In peace with all the world we live." J. W. Brayshaw and William Stringer also gave recitations, and a duet entitled "John Stout," was sung by Grace and Lucy Wallington. During the evening the young folks were addressed by Mr. Knowles, Mr. Wallington, and Mr. J. Garland. At the close of the entertainment each child was presented with an orange by Mr. Wallington, the superintendent. We may state that this school is in charge of the following teachers :—Mr. and Miss Podtnore, Mr. Wm. Ball, and Mr. Hawthorne.

CATIIOLIC SOIREE AT WARRINGTON.—The annual Catholic soirée was held in the Co-operative Hall on Tues- day evening, when about 100 hundred ladies and gentlemen assembled for dancing, which commenced at S•3O, and was kept up until after three the following morning, to an effi- cient band provided by Mr. Masksll, of this town. Mr. Potter furnished an excellent, supply of refreshments. The committee consisted of Messrs. T. Mather, J. Dolan, G. H. Tomlinson, W. Allen, T. Lytlagoe,, and J., Williams. Mr. Mather discharged the duties of M.C., "assisted by Mr. J. Dolan. The party was an enjoyable one and a. success, and reflecting great credit on the committee. WIDNES WESLEYAN IBIPROVRICENT CLAJ3B.—At the weekly meeting of the Oakland-street claSs, on Wednesday, Mr. J. Chadwick, read a paper on "The life of Joshua." CATTLE DISEASES IN CHESUlRE.—According to the latest returns furnished to the Chief Constable (Major Hamersley), there are at present no cases of pleuro- pneumonia in Cheshire, but a fresh outbreak of foot-and- mouth disease in the township of Hale, near Altrincham, is reported. Here two animals have been attacked, and are at present under treatment. There are no cases of swine fever. . ST. HELENS CORPORATION WATER BlLL.—This bill, which seeks to empower the mayor, aldermen, and bur- gesses of the town of St. Helens to make and maintain additional waterworks and to borrow money, came on Thurs- day before Mr. Frere, one of the examiners of the House of Commons, to comply with the standing orders of the House. The proceedings were adjourned until yesterday. THE SUBSIDENCE POLL AT NORTHWICH.—Messrs. Cliff and Hughes, members of the Northwich Local Board, have received a communication from the Local Government Board in reference to the surcharge of £5O, representing the expenses incurred in taking the poll of property owners and ratepayers of the district in connection with the promotion in Parliament of the Cheshire Salt Districts Compensation Bill. The Board are of opinion that the disallowance and surcharge were lawfully made for the reasons stated by the auditor, but they have, in the exercise of the equitable juris- diction conferred upon them by Act of Parliament, remitted the surcharge, and have forwarded a ceertificate giving effect to their decision.

_ PADOLTE 'WESLEYAN MUTUAL LiThOVEMENT So- curry.—" Corinth and St. Paul" was the title of a very interesting and instructive lecture given to a large audience of the members and friends of the above society on Tuesday last, by the Rev. Joseph Agar Beet. The lecture commenced with a vivid and portraiture of Corinth, its situation, its trade, and its immorality, and concluded with a graphic description of the various scenes connected with Corinth in which St. Paul took part, the work of early Christianity therein, the sins of some of its professing Christians, and the epistles written to them by St. Paul. Many valuable lessons were deduced from the narrative, and at the close of the lecture the appreciation of the audience was testified by loud applause. On the motion of Mr. Arthur Bennett, seconded by Mr. M. Shakeshaft, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Beet, who proposed a timilar vote to the chairman (Mr. William Bennett), which was seconded by Mr. Fred Wright, and carried with acclamation. BILLIARD 31 ATCII AT PRESCOT. On Saturday last a friendly game at billiards took place at the rooms of the Prescot Conservative Club, between 10 representatives of the latter and 10 of the St. Helens Conservative Association, and after a most exciting and well contested game resulted in a victory for the home team by six points on the total score. Play commenCed shortly after three o'clock, and ended about half-past nine. At six o'clock the visitors were entertained to tea by their opponents, and full-justice was done to the good things provided. The game, however, was kept going during tea, arrangements having been made for two of the players to go on so as to save time. Dr. Hall acted as captain of the Prescot team, and Mr. Mather •as captain of the St. Helens gentlemen. The scores were taken on behalf of Prescot by Mr. William Lloyd, the treasurer of the club, and by Mr:Mather on behalf of, St. Helens. The following is the score:—

FORESTERS' CLUB MEETING AT PRESCOT.—The annual meeting of Court "Earl of Derby," of the Ancient Order of Poresters, was held on Monday evening at the Derby Arms Inn, Eccleston-street. From the thirty-eighth financial report of the income, and expenditure for the year ended December 28th, 1881, it appeared' that in the sick and funeral fund account a balance of £9OB 13;10d was brought forward from the previous year, which, with .2210 103 id, made up by contributions, Sze., made the total receipts £1,119 3s 11d. The expenditure was as follows :—Cash paid sick members, £5B 17s 10d; district levy, £46 6e 6d; deaths, £37 18s; total, £143 2s 4d; keying a balance of £976 is 7d to the good, an increase on the year of £67 7s 9d. The receipts in the management fund amounted to £144 is 11E1, inclusive of a balance brought forward from the previous year of £BB 10s 7d.; the expenses reached £5l 8s 3d, leaving a balance in band of £92 13A Bd, a gain of £4 3s Lioi_the year. _Appropriation of balances :—On mort- gage freehold property, £500; Prescot Building Society, £502 15s 7d; Prescot Savings'. MR- BANTOCIC PIERPOINT'S CONCERT AT RUNCORN.*

This concert, which has bean looked forward to with much anticipation by the lovers of music, came off on Wednesday evening, in the Public Hall. Though the evening was A very unfavourable one, owing to the foggy condition of the atmosphere, there was a good attendance. No doubt the fact that the artistes comprised several well known names had very much.to do with this satisfactory state of things, which must be specially gratifying to Mr. Pierpoint when he remembers the well known saying, that a teacher does not receive honour in the locality from which he originally comes. The singers included Miss Clara Samuel!, soprano, whose fame as a highly popular soprano singer is firmly established ; Miss Emilie Lloyd, contralto, who is pretty well known and deservedly appreciated by Runcorn- audiences ; Mr. Henry Dunman, tenor, who has already won high honours at the Royal Academy of Music ; and last, though not least, Mr. Pierpoint, who is too popular in the district to need any introduction in our columns. There was also present Mr. • Frank Arnold, solo violin, a sub-pro- fessor at the insqtution just named, who is understood to be the favourite pupil of M. Sainton, the celebrated French violinist. Mr. W. I. Argent acted as accompanist. The programme, as announced, was a follows, though it had to be slightly varied owing to the fact that some of the lug- gage belonging to Miss Lloyd had gone astray : Serenade lii this hour " Pinsuti

Mr. Pierpoint Miss Lloyd and t The Sailor sighs „ Mr. Dunman B.dfe Miss Samuell "Non pilijnesta " Rossini Mr. Arn.)ld and t "Andante and Finale" t Mr. Argent i from concerto fJr violin, Mendelssohn Mr. Dunman..." Come into the garden, Maud ' Balfe Miss Lloyd "Gavotte from Mignon " Thomas Mr. Pierpoint " Thou'rt passing hence" 'ullivan Miss Samuell and "Of fairy wand ' (Maritana) Mr. Pierpoint 1 (By special permission.) Wallace Mr. Dunman " My own, my guiding star" Macfarren Miss Lloyd "Darby and Joan" Molloy Mr. Art>old and t "William Tell "...de Beriot k Osborne Mr. Argent Miss Samuell " Rose softly blooming" Spahr Mr. Pierpaint "The Boatswain's story" - Molloy Quartet "In this hour of softened splendour "—a quartette— was selected for the opening piece, and was given in a manner which at once won the attention of the audience, who impiediately settled down in the evident expectation of enjoying a rare treat. Mr. Pierpoint led off very wOl with Pinsuti's "I fear no foe," sung with an abandon which in the last line, "Strike, and capture make of me," won enthusiastic applause. ThG duet " The Sailor Sighs," by Balfe, was rendered by Miss Emilie Lloyd nod Mr. Dunman in a highly finished manner, which displayed what is too seldom seen in the ordinary run of public singers a most careful study of the meaning the writer of the piece intended to convey. This was beautifully shown in the line "'Tie she, 'tis she herself, she waves her hand," and the singers, we need hardly say, were rapturously applauded. Miss Samuell gave "Non pin mesta ' (Rossini), which showed to perfection the wonderful flexibility of her voice, which at times reminded us of the efforts of some of the great queens of song. Next came a charminc, piece of violin and piano- forte work (slendelssohn) by Mr F. Arnold and Mr. Argent. I One scarcely knew which to admire most. the wonderful skill of the finished violinist, whose whole soul was evidently lin his work, or the execution of Mr. Argent. The audience were evidently highly pleased. Mr. Dunman sang "Come into the garden, Maud "very sweetly, on the whole, but con- siderably too loudly in the last two lines of the charming compcsition. Miss Lloyd followed with "For ever and for ever" in which the rich tones of her powerful voice told with wonderful effect. She was enthusiastically received, and gave, as an encore, "Punchinello " one of her favourite pieces—which was beautifully sung Mr. Pierpoint gave with much pathos, Sullivan's " Thou rt passing hence," and was warmly received. The second part of the concert was commenced with the lovely duet "Of fairy wand," sung by Miss Samuell, and Mr. Pierpoint. Mr. Dunman was encored in " My own, my guiding star," and sang "My pretty Jane," with very delicate expression. Miss Lloyd next gave "Derby and Joan," and was recalled, when she sang "Caller Herrin," in a manner which we have seldom beard excelled. One of the "erns of the evening followed, being a magnificieut piece of violin playing from I "Guillaume Tell" (Rossini), by Mr. Arnold, and a nearly equally effective performance on the pianoforte, by Mr. I Argent. The audience were evidently entranced by the efforts of Mr. Arnold, who is destined to take one of the fore- most places of the day as a violinist. Miss Samuell next I sang, in splendid voice, "Rose softly blooming" (Spohr) ; and was encored, on which she gave "A bird in the hand," in such a charming manner, that she was Keealled and rendered, with much naivete, "Two is company." Mr. Pierpoint came next with " The boatswain's story," in which he received an encore, and replied with "Jack's yarn," for which he received most hearty applause. The concert, which has been one of the most successful of the season, concluded 1 with the quartette 'Calm be thy slumbers."
