LIBERALISM AT WIDNES.
The annual meeting in connection with the west division of the Widnes Liberal Association, was held on Monday evening, at Simm's Cross School, Mr. H. Brunner in tke chair.

Mr. H. B. SHORES. the secretary, read the minutes of the previous annual gathering, which were passed. The CHAIRMAN said in the General Committee, which numbered 40 members, of whom 10 were executive, there .were two vacancies, owing to Messrs. :Ellwell (hon. sec.) and W. B. Jones having left the neighbourhood. The whole of the committee would have to be re-elected by the members present, who would also have the power of filling up the vacancies. After propositions by Mr. Booth and Mr. Sadler, the names•of Mr. John Heath and Mr. E. Martley were added to the General Committee, which will be constituted as fol- lows :—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. W. Doward, J. Latham, T. Hughes, J. Bray, J. Dagnall, J. Powell, G. -Joynson, T. Brown T. Seed, S. Owens, G. Saxe, J. Newall, B. Brown, P. McKinley, J. Anderson, W. Sadler, J. Morris, T. Sadler, T. Jones, S. B. Stringer, J. Pye, G. Hesketh, E. Loines, T. Robinson, W. Hosker, J. Taylor, F. Lawrinson, J. William- son, F. H. Pankhurst, S. Sadler, H. Webster, S. K. Muspratt, D. Hirst, G. Davies, A. Powlson, J. Quinn, J. Heath, E. Martley, and H. Brunner. The members of the executive were then balloted for, and ! the following were chosen: Messrs. H. Brunner (chairman), S. Sadler, T. Seed, J. Hughes, R. Webster, W. Sadler, B. Brown, J. Sadler, and F. H. r ankhurst. On the proposition of Mr. Carlile, seconded by Mr. Booth, Mr. Shuttleworth was elected secretary for the next twelve months, in the 1) lace of Mr. Elwell, now of Bacup. Mr. CARLILE moved that Mr. Brunner be re-elected chair- man for the ensuing year, and that a vote of thanks be passed to him for his services during the past 12 months. When they looked at what Mr. Brunner had done for them, they would agree with him that he was the right man in the right place. They all knew and appreciated the services which that gentleman had rendered in the cause of Liberalism. Mr. WILLIAMSQX seconded the motion, and it was carried by acclaniation. Mr. BRUNNER, in responding, said he was very much In- debted to theta for the vote of thanks. His duties during the last year must have been extremely light, seeing that they had very little work to .do. He thought it quite probable that. during the present year they might find more work to employ them. Ho did not know whether they had noticed it, but the pros and cons of the question had been discussed in the p ipeis, as to whether or not we might have a dissolution of Parliament doling the coming year. It was an eventuality it was well to be prepared for. kilear, bear.) During the last revision they might congratulate them- selves on having done pretty well, the Liberals having inadq, a gain of 50. (Applause.) They had lost, he was sorry to say, from their midst, Mr. Martin Taylor, who had been of great assistance to them in many of the political fights they had for years past. If it should be that a general election came on be hoped they would fight their division again-. Though not successful last time they made a very good fight, and would, tie thought, be quite justified in fighting again. If they never fought they could never hope to win. He thought that this time they might expect to have a great Lumber of the farmers on their side. At the last general election they had many farmers on their side, and if all these did not vote for them they wished them well. Of coarse a great deal would depend on what question the dissolution took place. If the Government wept out on any question in regard to the land laws they might he sure that the farmers' votes throughout the country would be in favour of the Liberals. (Cheers.) Farmers in this country had not suffered so much as those in Ireland. Nevertheless they had suffered severely with the competition they now had to contend with from abroad. If the farmer were to live and pay his rates and taxes, some alteration must be made in the conditions under which he held his land. (Applause.) He next called their attention to the fact that they were to have an address delivered in connection with the Widnes Liberal Association, next Thursday, on the extension of the county franchise' by Mr. Joseph Arch. Mr. Arch, he believed, originally, worked as an agricultural labourer, or something of the kind. At all events he was a man who had educated himself, and must naturally thoroughly understand from what the agricultural interest in this country suffered • and, above all, he knew where the shoe. pinched in the case of the agricultural labourers. In November last it Vas arrange that Mr. Arch should address a meeting during the current month at Widnes; and on the 26th he would be among them to fulfil his promise. He thought that those who came to hear Mr. Arch would be very much pleased with him. He spoke well, and was thoroughly master of the subject of which he treated. Ile concluded by thanking them for their atten- dance there that evening. Several gentlemen present referred to Mr. Brunner's state- ment with regard to Mr. Martin Taylor, and said they believed it was not his intention to leave Widnes. This concluded the proceedings.

Another Public meeting of Liberals was held at the Albert Hotel, W'idnes, on Wednesday evening, for the pur- pose of electing the officers and committee for the following year. Mr. Joseph Morrison presided. The following committee for the division was appointed, viz. :—Messrs. J. L. Muspratt, T. Crosier, D. Wright, R. Fogg, Hamblett, Kidd, Robinson, Talton, Hirst, Deakin, F. Hurter, C. Stout, A. Speakman, J. W. Carlile, J. Riddle, W. H. Kershaw, Mr. Pritchard, J. Laithwood, J. W. Ware- ing, W. Powlson, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Y. Dale, J. Davies, J. Horrabin, S. K. Muspratt, J. Morrison, J. W. Davies, J. H. Lewis, R. Mercer, G. Rea, D. Forster, T. Dennett, A. Cowley, J. Brook, D. W. Hunter, A. Walker, W. Hartley, Hargreaves, jun., M. W. Gentles, and J. Hadfield. On the motion of Mr. CARLILE, seconded by Mr. Cuosurn; the following ten gentlemen chosen out of the general com- mittee were appointed the executive, namely, Messrs. J. Morrison (chairman), J. W. Davies (secretary), Crosier, D. Wright, R. Fogg, J. Hamblett, Robinson, D. Hirst, J. W. Carlile, and W. Gentles. Mr. CAELILE Moved a.vote of thanks to the Chairman for his services during the past year, and added as a rider a resolution that he be re-elected for the ensuing year. (Ap- plause.) During the past year Mr. Morrison had served them well. In him he considered they had the right man in the right place, and he therefore thought they could not do better than re-elect him (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. Monuisox said that before the resolution was put to the meeting he should like to explain his feelings a little. Though he had a very high opinion of the present Govern- ment as far as the general policy was concerned, still there was one part of their policy upon-which be must divide from them. On their foreign policy he agreed with them. The point at which he joined issue with the Government was in regard to their coercive measures towards Ireland. He did not deny that they had had some reason for the action they had taken; but he did not think they had suffi- cient cause for incarcerating men in gaol without trial. He thought that the crimes laid against Ireland were exag- gerated and misrepresented. They found Mr. Herbert Glad- stone saying that they were exaggerated. He felt he must strongly condemn the manner in which the Government were ruling Ireland. He alluded to the police circulars offering bribes to informers and what had recently occurred between the poliz.e and the .Archbishop of Cashel. He had thought it right to make this explanation, as he doubted whether it was fitting for him to remain chairman of that committee when on this important question of policy he differed. In his opinion the coercion policy had done more to embitter the feeling between the two countries than any- thing since the Act of Union. Having these feelings he questioned whether he could continue to be the chairman of the district committee. He was extremely obliged to them for their thanks. Mr. H. B. SHORES remarked that, lest they should be biassed by the explanations Mr. Morrison had just given in regard to his views, he might remind them that Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., held the same opinions as those just enun- ciated by Mr. J. Morrison. But after he had stated in the House of C6mmons that be could not support the coercive policy of the Government, his sound Liberal principles generally were sufficient to warrant his re-election as Presi- dent of the National Liberal Federation. Ile thou4ht they too would see their way to re-elect Mr. Morrison. Mr. GENTLES had great pleasure in seconding Mr. Car- lisle's motion. He thought Mr. Morrison was justified in feeling warmly for the people of Ireland, but at the same time he must admit that the Government had tried to do their best. The motion was unanimously carried, which was ackno ledged by Mr. Morrison. Mr. CARLILE proposed the re-election of Mr. J. W. Davies as secretary for the forthcoming year, and coupled with it a vote of thanks for his past services. He was sure they were all very much obliged to him for the manner in which he had carried on his duties, and he was therefore extremely pleased to move his re-election to the post. Mr. HIRST seconded the motion, which was also carried. On the motion of Mr. WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. GENTLES, Mr. Heaney was re-appointed as the Cuerdley representative of the committee. At the same time a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Heaney. The proceedings then terminated.

PADGATE CHURCH CONGREGATIONAL TEA. PARTY. - The annual tea meeting in connection with Padgate church was held a few days ago in the Schoolroom. There was a large attendance, and the proceedings passed off very pleasantly. Among those present were the Rev. W. H. Williams (the vicar) and Mrs. Williams, Mr. and Mrs. Beamont, Mr. Royston, Mr. Pennington, the Messrs. Houghton' the Messrs. Bennett, Mr. Yates, Mr. George Williams, Mr. Hamson, Mts. Turner, the Misses Turner, the Misses Crawford, Miss Lees, and Miss Hamson, Szc. In opening the subsequent proceedings, the Vicar remarked that their parish life was certainly most encouraging. Harmony everywhere prevailed, and goodwill reigned supreme amongst them all. Still it had not been all sunshine. They had been obliged to close their school for several weeks owing to the prevalence of the epidemic, but he was happy to say that no case bad proved fatal, and that they were again in a flourish- ing condition. After a few remarks by Mr. Beamont, the entertainment was then proceeded with, end was contributed to by Miss Ellen Turner, Miss Sarah Turner, Miss Lees, Miss Hamson, the Misses Wrighson, Messrs. Harding, John Williams, Jenkins, George Williams Hamson, Jos. Monks, Masters Leslie Wrighton and William Wood; and the Vicar. The singing of the National Anthem brought the entertainment to a close. On Saturday evening a tea party was given to the children of the parish Sunday and day schools. After tea an entertainment was given, and was concluded by the distribution of prizes.
A RUNCORN CONTRACTOR CHARGED
WITH FRAUD.

• At the Liverpool sessions on Wednesday, John Jones (54) formerly a clerk in the employ of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, and John Beckett (58), contractor, Runcorn, surrendered to their bail on a number of charges against them of having fraudulenty obtained the sum of Li 13s. Gd. and other amounts, the moneys of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board. Mr. Carver and Mr. PicHord appeared on behalf of the Dock Board •, Mr. Charles Russell, Q.Ce M.P., and Dr. Commins, M.P. (instructed by Mr. R. Bremner), represented Beckett; and Mr. Lumb (instructed by Messrs. Moore and Spence), represented the prisoner Jones. On the advice of the counsel, both prisoners pleaded guilty. Mr. Russell said the prisoner Beckett had pleaded guilty upon his advice. His honour would have noticed that the indictment charged the prisoners with having obtained large sums by false pretences, but, as a matter of fact, these sums represented the entire price of certain cargoes of gravel which Beckett had con- tracted to deliver to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, 1 and by far the greater part of it was properly owing to I him. In point of fact, the excess tonnage of the cargoes of the the three vessels mentioned in the indictment—viz., the Tarleton Lass, the Countess of Kerry, and the Harvest Home—was in one instance as much as 14 tons, in another 18 or 19 tons, and in the third 11 tons, representing alto- gether about 44 tons of gravel for which he was paid by the Dock Board more than he was entitled to. In respect of that, however, the only sum that the prisoner Beckett received was 3d. per ton, or altogether on these three vessels the sum of lie. Beckett, who at one time was master of a flat, carried on business as a contractor at Runcorn, and for some time had contracted with the Dock Board for the supply of gravel Co be used at their new dock works. The gravel was obtained from WAlney Island, near Barrow-in-Furness, and was supplied by Messrs. Hunter and Son. In the three cases mentioned in the indictment, Beckett eugaged small vessels to bring the gravel to Liverpool, paying 2e. di. per ton of freight. For the gravel he paid is. per ton, and as the Dock Board paid him 3s. 9d. per ton, he had only 3d. per ton of profit. There was no proper mode of loading these vessels at Barrow-in-Farness, but they were grounded and so much of the cargo put in, the remainder being shipped after they were floated. There was also no mode of ascertaining their weight with any accuracy, but a rough calculation was made of how much was on board from the carrying capacity of the vessels. Messrs. Hunter were not particular about ascertaining the exact weight 9f the gravel, as its intrinsic value was very small, and they could say that they were aware that they gave more that) the tonnage stated in the invoices. The vessels were taken to whatever part of the dock works the gravel was required, where it was weighed by the Dock Board workmen along with the waggons into which it had been put. The weight was recorded by two weighers, the prisoner Jones being one of them. After the gross weight was ascertained, it was necessary to deduct from it the tare of the waggons, and for this purpose recourse had to oe made to a list which contained the weights of the waggons. The weights of the respective waggons were tajeen from the list and then deducted from the gross. His Honour would see that in that way there was room for mistakes occurring, especially when the' weights of the waggons varied as much as llewt. Until about 18 months ago, the prisoner Beckett was supplied with such weights by the Dock Board weighers, but since then the weights had been sent to the overseer in charge of the dock works, who forwarded them to Mr. Lyster's office, where Beckett obtained them, and made his charges accordingly. When taken into custody' Beckett voluntarily made a statement, from which, to his (Mr. Russell's) mind, it was plain that he was certainly guilty of the offence with which he was charged. The learned counsel then read Beckett's statement, in which he said that he had had suspicions that the weighers were returning • over-weights, and that hd spoke to the prisoner Jones and another weigher about it, advising them to be cautious, as they were old men, and he would not like them to be put away at their tithe of life. They said their weights were correct. Beckett employed a man named Heppens to make out his accounts, and he also entrusted him with paying the captains of the flits and other vessels which brought the gravel. The prisoner Beckett subsequently made another statement, and it appeared plain from it that be was unquestionably culpable The captains of the vessels got the greater part of the overcharge' and Becket* only benefited to the extent of lls, in the cases against him. Without any suggesting or prompting of the bock Board, Beckett. had expressed his desire to make restitation as far as possible to the board. In view of that offer, Mr. Carver, on behalf the Dock Board, would state that they had no desire to press for punishment, and he (Mr. Russell) asked that Beckett should be allowed out on the same bail as before until the next sessions, in order that he would make such restitution.—Mr. Limb, on behalf of Jones, slid it en- deared from the evidence that Jones, who had been in ,the employ of the Dock Board for six years as weigher, must have been tempted by the captains of the vessels bringing the gravel, who got most of the money received from the overweight. One of the capteins, who knew the capacity of his vessel to be 189 tons, stated in his cross-examination at the Police Court that he received tonnage money for 201 tons, that for the overweight he received 2s 6d per ton, and that he sometimes paid Jones 5s or 7s Gd to make the cargo weigh as much as possible. He therefore submitted that Jones had been tempted to do this by the captain. Jones was very sorry for what he had done, and he hoped his honour would give him as lenient a sentence as was consist- ent with the ends of justice; or perhepe he would see his way to postpone sentence until the next sessions.—Mr. Carver said the Dock Board did not institute proceedings with the view of recovering the meeeey ; but they were perfectly con- tent to leave the matter in • his honour's hands.—The Recorder said lie would pestpone the sentences of both prisoners until the next sessions. Mr. Carver, he thought, had very properly acceded to the offer of Beckett. While he (the Recorder) would not pledge .hiintailt to any course which he might pursue at the next sessions, he thought that meanwhile Beckett should not only endeavour to pay back what he had himself benefited by the overcharge, but also for what he had been the n'teans of enabling others to obtain. He would allow both prisoners to go out on bail of two sureties of £25 each. The Recorder then told the pri- soner Jones to be prepared to pay any fine at the next ses- sions he might impop upon him, for he would not like to send him to prison if Beckett was not sent there.

div.p: RUNCORN SAYINGS' BANK.

The annul meeting of the trustees and managers of this bank, was held at the offices, High-street, on Tuesday after- noon. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were I also present the Revs. 'Wm. Preston, Evan Willi ime, and Messrs. John Simpson, John Brundrit, W. Whittaker Walter Jones, and W. F. Sallteld (actuary.) Mr. SALKELD read the, minutes of the last meeting, which were signed and confirmed Ile also read the report and statement of accounts (which will be found in our advertis- ing columns) for the year ending November 20th, 1881. The four auditors have examined the books and accounts frequently, and I beg to submit their:certificate of the correctness of them. At the Winchester Assizes, a Southampton solicitor, named William Henry Newman, aged 76, ras found guilty on a charge of having converted trust money to the amount of £14,000 to his own use. Sentence was deferred, pending the raising of a point of law.
LIBERAL DEMONTRATION IN WEST
CHESHIR E.

I A great Liberal demonstration was held in Crewe Town : Hall on Thursday night, when the building was crowded. IThe Rev. W. Mellor, president of the Crewe Liberal Asso- ' elation, presided, and .was supported by Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., J. Tomkinson, C. VV. Latham, Alderman McNeill (Mayor of Crewe), and Councillors Wallis, Eaton, Allman, Pedley, dm The CHAIRMAN said they had met to express their con- tinued and unabated confidence in her Majesty's Government. (Appluse.) Their confidence in the man.who had com- posed that Ministry remained unbroken and undiminished— (cheers) ;—and the whole of the Cabinet, from the illustrious chief of the empire, Mr. W. E. Gladstone—(loud cheers),— down to the unsalaried Junior Lord of the Treasury, had the full confidence of the people in their principles and policy —(bear, hear,)—principles that were well known and recog- nised by the great Liberal party at large. (Hear, hear.) To take a glance at the position of the Liberal party for the , West division of Cheshire, he might inform his audience that ' that they had made a clear gain ;of 1,003 votes since the last general election—(loud cheers),— 60 of which were gained in: the polling district of which Crewe was the centre. (Renewed cheers). At the general election for West Cheshire Messrs. West and Crompton, the Liberal candidates, were beaten by a majority of 760 votes—by no means large con- sidering the past history of the constituency—but at the by- election, which took place subsequently, owing to the death of Sir Philip Egerton, Mr. Tompkinson was only beaten by 380 votes, being just half of the previous majority. (cheers.) Seeing that, he was 'sure they would own he had a reason for introducing Mr. Tomkinson to them as one of the future 'liberal members for West Cheshire. (Loud cheers.) ' Mr. JAMES Toeneriesos, who was greeted with loud and prolonged cheering, moved," That this meeting hereby ex- presses its unabated confidence in Her Majesty's Govern— ment, believing that all legislation of pressing importance, including such measures ae the reform of the land laws, local county government, and household franchise of the counties, will receive their early attention." (Cheers.) He believed that the present Government was the most con- scientious, the most just, and the most hard working one they had seen for many a day—(cheers)—and with its present chief at its head it was abundantly able to keep within those questions which beset it. All people, he need hardly say so, were not of the same opinion ; in fact, some people had charged Liberal Ministers with every sort of malpractice. Mr. Gladstone had been compared to Mr. Per- nell, and the leading statesman of the Opposition had . stated that he did not think there was anything in their 1 condition which justified a difference between a resi- dence in Downing-street and one in Kilmain ham Gaol. (Laughter.) First of all, the Ministry had been charged with beveng promised great things end done nothine, next will having initiated a pelicy of spoliatien, and thirdly with , having, by their concessions truckled to agitation. If that were so he would not be standing on that platform as an apologist of the Government; but he felt perfectly convinced in his own mind that justice had been the only guide of the Cabinet. (Hear, hear.) As regarded the first charge, that of broken promises, everybody but the greatest enemy of the Ministry would admit that the in- dustry, energy, and will of the Government to pass reform was unquestioned; and, indeed, more work had been done since the last general election than during the whole of the six years of Conservative rule. (Loud cheers.) With re- gard to the second charge—that of spoliation—he would be the last man to say a word against Irish landlords, being an English landlord himself, and having no interest in Ire- land; but although the great majority of landowners in the sister isle had no doubt done their duty, there was abundant evidence to show that quite a sufficient percentage took un- , due advantage of the tenants committed to their-charge, and ; th us made the recent exceptional legislation absolutely reeces- I sary. (Hear, hear.) The Irish Land Bill was simply a mea- sure to protect the rights of property of both tenant and landlord—(cheers)—; and now that the Act was in working order, there was a terrible outcV that the Sub- Commissioners in some of the districts had been reducing the rents. - The landowners' panic, he ventured to think, was rather premature merely for that reason. (Hear, hear). Because a reduction of 24 per cent. had been made, on an average, at the beginning, he did not think that a similar reduction would be made throughout Ireland. On the contrary, it would be found in the majority of cases that the decisions of the Sub-Cosemissioners were quite fair, and in several cases already the rents bad not been reduced, but the petitions of the tenants had been dismissed instead. As to the third charge which the Tories had brought against the Government about concessions to agitation, he did not know that any measure had ever yet been passed which did not follow agitation. (Heir, hear). What about the Re- form Bill of 1832, and Catholic Emancipation? (Cheers). But then the Tories said, "You always give in to agitation ; but we were a strong party, and said, 'No, we mean it.'" (Laughter). What about the Land League? That body of agitators was started by Michael Davitt whilst the Con- servatives were in office, and yet the then Government had allowed it to grow unchecked. (Hear, hear). He ((lie speaker) did not say that the Tories ought to have can- celled Davitt's tieket.of-leave at the time, but it was not fair for the Opposition to turn around now and say " You ought to have nipped it in the bud," when they could have done it at the outset vvith but little difficulty. (Loud cheers). If the nation sent in a Con- servative'Government to-morrow what would be their pro- gramme ? (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He defied the subtlest intellect to make out what their programme would be. (Renewed laughter). The Marquis of, Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill—(laughter)—were opposing the Lend Act as the greatest measure of spoliation ever passed, and they had compared Mr. Gladstone the Marquis of , Hartington. and Mr. W. E. Ferster to Dick Turpin, Claude Duval, mid other disreputable characters. (Laughter.) Yet those very same erratic noblemen had not only expressed themselves in favour of the measure in its entirety, but declared that they would vote eyen for a further extension eif it. (Loud laughter.) Seriously speaking, there never I had been such a case of political destitution as those gentle- men were in at the present moment—(renewed laughter)— 1 and Liberals must not, therefore, be surprised if a little dirt was thrown. In conclusion, Mr. Toinkinson said he would. like to see the feudal shackles knocked off the people of the United Kingdom, so that the fullest free trade in land that 'was possible might occur. (Cheers.) Other great measures 'that would be acceptable were the reduction of the county to the borough franchise, and the adoption of more stringent 'measures for the prevention of corrupt practices at elections, I(Loud cheers.) Mr. LATHAM, in seconding the resolution, said the election in the North Riding of Yorkshire was a highly important one, as being the first fair stand up fight between the land- owner and the land occupier. (Hear, hear.) Hitherto landlords had been in the habit of bringing up their tenants behind them to vote for the Conservative or Whig candi- date, but he hoped the spirit that now animated the Northern 'tenantry would break that combination. '(Cheers.) God grant that the counties might return to the proud position they occupied just before the Reform Bill of 1832, when Liberals were returned in contradistinction of the Tories, who bad been previously sent to Parliament. (Cheers.) The most important question to be considered on the reas- sembling of Parliament was the- alteration in some way of the procedure of the House—(hear, hear,)—and he balieved it very possible that there would be such a combination of Conservatives, weak-kneed Liberals—(hear, bear,)—old- fashioned Whigs—(laughter)—and discontented Radicals on the question as might compel Her Majesty's Government, if they wished to do anything, to appeal again to the constitu- encies, in order to know whether the electors wished Parlia- ment to be a farce or a reality. (Loud cheers.) Cheshire county was never heard inside the House of Commons, and he sincerely trusted that when the time came the electors would do their duty by returning Lilieral representatives. (Cheers.) If such a miracle ever took place as a Cheshire county member speaking inside Parliament, then a similar 'achievement would only have been done once before, and then by a certain animal. (Loud laughter.) He would ask those before him, in finishing his observations, if a small body of men of different parties, and for different objects, 8110111 d be allowed to unite together and prevent the action of Parliament, and to stop measures being passed for which the whole country was asking. (" No," and loud cheers.) Mr. W. S. CAINE M.P., who met with a very cordial re- ception, supported the resolution. While their own future member (Mr. Tomkinson) was speaking, he said, •he was : forcibly reminded of a conversation that passed between a , Conservative and a Liberal some time since. The Tory , asked, " Why do you Liberals, when you get on your plat- ' form, always refer to the past?" The Liberal answered by asking, "Why do you Tories never refer to the past" (a laugh) ? . The answer was that the Liberals had a past of which they were proud, while the Tories had a past of which they were greatly ashamed (cheers and laughter). During the last ten years, for in- stance, the Tories had had seven years of rule, and their record was a very poor one (hear hear.) He contrasted the foreign policy of the Tory Government with that of the present administration, and showed the vast difference which these policies made in the expendi- ture of the nation, and quoted a large number of figures in support of his argument, showing that the expendi- ture under Mr. Gladstone's C'eovernment was much less than. under the Tory Ministry. Then as to the malt tax, the Tories were very fond of posing as the farmers' friends; yet why did they not repeal the malt tax when in power? It could have been easily done for their friends, but it was left for Mr. Gladftone to do, as the first thing when he returned to power. (Cheers.) The Liberal -party were not ashamed of the past, and referred to it with pride whenever they had an opportunity of doing so, while to the future they looked forward with confidence and hope. (Loud Cheers.) The resolution was carried unanrmously.

Sr. HELENS WESLEYAN IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. —On Wednesday evening, Mr. Brearley read a paper on "Inventions" before the members of this association. The Rev. W. G. Pascoe occupied the chair.—Mr. Brearley said that every man more or less possessed the power of inven- tion. He spoke of the wooden skewer, and remarked that probably that article had suggested the übiquitous needle, which had now reached so high a state of perfection. There were in England great drawbacks to those who desired to put their inventions into practical operation, and he instanced the patentee office, and the high fees, as deterrents to those , who wished Eo make use of their inventions. Mr. Brearley I said that the Americans were ahead of us in this respect, the I fees in America being low, which, of course, encouraged the inventive and practical faculties of its people. He gave in- stances of how mechanics, through want of means, were unable to give the public and themselves the benefits of their inventions.—A discussion took place, in which Messrs. Else, I R. Coop, J. J. Cook, Green, and Ackerley took part.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The appointment of Prince Leopold Duke of Albany, to- be a colonel in the army is also gazetted. Last night's Gazette contained notice that at .the end of six days the Speaker will issue a new writ for the vacancy at Preston.
Charles Dillon, of Ballymaeura, was arrested yesterday on a charge of having used seditious language at the railway station, Ball wasloe.
Cornelius Brosnahan, of Ballymaho, county Kerry, com- mitted to Limerick gaol under the Coercion Act on October 21st, was discharged yesterday, by order of the Lord Lieu- tenant.

The Mayor of Birmingham has granted the us of the Town Hall to the Salvation Army for a demonstration next week only on the understanding that they indulge in no open air processions, General Booth having announced after the riot at Sheffied that he want& "a big drum to beat up Birmingham."

A branch railway and a new pier, the former connecting the latter with the Milford station of the Milford and John- stone Railway, were opened on Thursday in the presence of Mr. IV,Davies, M.P., Admiral Stokes, Sir Charles Bright, and a number of gentlemen interested in the development of Milford as a seaport for the Atlantic trade.

The now well-known David Connell, alias "Captain Moonlight," has turned approver against his companions in crime. Connell pleaded guilty at Cork Assizes, on Thurs- day, to a " Whiteboy " offence, and was put back, the Crown counsel intimating that the convict was about to give im- portant evidence against his associates, of whom there are about twenty in custody. . The Miners' National Association have drawn up a circa' a letter to all colliery owners, pointing out that a large per centage of non-fatal accidents prove fatal tNeugh want of proper attention, and they therefore recommend masters to provide a special small house where all needful appliances shall be kept in case of any serious colliery disasters. At the Liverpool Sessions, yesterday, three youths, named Copper, Cuthbert, and Creighton, were charged with frapds ,on an hotel keeper. They ran tiway from home at Carlisle, inrending, to go to London, and travelled to ,Liverpool on the roof of a c trriage of an express train, managing to escape detection. Iu Liverpool they took private rooms in an hotel, and left without paying. A poitinanteau was left behind, hein:t• filled vial bricks and WaNta paper. Th,y returned Louie, being penniless. Sentence was deferred. A crowded meeting of holders of Turkish bonds was held at the City Terminus Hotel yesterday, when the Right Honourable Robert Bourke, detailed the result of his mission to Turkey, and explained the scheme which had been accepted by the Po7te for the liquidation of the bond- holders' claims, details of which haVe been already pub- lished. In some of the later loans they bad 'found that for a £lOO bond the Turks had received from 11 to 25 per cent. An amendment, proposing a committee to draw up an amended scheme, was rejected by the meeting.

Those of the crew of the Dotterel who have been sum- moned to London are two from Devonport and a third from Portsmouth, to give testimony in connection with the disaster to the vessel. The men are expected in London to-day, and a private inquiry will he instituted at the Admiralty as rerding the matter. This course has been brought about by the recent explosion of exsistine seccative on board H.M.S. Triumph, as the account appears to have furnished a true solution of the Dotterel disaster, it being known that the explosive was on Ward, and that some had escaped from a cask.

Last night Mr. J. L. Toole and his company had the honour of appearing before their Royal Highnesses Prince and Princess of Wales and a distinguished and numerous company at Sandringham, the pieces selected being "The Steeplechase," "Our Clerks," and "Ici on parle Frangais." After the performance Mr. Toole and his company sat down to supper. The. Prince of Wales was present, and in a few , graceful remarks, after arinking Mr. Toole's health, thanked the company for the pleasure they had given, and compli- mented Mr. Loveday for the way in which the arrangements had been carried out.

Miss Bridget McCormick, a member of the Dublin Ladies League, was arrested yesterday in Tuna, where for the last ten or twelve days she has been on special business in connection with the League, and working energetically. The authorities were made aware-of her movetnents, and after a private enquiry kad been held in the Police Bar- racks a warrant was issued, and Miss McCormick was arrested at Shank's Hotel. She was asked to give bail for her future good conduct but refused, Ind was therefore com- mitted to gaol for three months. An immense crowd fol. lowed the lady from the hotel to the barracks, and cheered the Land League loudly. Three farmers named Denis and Michael Murphy and Andrew Macnamara, who took part in the demonstration, were arrested, and sent to prison for six months on refusing bail. The four prisoners were con- veyed to Limerick.
MR. GLA.DSTONE ON THE NORTH RIDING ELECTION.

The following letter has been received from Mr. Glad- stone's secretary :-101, Downing-street, Whitehall, 16th January, 1882. Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Gladstone to thauk you for your letter of the 11th inst., and the reports which you have sent him in connection with the contest in the North Riding.. Mr. Gladstone has learned waif/great satisfaction that Mr. Rowlandson has been so favourably received, as he feels a cordial interest in his success, both bccause he is a Liberal and because he belongs to that body of tenant farmers whose interest Mr. Gladstone desires to see amply, as well as ably, represented in Parliament at this juncture, which is so important to them.—l am, Sir, your obedient servant, HORACE SEYMOUR —Both parties are actively pursuing their canvass in this constituency, and both are hopefully looking to a buccessful resnit on Tnes- dav next.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

SOCIAL GATHERING OF WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS.—A very successful gathering of teachers of the Trinity Wesleyan Sunday school took place on Thursday evening, when about 100 teachers and friends assembled in the schoolroom adjoining the chapel for social en- joyment and recreation. The idea is a somewhat novel one for Frodsham, as gatherings of this kind are of rare occurrence, and social life appears to have been confined, in the past, to very narrow limits. The rising g. neration are, however, of a different opinion, and the results will doubtless be shown in the future, by the prosperity of the institutions to which they belong, arising from the prac- tical application of the well-worn axiom:that " unity is strength," and in Sunday school work, particularly meet- ings of this kind, are essential. The schoolroom had under- gone an entire metamorphosis, and under the busy hands of the ladies and their willing assistants, presented the appearance of a family parlour, the walls being hung with pictures, texts, flags, ttc., and decorated with an abundance of evergreens. Refreshments were plentifully provided, and quite a museum of curiosities and works of art repre- senting all parts of the world had been contributed by the teachers and friends, in fact we were not previously aware that Frodsham was such a treasure house. The following ' programme was gone through during the evening :—Open- ingbbymn, " Hark what means;" prayer and address t y the Rey. J. M. Bamford; part song' "Spring ;" report by the Sunday school secretary, Mr. Samuel Sharp; pianoforte solo, Mics C. Kent ; song and chorus, Mr. J. Jones; part son', "Softly falls the moonlight ;" pianoforte duet, Mr. Albert Walker; song, "Remember now thy Creator," Mr. James Kent ; part song, "Lovely night ;'; song, " Naza- reth," Mr. Albert Walker ; address by Mr. Proude. Miss C. Kent and Mr. Albert Walker accompanied efficiently throughout. The part songs were rendered by the Misses Edmonds, Ada Turner, M. Walker, L. Proude, and Messrs. Thomas Sant, James _Kent, John Jones, and D. Maddock.

PROPOSED NE )y CHURCH FOR DIITTON.—The parish- ioners of Dutton, in the district of Little Legh, have for some time felt the want of a new churchi in place of the present somewhat dilapidated iron church, and a meeting was held at Dutton, on Tuesday, to consider a design, which had been prepared by Messrs. Li naker and Davies, architects, Frodsham. The proposed church is in the late perpen- dicular or Tudor style and consists of nave, toaccommodate 150 persons, chancel, vestry, and organ chamber. The ex- ternallralls will be built of patent bricks, and the windows will contain tracery formed of terracotta. The gables con- sist of English oak framing, the interstices being filled in with white cement panels. The roof will be covered with red tiles, and at the apex of the west gable an oak turret for one bell, and surmounted by a vane will be erected. It is to be hoped that sufficient funds will be forthcoming to enable the parishioners to commence the work in a short time.

FRODSHAM CATTLE MART.—Mr. J J Steward held his usual fortnightly sale at the Queen * 's Head Hotel on Tues- day. The stock corriprised 25 fat and store beasts, 80 prime fat sheep, and 10 fat calves. There was a numerous attend- ance of buyers from Warrington, Runcorn, Chester, and the stock realised good prices. Three fat beasts from Mr. E. G. Steward fetched £l7 is, £lB 2s ed, £25 15s; two fat beasts from Mr. W. Lowe, of Sutton Hall, were sold for X 24 and £2l 103; calves averaged 30s; two pens of sheep from Mr. J. Higson made 65s and 68s; 20 fat Scotch wethers from Mr. J. Andrews averaged 38s; 20 Leicesters from Mr. E. G. Steward averaged 425; other sheep sold from 35s to 70s.

BREA= or PROMISE.— At Lancaster Assizes, on Tuesday, before Baron Pollock, in the case of Cummings v. Brumwell, which was an action to recover £l,OOO for breach of promise of marriage, and £7OO for goods sold and de- livered, Mr. Russell, Q.O ,stated that with the consent of both parties the record would be withdrawn, a settlement having been come to. The parties reside at Kendall, plaintiff being a widow and defendant a young medical practitioner. The sum agreed upon was £BOO, to include an costs.
