div.head: THROUGH THE HEART OF ENGLAND.
div.p: THROUGH THE HEART OF ENGLAND.

A trip to the Midlands by means of the Midland Railway from Warrington via Manchester, is one of the pleasantest rides that the lover of the picturesque could possibly enjoy. No sooner does the train leave the great " Cottonopolis than the scenery becomes gradually more and more interest- ing and beautiful, until at length we find ourselves-entering that singularly beautiful county of Derby. This part may well be called "The heart of old England," but it is a very stony heart indeed for we are rapidly whirled along for many miles over viaducts, through tunnels cut through limestone rocks, whilst the pretty views of quarries, mills, factories, reservoirs, lovely valleys, carefully laid out burial grounds, rivulets, &c., as we emerge ever and anon from each tunnel cannot fail to interest every beholder. Although whea at the Peak Forest the eye of the traveller sees scarcely a single tree or shrub but the fields divided by stone walls, yet he very shortly afterwards finds lying tefore him, as he passes Bakewell and a number of other small stations, a magnificent panorama of lovely green slopes dotted with trees, and as he comes nearer the well-known and popular resort called Matlock Bath—the English Switzerland—he is here able to gaze upon a landscape which is not to be surpassed by that of any other part of the kingdom. From here to Derby the traveller on the Midland Railway, especially if he has any poetry in his soul, is able to enjoy a succession of views of the most beautiful scenes of hill and dale, rock and river, peak and forest, as must fill him with delight, and cause him to be loud in his praises of the beauty of our dear "old native land." Arriving at Derby, we remain here for a few moments for refreshments, and we think that a word of praise is certainly due to the Midland Company for the way in which they have endeavoured at this and other large stations on their system to minister to the wants of the public. Temperance men and others who are not abstainers from intoxicating drinks have complained, loudly and lowg, about the extortionate charges made at railway stations for tea and coffee and other beverages, and the obstacles that are thrown in the way of drinking either of the former after you have had them. At Derby we find pretty little page boys attending every train with cool and refreshing glasses of milk and other refreshments at moderate charges, and, judg- ing from the quick sale, they art heartily appreciated by the occupants of the various carriages. Leaving Derby, we proceeded along part of the beautiful and fertile valley of the Trent into Burton-on-Trent, where there are so many well-known brewers. Here we could not help noticing the charming scenery which lay on both sides of the line all along to Birmingham, the great metropolis of the midlands. Shortly after leaving Barton we bad a fine view of the pretty villages of VVichnor, Walton, and Barton, the former of which is situated on an eminence in a beautiful wood tract of country. We had also a good view of the Trent as it runs under the line between Crosall and Wichnor. In the church of Croxwell, with its ivy mantled tower, which is seen embowered in trees, is a beautiful work of Chantrey, the sculptor, and near the edifice is a tumulus, enclosed by trees, full of human remains. Shortly afterwards we passed over the Tame, and entering Staffordshire, came to the ancient town of Tarnworth, with its venerable castle, of which we had a splendid view from the line. Here also there is a handsome old parish church, several chapels and an almshouse endowed by Thomas Guy, the founder of Guy's Hospital, in London, and near here is Drayton manor, the seat of Sir Robert Peel. It was here that the Earl:of Richmond halted on his march to Bosworth field, thus to inspire his forces for the coming conflict :

This foul swine Lies now even in the centre of this isle, Near to the town of Leicester, as we learn. From Tamworth thither is but one da* march, In God's name, cheerily on! Courage, friends, To reap the harvest of perpetual peace By this one bloody trial of sharp war." Rapidly passing through a beautifully wooded and well cultivated country we soon got to Castle Bromwich, a small town seated on a gentle acclivity and surrounded by pictu- resque scenery, where we were told was the seat of the Earl of Bradford, and shortly afterwards entered Birmingham, "the toy shop of the world." Having spent a few hours here visiting the various public buildings and some of the principal manufactories' we resumed our journey again by the Midland line through scenery very similar to that which had gladdened our eyes between Derby and Birmingham, now on our way into Worcestershire. Leaving New-street Station, Birmingham, which it should be noticed witnesses the arrival and departure of above 300 trains daily, by a tunnel we shortly emerged upon a network of sidings and junctions across the Great Western and London and North- Western lines, and soon came out to Camp Hill, Black% ell, and Barnt Green, where we saw some elegant mansions belonging to the Birmingham merchants, and reached Bromsgrove, pleasantly situated on the banks of the Salwarp— a place that was a royal demesne at the time of the Conquest. After leaving Bromsgrove we arrived at Stoke Works and Droitsvich, the former being celebrated for its large salt works, and the latter for the brine springs with which it is supplied, and where it is estimated that 30,000 tons of salt are annually produced. The water from the springs is more strongly impregnated with brine than sea water by running over salt rocks that underlie Droitwich. The water is pmmped into large pans which are then placed over large fires, and as the water evaporates the salt crystalizes first appearing in light flakes upon the surface and afterwards settling in solid masses at the bottom of the pans. It is then placed in wooden moulds and conveyed to the drying room or store. These springs are visited by large numbers of invalids yearly for their medicinal properties. Leaving this town, we in a very short space of time reached Wo-coster, one of /the most ancient episcopal cities in the kingdom. Here we spent some time in visiting; the ancient cathedral, numbers of churches, the Trinity Col- lege, the Grammar School, the Guildhall, and wound up with a row upon the Severn, which runs through the city, and is crossed by a bridge of five arches. We returned to Birmingham and back to Warrington by the same line of railway, heartily enjoying the scenery on the other side of our route quite as much as we had done that on our outward journey, and feeling satisfied that those friends who love the beautiful cannot do better when visiting the Midlands than _
to go through the heart of England, as we did, by way of the Midland line, when they will say that the half of what they will see and enjoy has not been told them. RAMBLER.

div.head: PRESCOT CONSERVATIVE an BILL
div.p: PRESCOT CONSERVATIVE an BILL

The first annual ball under the auspices of the Peescot Conservative Club took place in the Association-room, Derby-street, Prescot, on Monday night, and was in every respect, so far as appearances were concerned, a complete success. The principal object of the club in giving the ball was to bring the members and their friends together for the purpose of spending a pleasant and enjoyable evening on the "light fantastic toe," and it is pleasing to notice that this desideratum was fully achieved, the invitation meeting with a ready and courteous response. The room was very tastefully and artistically embellished for the occasion with evergreens of various kinds, plants, &c. In the niches of the wall at one end of the room were hung the portraits of the fate Lord Derby, Lord Beaconsfield, and the present Marquis of Salisbury, each of which was surrounded by a wreath of 'Ye', that of the Knowsley lord being surmounted by an) imitation of the crown. In the niches at the other end of the room were affixed escutcheons of the arms of Great Britain, while the doorway and passage leading from this portion of the room were literally blocked up with a very nice collection of stove and greenhouse plants kindly lent by Mr. W. L. Evans, chairman of the club. Festoons ccn- structed of small links of different coloured paper were sus- pended in a graceful manner from the four corners of the room to the 32-light chandelier in the centre, wbilethe walls were adorned with similarly made material. Altogether, the general appearance of th, soon was vastly improved, and when dancing commenced later in the evening the sight was animated and picturesque in the extreme. The decorations were carried out by a committee consisting of Messrs. P. G. Twist, E. Range, W. Lloyd, H. McCarthy, and Jos. Preston, and reflected much credit upon their taste and skill. Messrs. J. and F. Williams, builders, erected the band stage, and covered it and the seats round the room with red cloth. In an adjoining room refreshments to suit the tastes of the most fastidious individuals were provided by Mr. W. E. Beau- mont, of the Royal Hotel, whose catering for public enter- tainments is highly appreciated. There were two cloak rooms, one for the gentlemen and the other for the ladies, the former being in charge of Mr. James Ronghsedge, manager of the club, and the latter, under the care of Mrs. Mercer, of Derby- street. Altogether the arrangements were of an admirable character, and nothing was left undone by the committee that was thought would conduce to the success of the under- taking and add to the comfort and convenience of the dancers, of whom there were over 100 present, including Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., and Mrs. Evans and party, Mr. Thomas Evans, Mr. A. F. Evans, Mr. and Mrs. J. D. Banks, Mr. and Mrs. F. H. Kendall, Mrs. Miss and Mr. Driffield, Dr. Hall, Dr. Henry Gerst and Mr. W. Gorst (Huyton), Dr. S. Green and Mrs. Green, Miss Nellie Coates, Mr. J. T. Hall, Mr. F. Smith, Mr. James Be Ty, Mr. Henry Cross, Mr. J. K. Slack, Mr. and Mrs. Beecham and friend, Mr. Joseph Preston and Miss Pibus, Mr. John Goldsworth, Mr. William Goldswortf., Mr. Clegg (St. Helens), Mr. C. S. Worthington and Miss Berry, Mr. Charles Barlow,Mr. F. Evans, Mr. Lacklend, Mr. and Mrs. P. G. Twist, Miss Twist, Mies E. Critchley, Mr. H. McCarthy and Miss Brandretb, Mr. C. Dyson and Mr. S. Dyson, Mr. C. W. and Miss Brown, the Misses Baker (Woolton), Mr. Roby, Mr. Foster, and Mr. J. Hubberstev (Rainhill), Mr. A. Scarisbrick, Sze. Dancing commenced about half-past eight and was kept up with unflagging spirit till about four o'clock the following morning, the music being supplied by Martin's quadrille band, of Liverpool. Dr. Hall officiated as master of the ceremonies and per- formed the duties with his usual tact and skill ; and was ably supported by Mr. Wm. Lloyd as deputy MC., and everything passed off satisfactorily to all. A word of praise is due to Mr. Edmund Range, the secretary of the ball com- tnittee, for the zeal and assiduity he displayed in his endeavours to make the ball a success._

----- Writing to a Welsh farmers' club, Mr. C. R. M. Talbot, M.P., remarks that in his opinion the creation of small freeholds would be a serious blunder. Ile adds his belief that farmers' clubs would gain nothing but lose something by adherence to the Farmers' Alliance.

div.head: LANCASHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.
div.p: LANCASHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.

The General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the Hun- dred of West Derby were commenced on Tuesday, in St. George's Hall, Liverpool. The Earl of Derby presided, and the following magistrates were present :—Sir Richard A. Cross, M.P., Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss, Sir Thomas Earle, Lieut.-Col. J. Irtlancl Blackburn, M.P., Messrs. J. A. Tobin, C. Bright, T. Comber, W. Smith, H. B. Gilmour, T. H. Ismay, R. Nicholson, J. Pearson, R. Formby, jun., G. Mc- Corquodale, John Bibby, R. Fletcher, T. Knowles, M.P., T. J. Gillespie, John Hayes, H. Bleckly, H. Perkins, W. B. Forwood, H. Bright, F. Hollins, W. C. Holt, G. Artingstall, C. Barnes, T. Brocklebank, A. Castellain, R. Withers, E. K. Muspratt, P. Stubs, R. D. Pilkington, jun., J. Prescott, A. R. Gladstone, W. J. Fernie, W. Dent-Dent, and D. Gamble. The calendar contained the names of 53 prisoners, of whom 42 were charged with felonies and 11 with misde- meanours. The educational description of the prisoners showed that 17 could neither read nor write, 7 could read, 23 conld read and write imperfectly, while 6 were not educa- tionally described. The noble Chairman, in charging the grand jury, said he was happy to be able to inform them that the calendar on the occasion of the present sessions was an unusually short one. They had not more than about one-half the number of cases that came before them on a recent occasion of the same kind. Forty-two persons were charged in the calendar with felon- ies and eleven with misdemeanours. Whether that veri, considerable diminution in the cases arose from accidental circumstances, or was really a decrease of crime, was more than he was able to say: but it might be from the short time which had elapsed since last sessions. Whatever the cause might be it was a gratifying fact. All the cases, so far as he was able to judge from the list, were of the most ordinary kind, the majority of them being, as usual, offences against property and charges of fraud by means of false pretences. He was glad to observe that there were no cases of indecent assault; and, on the whole, he might congratu- late them that their labours would be lighter than usual. RATES FOR IHE WEST DERBY HUNDRED. It was agreed to levy the following rates upon the various divisions of the Hundred of West Derby for the ensuing half-year :—West Derby, police, lid in the making a total of £l6OB 2s 7d; Bootle, police, 2d in the £, total £2296 198 81; Ormskirk, police, lld in the £. total £1309 , 2s 43. ; Pres Cot, police, 111 d in the X, total £4027 us; War- rington, police, 41 in the X, total £1462 14s 103.; Wigan, ! police, 2d in the X, total £2676 12s &l; West Derby Hun- dred, bridges, 1-16 d in the £, total £617 Gs lid; West Derby, main roads, Id in the £, total £2487 Cs 46; hundred riots, 1-534 in the -X, total £435 Os 43.. CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.

Capt.ain Moorsom, the chief constable of the county, pre- sented the following report :—I have the honour to lay before you the returns of crime, 6;:c., in the county of Lan- caster police district for the quarter ended 31st December, 1881. The number of apprehensions by the police have been 4613, as compared with 5160 in the preceding quarter, and 4094 in the corresponding quarter of the year before; the decrease of 547 in comparison with the former quarter being principally shown in the apprehensions for drunken- ness (304). common assaults (105), and stealing fruit, &-c. (98); the increase of 519 in comparison the December quarter, 1880, being chiefly accounted for in the increased number of persons apprehended for vagrancy (222), larceny, simple—Summary Jurisdiction Act—(lo2), other larcenies indictable (59), and drunkenness (78). The summonses by the police have been 5173, as against 5426 in the preceding quarter, and 5015 in the corresponding period of 1880, be- ing 253 less than in the previous quarter, and 158 in exc'2ss of the December quarter in 1880, the decrease of 253 being shown in summonses for drunkenness (216) and breach of the peace (47), the increase of 158 being accounted for in summonses for drunkenness (160). The summonses by parish authorities and others have been 5936, as compared with 7796 in the preceding quarter, and 5849 in the corres- ponding period in 1880, the decrease of 1860 being chiefly shown in summonses for non-payment of rates (1329), com- mon assaults (276), and breach of the peace (46), the increase of 87 being more than accounted for in summonses under the Elementary Education Act (194). On the Ist of January, 1882, the strength of the force was reducedly 15, consequent on the formation of a separate police esablish- ment in the borough of Accrington. The present strength of the police force i# 1318 of all ranks, the augmentation sanctioned by the court of adjourned annual session on the Bth September last having, on the 14th of December, received the sanction of the Secretary of State. The general health and conduct of the constables have been good.

div.head: STOPPAGE OF A ROAD AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: STOPPAGE OF A ROAD AT WARRINGTON.

Mr. E. Sutton, barrister, Manchester (instructed by Mr. W. H. Brook, Town Clerk of Warrington), applied "for an order for stopping up the road leading from Howley-lane to the side of the river Mersey on the easterly side of Howley Quay, in Warrington, from the easterly end of Navigation- street to the point at which such road abuts upon or adjoins the side or bank of the river, and for turning and diverting the said road into a new road, 36 feet wide, also commencing at the east end of Navigation-street, and extending to the point on or near the river side to which it is proposed to continue the stopping up of the existing road; and also for an order for stopping up the footpath running from the river side near the westerly side of Howley Quay to a point about 120 feet from the easterly end of Navigation-street, thence along the said street to Howley-lane, and crossing the said lane, thence in an easterly and sonth-easterly direction to the point at which snch footpath adjoins the above-mentioned existing road near the river side on the easterly side of Howley Quay, and for turning and diverting the said foot- path so proposed to be stopped up into a new footpath six feet wide, commencing from the same point, near the westerly side of Howley Quay, at which it is proposed to begin to stop up the existing footpath, and extending northerly in a straight line to the west end of Navigation-street, thence run- ning the whole length of Navigation-street and forming part of such street to Howley-lane, and crossing the said lane, thence continuing along the north side of the proposed new road to or near the point at which it is proposed to con- tinue such new road on the easterly side of Howley Quay." —Mr. Sutton said he believed there was no objection to the application, which was perfectly in order.—Lord Derby: Is there no notice of appeal.—The Clerk of the Peace: We have received no notice, my Lord.—Lord Derby: Then the appli- cation is granted. After the conclusion of the county business, the court was divided for the trial of prisoners, Lord Derby presiding in the first court and Mr. Edward Gibbon in the second. SENTENCES AND ACQUITTALS.

Frank Minton, 19 years of age, labourer, pleaded guilty to having, at Warrington, on the 24th December, stolen three pairs of boots, the property of Elizabeth Booth, and was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment. Thomas George Moore, 18 years of age, a labourer, and William M'Allister, 16 years of age, labourer, pleaded guilty to haying, at Huyton, on the 30th December, stolen a flannel shirt, the property of Charles Green. There were previous convictions against both prisoners. Moore was sentenced to nine months' and WAllister to six months' imprisonment with hard labour. Patrick Edwards, 21 years of age, tailor, pleaded guilty to 1 having, at Warrington, on the 26th October, stolen five 1 sovereigns in gold and 26 shillings in silver from the dwell- ' ing-house of Michael Gannon, and was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment with hard labour. In the case of Sarah Kerley, 15 years of age, of no occu- pation, who had been charged with having, at Widnes, on the 6th June, broken and entered the dwelling-house of John Ward and stolen two pieces of lace and a gold ring, the pro- perty of Mary Ana Hampson, the grand jury threw out the bill. THE IDENTIFICATION OF THIEVES AT WARRINGTON.— Joseph Corcoran (22), a labourer, and Thomas McHugh (30), hod-carrier, were charged with having at Warrington, on the 29th November last, feloniously stolen three grey mixture woollen shirts, the property of Thomas Dale, of Warrington. ' Mr. E. Sutton (instructed by the Town Clerk, Mr. Brook) prosecuted on behalf of the police. Mr. Gee appeared for McHugh, and Mr. Lancaster for Corcoran.—Samuel Daul- man, oil and colour merchant, 112, Bridge-street, Warrington, said that on the afternoon of the 29th November he was en- gaged in putting in three squares of glass in a warehouse on Frar's Green. He Saw McHugh came out of Leyland's- yard and go into Friar's Green, where he srood several minutes; when he was joined by a man whose face he could not see, as witness was standing on top of a ladder 14 feet long. He went on with his work, and when he looked again he saw McHugh coming towards him. McHugh passed underneath the ladder; the other man passed on the outside. They then went into Leyland's-yard, and he did not see them again till he saw them in the Police Court. He would not undertake to say he saw Corcoran.—Cross-examined : He thought the man he saw was a little taller than Corcoran. —He could see one man's face better than the other because it was exposed. He had no doubt that one of the men he saw was McHugh. The other man was wearing a scarf and a " billycock." Th 3 man thought he was doing a "clever .bilf by holding down his bead and trying to escape unob- served. His face could not be seen. His attention was not occu- pied too much to prevent him putting in the panes of glass.— Maria Frances Marsh, fustian cutter, of Rose and Crown- street, Warrington, said' Mr. Dale's shop was at the corner of Rosa and Crown-street. On the 29th 'ovenaber she saw the prisoners, whom she had known previously, between three and half-past three o'clock. She was coming down Friar's Gate. McHugh was standing near the provision shop a, the corner. She crossed into Bridge-street, when she saw Corcoran pick up one or two shirts from a hook at the prosecutor's shop door. She csuld could not tell how many. He then put them under his coat, crossed the street, and McHugh, who was standing by the provision shop window, joined him. IWtHugh could easily see him commit the offence. They then went away together on to Friar's Green and into Leyland's-yard. When she first saw Corcoran he was in the act of lifting the shirts from the hook.—By Mr. Lancaster: When' she first saw Corcoran she was about three yards from him.—Mr. Lancaster: Bridge-street is one of your most important streets, is it not P—Witness : Yes, but it is a very narrow street.—Mr. Lancaster: I am sorry for Warrington if that is the case.—Witness said Corcoran was subsequently brought to her house by the police. She recognized him at once as the man who had committed the robbery. A lamp was held before him.—Re-examined: Cor- coran once lived near her, and she frequently saw him and knew him well. Had seen McHugh in the street several times. McHugh noticed her on the day of the robbery.-- The prosecutor said be was a gentleman's outfitter' in Bridge-street, Warrington. On the 29th November he had exposed for sale several shirts which were hanging on the window case outside the shop door. Shortly after three o'clock Constab'e Crickett drew his attention to the shop window, when he missed three shirts. He had seen them about an hour before that time. They had not been sold to

div.head: EXAMINE-R, SATURDAY, JANUARY 21, 1882. ST. HELENS TOWN ouNca.
div.p: THE EXAMINE-R, SATURDAY, JANUARY 21, 1882. ST. HELENS TOWN ouNca.

anyone.—The Chairman: Were the shirts within reach ? Witness: Yes, they were at the bottom of the window.— Ellen, wife of Joseph Lingard, 120, Bridge-street, Warring- ton, said McHugh passed her, carrying some shirting under his coat. He was alone. Cross-examined: Had known McHugh for several years, and saw him nearly every day.— P.C. William Crickett said he arrested the prisoners in Bull's Head yard, off Bridge-street, on the 29th November.—Cross- examined : They asked him what they were wanted for, and he told them he should tell them on their arrival at the Police Station.—Mr. Lancaster, on behalf of Corcoran, said there was no doubt the shirts were stolen. He did not know whether they were taken by McHugh; his friend Mr. Gee would have to deal with that matter. The only evidence against his client was that given by Marsh, who, he admitted, had given her evidence in a highly creditable manner. But she had not seen him for three years previously, and she might have been mistaken as to his identity. He thought the police acted most indiscreetly in not allowing his client to have been selected by the witness from a number of other men; instead of that he WAS taken alone to the witness's house. That was a point to which attention had been fre- quently called in the law courts, and no doubt the learned Chairman would have something to say about the matter. He called Thomas Rush, a rag-gatherer, who said he, Corcoran, McHugh and others were in the Currier's Arms on the afternoon in question from three to four o'clock. They never left him during that time.—Michael Mulkearn, labourer, gave similar evidence.—Mr. Lancaster said there was absolutely no evidence, except that given by Marsh, connecting Corcoran with the robbery. None of the shirts had been traced. What had become of them? Mr. Sutton said the inn referred to was only 300 yards from the shop of the prosecutor, and it was quite possible for the prisoners not only to have committed the robbery, but also to have been drinking with Rush and Mulkearn. Miss Marsh's evidence had certai—ly been very clearly given, and the jury would be perfectly justified in acting upon it.—Mr. Gee, in defence of McHugh, said there was no evidence to prove that the prisoners were companions on the afternoon in ques- tion. The jury must be satisfied that they were not merely companions, but there was actually complicity, or an agree- raent between them that the articles should be stolen, which the prosecution had failed to make out. The evidence, as far as McHugh was concerned, merely rested on supposition. There was a missing link in the evidence, and it was that the shirts had not been found. He contended that the case had sot been carried further than the point that " someone " stole the shirts. Orm of the prisoners, it was said, was seen with some shirting partly concealed under his coat, but he had not necessarily stolen it. He might have been on his way to the pawnshop.—The Chairman did not agree with all that had been said in defence of the prisoners, but there was one point in which he thoroughly agreed, and:that was as to the man- ner in which the prisoner Corcoran was identified. If a correct account had been given of it, he had no hesitation in saying that it was done in a highly improper manner, and, as far as his experience, went, in a most unusual manner. The ordinary and proper way to identify prisoners was to place them amongst others, and let the person identifying them take a fair view. The police should not hold a lamp in front of a- particular person, and ask "Is this the man ?" He could hardly believe that the magistrates had got quite a correct account of the matter; at all events, it was sufficient for him to say that if correct it was a kind of thing that he hoped would not occur again in the West Derby Hundred, in Warrington, or in any other part of the county with which ha had to do. Referring to the evidence ,he said that if the jury believed the evidence of the young woman Marsh, there could, he thought, be only one course open to them, and that was to return a verdict of guilty. Evidence had been called to show that the prisoners were in a public- house at the time of the robbery. He did not attach much importance to it, because they might also have been in Bridge-etreet at the time of the rob- bery, the public-house being so near at hand.— The jury returned a verdict of guilty against both prisoners —McHugh was then further charged with having been previously convicted of felony.—The Chairman, in sentenc- ing the prisoners, said Corcoran had been discharged several times—whether it was owing to his good luck he could not say—but he had now been found guilty. He must say that he thought an improper temptation was held out to people by exposing goods for sale at shop doors and windows. No one looked after them, and there was a temptation to steal. It was at the same time quite true that people ought not to avail themselves of the facility thus afforded. Still the temptation ought to be taken into account in passing sen- tence. He should do so, and as Corcoran had not been pre- viously convicted of a si miler crime he would only be sent to prison for six months with hard labour. McHugh had been several times imprisoned, and he would now be com- mitted to gaol. for 18 months, to be followed by three years' police supervision.—McHugh : Have mercy on us !—Cor- corn : lam innocent, and the police know it. It will do them no good, I can tell you !—The prisoners were then removed.

John Power (17), labourer, was sentenced to nine months, and Robert Power (15), also a labourer, to four months' im- prisonment, for having at Widnes, on the 30th December, stolen a hen, the property of William Harvey. Patrick 111'Loughlin (19), collier, was acquitted on a charge of having at Golborne, on the 18th November, stolen 25. 6d. in money, the property of Ann Pilling. John Houghton (52), labourer, was charged with having stolen at Warrington, on the 26th December last, two cart-arms and two bushes, the property of John Barlow; and James Tomlinson was charged with receiving the same knowing them to have been stolen. Tomlinson was acquitted, and Houghton was sentenced lo six months' imprisonment. Sarah Ellen Ward (14), was ordered to be detained in custody for three days, for having at Widnes, on the 16th Nov. 1881, felonionsly broken and entered the dwelling-house of Elizabeth Jones, and stolen therefrom one pair of clogs, one woollen shawl, one necklet, and fourpence in money the property of the said Elizabeth Jones. * William Winrow (35), labourer, six months' imprisonment for having at Windle, on the 31st October, 1881, broken and entered the shop of William Brown, and stolen therefrom 111 pounds weight of beef.
LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wednesday, Mr. H: H. Lacey presiding. There were also present—Alderman Ciamble; Councillors Hanson, Brook; and Messrs. Sinclair, Cotton, Dromgoole, and N. Lacey.
CHAIRS FOR THE LADIES' ROOM. It was decide to get a dozen chairs (cane-bottomed), at 3s. 10d. each, for the laaies' reading room.

THE COLONEL MAKES AN EXPLANATION. Alderman GAMBLE: I suppose the committee will blame me for moving that the Council should aot sanction the minutes of this committee. It was done simply on the ground that they objected to the words appointing a boy for the library. They objected to the appointment of a boy who was to be free from the supervision of a responsible man. At first the objection was made because it stated that the boy should do such and such work, apparently quite independent of the librarian; and in the second place the resolution was modified a little, but seemed to bear the same interpretation that the boy was to be in some degree free from the super- vision of the librarian, and the Council thought that such a method was not generally adopted by the Corporation in any of the establishments. They thought he ought not to be under the supervision of the committee, but of the librarian. Of course, the librarian is under the committee, and is bound to follow their orders. It is for the librarian to get orders from the committee, but not the boy; and I think the Council will held to the same opinion. Mr. DROMGOOLE : Perhaps leaving out the words will meet the case. It is unnecessary for this discussion to go before the public; it has been Wore the public too much. Mr. SINCLAIR : I move that a boy be engaged as an assis- tant to the librarian at ss. per week. Mr. HANsorn I second that.—Carried. Mr. DROINIOOOLE : There was really no question in this committee about the direction of the boy, and it was on account of the peculiar circumstances of the case that the committee felt themselves placed under at that time. Mr. CRACK said that a resolution was referred back at the last meeting of the Council in reference to having news- papers in the reading room of the library. Mr. BROOK: I think it is a great mistake. Mr. DROMGOOLE : How much do the newspapers come to altogether? Mr. BROOK: Two shillings. I think it was a great mis- take to refer that resolution back. For one thing, what are you going to have in this room (ladies' room)? You ought to have the Queen and a few other papers. Mr. DROMGOOLE : I think, Mr. Chairman, if you will allow me, it seems somewhat unseemly to raise a discussion so soon after the action of the Council, and if you allow the matter to stand over a little time perhaps those gentle- men of the Council who take a generous view of this matter will reconsider it; and in a little time the matter may b 3 re-introduced under fresh auspices. The CHAIRMAN: I think myself that as a great majority approved the resolution it will be best to allow it to drop for a time. _ _ _
Mr. SINCLAIR : I suppose it is a polite way of informing us to let it stand over a little. It can be brought on again by this committee. _

Alderman GAMBLE: The Council believe that this com- mittee were about equally divided. Mr. DROMGOOLE : There was no hand held up against it. Mr. SINCLAIR: But there were only two for it. Mr. DROMGOOLE : If the committee had no objection, I would put in this room papers until the Council took the matter in hand; and perhaps somebody else will do the same. Alderman GAMBLE: Well, I wouln't do that. You can- not suppose that the Council object for the sake of the cost of the papers. The Council certainly do not object to the introduction of those papers on account of what they would cost, but they did not think it would conduce to the pur- poses for which the library was intend.d. .MR. DROMGOOLE : The papers are for the reading room, and the reading room should not be confounded with the library. It is the only reading part of the library. Alderman GAMBLE: The borrowers is the reading part of

the library. Mr. BROOK: What must we have in this room (ladies) ? Mr. SINCLAIR : For the books they want to read. Mr. DROMGOOLE : They get their books and go away. But it is no use carryine• on this unseemly discussion. Mr. COTTON: There is another question likely to arise— the political• view—and we should want the whole boiling of it. Mr. HANSON' : I think it is better not:to:discuss it. The matter dropped. BARE BOOKS. Several rare and valuable books on local history obtained from Mr. Percival Pearse, of Warrington, were placed on the table for the committee to make selections therefrom, and it was ultimately decided to obtain " Espinnass's Lan- cashire worthies," and " Portico of fragments. Mr. DROMGOOLE said that Mr. Pearse gave them a quota- tion that a fac-simile edition of the early copy of Shakspere originally at £B, could be obtained for £5. The book was a reproduction of the 1620 edition. That edition was photo- graphed, and the book in question was a reprint from the photograph. It was a large quarto edition. Mr. SINCLAIR : I don't think we have antiquarian people amongst us to raise money for it. Mr. DROMGOOLE : I think we ought to have it in the library. Mr. Corrox : Of course it is not the copy of Shakspere simply, but a curiosity. Mr. DROMGOOLE : That's it; the curiosity, and to students of Shakspere it may be interesting to look back and see how the original was written. They are very scarce now. We erquired of the librarian at Wigan, and he said they had great difficulty to get one. That is the reason why we urged Mr. Pearse to search one up. Mr. BROOK: I move that we get one. Mr. DROMGOOLE seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr. Sinclair did not vote. USEFULNESS OF THE LIBRARY.—MEMBERS WINGS CLIPPED. Mr. DROMGOOLE : There is a mistaken notion in the Council, and perhaps in the minds of others in the town, as to the value of this library as an institution—perhaps I may be permitted to use the words given to me by a gentleman whom I met in the street the other day, "a humanising institution." There was much negligence shown in its im- provement and extension. Perhaps many persons are of the idea he is. If we had a turn—stile at the door, or a sort of tell-tale, so that the number of persons who visit the library could be ascertained accurately without any chance of the figures being trifled with, I think it would be a fact to show to the public the usefulness cf the institution. To mem- bers of this committee who are earnestly and devotedly giving their time day by day to the building up of the library and promotion of the usefulness of the reading-room, it is somewhat painful io have every little improvement they suggest, every little condition they feel necessary, carped at and curtailed, and sent back and all that sort of thing •, and the feeling of uncom- fortableness raised in the town in consequence. It is the only institution in the town finding intellectual food for the general public, and I think it ought to be supported as far as possible instead of having obstacles thrown in its way, and contentions raised about nothing. The CHAIRMAN: It is a very valuable and humanising institution, and the point mentioned by Mr. Dromgoole has been several times before the committee, but it has not met with general approval. It would be of great interest to those who were very much interested in the library. Mr. HANSON asked if that could not be done by means of a boy. The course raised by Mr. Dromgoole would entail structural alteration, and the members of that committee knew that there had been considerable feeling in the Council in regard to structural alterations originating in that com- mittee. He thought that was unnecessary, as a record might be kept by a man or a boy. Mr. SINCLAIR : I am not aware that the Council have re- fused to spend money on the library. I know there has been discussion about something which belonged to other departments. There is nothing extravagant in the altera- tions made by this committee. The whole outlay with respect to dry rot has been attributed to having arisen from the action of this committee, but with the exception of those comments I know not anything. As the gentleman who moved the rejection of the minute of the Library Committee, has just said, he did not do it on account of the expense, but on account of unsuitability. Mr. DamtdooLE : But the Council did not say why it did not confirm the recommendation; and I think remarks have been made in the Council which have been intended to apply to other than structural alterations, which have taken place in this room and corridor. We have been charged— and I think our chairman could not help but feel it—with tinkering for four years. Mr. SINCLAIR : But the alterations did not:occupy all that time.

Mr. DROMGOOLE ; But these alterations have only been going on three months, and the tinkering is said to have gone on for four years. Mr. HANSON said both the Parliamentary and the Library Committees had the matter in hand and the two things were mixed together. Mr. SINCLAIR said the Library Committee did not order and never had power to order structural alterations and he remembered Mr. Hart showing them the plan which had been before the Parliamentary Committee, for their approval. Mr. NEWTON LACEY : That is to say no work saving been done here can he charged solely to the -Library Committee. Mr. SINCLAIR : That is so. Mr. DROMGOOLE : Supposing Mr. Sinclair hag expressed pretty accurately the opinions of this committee, I will allow the mattr to stand over a little time. (A laugh.) A PRESENT.

It was stated that Mr. Sinclair had presented to the Library 50 volumes of the "Minutes of the proceedings of Institution of Civil Engineers, with abstract of lectures," and an index to the whole. Some discussion ensued as to whether the books should be placed in the Lending Library or in the Reference Library, Mr. Sinclair preferring the former, but attaching no con- dition to his gift.—Mr. CorroN moved that the work be put in the Reference Library.—Mr. DROMGOOLE seconded the motion which was negatived. THE RULES.

The committee decided (subject to confirmation by the Coutcll) to alter the number of days allowed for reading a book, from 14 (4oys to seven days, and a halfpenny instead of a penny fine for each day over the seven. It was also decided "that at the end of the 4th week after the issue or renewal of a book, application be made to the borrower's guarantors for the return of the book, or payment of its value, and for payment of all fines." It was decided "that all books be returned for the annual stocktaking, of which due no.ice will be given."
LIBRARIAN'S REPORT.

The LIBRARIAN reported that 1,431 books had been issued from the Lending department during the month, and they were classified as follows :—Biography, 2; travels, 172; natural history, 122; science, 139; theology, 179; poetry, 74 ; fiction, 2 ; political economy, 6 ; fine arts, 27 ;. general literature, 708.—Sunday attendance bad been as follows: 116; closed ; 53; 61; total, 235; average, 78 3. PAVING, Sx., COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of the committee was held on Wed- nesday afternoon, Alderman Johnson presiding. There were also present the Mayor (Mr. B. Pilkington), Alderman Gam- ble, Councillors Jamison, Foster, Baxter, Wilcock, Belsher, Walker.

• Mr. CRIIIC (Deputy Town Clerk) submitted resolution of the Gas and Lighting Committee in regard to the land pro- posed to be taken as a store yard in the gas works yard. It was resolved that the Surveyor and the Gas Works Manager a.rrange as to the exact area to be taken, and that a plan be kept in the Surveyor's office.

div.head: ALLEGED ILLEGAL SEIZURE OF GOODS AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ALLEGED ILLEGAL SEIZURE OF GOODS AT ST. HELENS.

At the Liverpool County Court, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, and a common jury, the case of Jennings v. Hickey, Dobson, and others, was heard. The plaintiff, Albert Jennings, a grocer and provision dealer, lately cirrying on business in a stall in the Market Hall, St. Helens, claimed compensation from the defendants for wrongfully breaking into his stall and removing and selling his goods. Dr. O'Feeley (instructed by Mr. Nordon) appeared for the plaintiff; Mr. W. F. Taylor (instructed by Mr. Riley) appeared for Hickey; and Mr. Riley represented the defendant Dobson. The case for the plaintiff was that in the beginning of July, 1880, he borrowed £3O from Mrs. Hickey, one of the defendants, at whose house he lived. In acknowledgment he gave her a document, stating that he agreed to give her 'full and complete control over all his goods and stock-in-trade, situate on the stall occupied by him." On the 10th July the plaintiff found himself in difficulties, and decided to file a petition for liquidation of his affairs. He went to Mr. Riley, solicitor, but he came to no arrangement with him on the subject ; and he went to another solicitor in Liverpool. On the samg afternoon, when he returned to St. Helens, be found that his stall had been broken into and the whole of his goods had been taken away. These, together with a pony and harness, had been sold, the value put on the goods and the pony by the plain- tiff being £lBB. He afterwards discovered that the goods had been seized by Dobson, an auctioneer, at the instance of Mrs. lEckey, who acted under the document he had given her for the loan.—Mr. Jennings, after giving evidence to this effect, was cross-examined by Mr. Riley. He said he was perfectly sober on the day of the seizure, and had been sober for a long time previously.— Mr. Riley : Had not your drunken habits been spoken of ? —Plaintiff: That was the first few months I was in busi- ness.—Plaintiff denied that he had given instructions for anyone to say that the goods in the stall were not his in the event of anyone coming in his absence, or that he had said the goods would "come in again," when his bankruptcy business was over. Before his petition, he did not sell to his neighbours in the market at ridiculous prices.—An assistant named Fairbrother, who had been in the employ of the plaintiff, said that the latter had sometimes come to business in a drunken state, and this had had the effect of driving his custom away. There was about £5O worth of stock on the stall.—Further evidence having been given, Dr. O'Feely addressed the jury on behalf of the plaintiff, arguing that the statement as to the loss of his goods that he had made was evidently the statement of an honest man who attempted to arrange everything for the benefit of his creditors in a time of difficulty. Even the rtsult of this action would be, if a verdict were found in his favour, for the benefit of his creditors.—Mr. Riley was about to address the jury on behalf of Swift, when Dr. O'Feely said he would withdraw the case against that defendant. Mr. Riley accordingly was not allowed to address the court on behalf of Swift. The case had previously been withdrawn against Mr. Riley him- self, who was originally one of the defendants, and the judge held that there was no case against Dobson, and the only remaining defendant was Mrs. Hickey. His Honour pointed out that the.seizure of the goods on the stall was justified under the document held by Mrs. Hickey, but in relation to the seizure of the pony and harness, and some other goods at the plaintiff's house, there appeared to be no defence.—ln respect to the seizure of those goods not at the stall, the jury found a verdict for the plaintiff for £2o.—His Honour refused to make any order as to costs.

div.head: LITER ITUR F.,
div.p: LITER ITUR F.,

THE VERY WORDS OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST (Lon- don : Henry Fronde, 7, Paternoster Row).—ln this little work issued from the Oxford University Press, we have the Saviour's own words gathered from the four Gospels accord- ing to the authorised version (1(311), with marginal quota- tions from the Revised Version wherever the latter version has thrown a distinctly fresh or stronger light on any pas- sage. The idca of gathering together the very words of Jesus is a very good one, and no doubt will be of use to many, and especially to invalids, that being the intention of the publisher. To aid the memory, an sffort has been made to group together those short detached passaaes which bear on the same subject, setting forth as far as possible each topic on its separate page, whilst a useful index of subjects and texts is appended. The work is well printed, and strongly and neatly bound in cloth.

div.head: BOUND TO RAVE FEVER.
div.p: BOUND TO RAVE FEVER.

Mr. tun' submitted plans of a proposed improvement of the brook near the branch of the London and North- Western railway, lying between the Hardshaw Brook chemi- cal works and Mr. Kurtz's works. He said that both com- panies had each agreed to defray one-fourth of the cost, but be had not yet received a definite reply from Mr. Kurtz. The total cost would be about £4OO. Dr. JAMISON said the whole question of tho brook wanted looking into. When the brook was flooded the outlets of the sewers emptying into the brook from Westfield-street to Spray's Bridge was covered with water; the sowage matter was unable to proceed, and consequently they were bound to have fever. According to the report of the officers they were bound to have fever.

The MAYon.: The evil exists, according to you, round about St. Thomas's Church; those are the sewers to which you refer ? Dr. JAMISON : Chiefly. The Maxon. ::Exactly. Then between Spray's Bridge and Westfield-street, where these sewers have their outflow into the brook, we have spent a great deal of money in putting in an intercepting sewer. What is the use going on spend- ing money if it is not effectual ? Why has it not had due effect? There is plenty of fall from Westfield-street bridge to take away all the water. Mr. WALKER remarked that all that property was built too low.

Mr. HART said they could not possibly begin at a peint, say, in Westfield-streeet, and give a sufficient amount of fall for the brook. There was no fall at all. There was only 16 inches of rise between Westfield-street and the length of the brook to Spray's Bridge. Out of that, 12 inches was take,n in Talbot-street. In time of flood and heavy storm the water rose higher than the outlets of the sewers, and the sewage matter was held in, and mud got in. An intercept- ing sewer was put in, and that did a little good. The best thing to do would be to lower the brook at Boardman's Bridge, cut a straight line from there to Ashcroft's Bridge, terminating at the intersection of Hareshaw and Sutton Brooks, near Mr. Kurtz's waste heap. Then follnw the line through the culverts in the gas works yard, besides Messrs. Dogfish's works, and so on through Westfield-steet to Spray's Bridge. This would cost £4,800.—1t was remarked that would be a great undertaking. Dr. 3.Amisox did not think they ought to do it in piecemeal, as they were bound to have fever unlesJ something effectual was done.

The MAYOR said they ought to do what they could, but as to being " bound " to have fever, a comparison on the question of fever would be made between St. Helens and other towns. Besides, the most part of fever recently was round the Town Hall. . Mr. BAXTER: Do you believe in that prognostic that we are bound to have fever? Dr. JAMISON : I don't see how it is going to be stopped according to the statements made here by the officers. The MAYOR: How many of the sewers are blocked up? Mr. HART: Every sewer in the town. These sewers are now totally lost in mud. The MAYOR: Why are they not cleared out in dry weather? Mr. HART: There are many hundred tons of sand— The MAYOR: Many hundred tons of sand! Mr. HART: Yes, I have no doubt. The MAYOR: Why are they not flushed regularly? Mr. HART: We have no means. We can only put a a three or four inch hydrant in, and this is of no use what- ever. _ _

The MAYOR did not think them was anything like the quantity of sand in the pipes, and if they were flushed and looked after in dry weather things would be a great deal better. But because everything was not exactly what sani- tarians would wish in regard to the brook, that ought not to prevent them from doing the' very best they could, and it seemed to him that measures could be taken to clear out the mouths. The CHAIRMIN: Have any of those sewers been con- structed since you came? Mr. HART: Not one of them, sir. They would he done in Mr. Ross's time. Mr. Hart mentioned that Lowe-street sewer was altogether insufficient in size and capicity for the work it had to do. At the MAYOR'S suggestion a special meeting of the whole committee was ordered to be convened.

div.head: WIN SFORD.
div.p: WIN SFORD.

_ OVER SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.—In anticipation of the election of this Board, a circular has been signed by many of the ratepayers calling on the Mayor to call a public meeting to consider and arrange, if possible, to make the necessary changes so amicably that a contested election may be avoided, and the pockets of the ratepayers be saved at least in that instance, if not by the Board's working. SALT TRADE.—The past year gave us in the early part a demand for salt which taxed the full capacity to supply. In I fact, at one time there was not a sufficient supply of brine to I meet the wants of the manufacturers. However, the exports in autumn became circumscribed owing to the extraordinary storing season, and the consequent loss of much of the ship- ping usually available for salt exportation. The loss of the ships will be seriously felt, so that friends abroad need not calculate upon the ordinary tonnage as per sailing ships, but take that imposed by steamers which may have to supply their place. Prices have ranged at a very low figure during the year, since there is no arrangement among the salt pro- prietors to accommodate the supply to the demand. In spring and summer the price of common salt was usually oscillating between ss. and ss. 6d. at the works, but later on it fell to 4s. and 4s. 6d. Calcutta salt has become very cheap, owing to a great extent to the indifference of shippers to quality. This may be visited upon the Calcutta market by a corresponding appreciation. At least experience has taught that lesson. India stands foremost in the list of our customers, and if the long-looked for and and promised total equalisation of the duties takes place, it will give a great additional stimulus to our trade, especially as the rapid in- crease of internal communication by railways will vastly develope the trade with the seaboard. America has upon the whole presented but very unsatisfactory results. The great rise in freights has operated seriously upon the salt trade. It has given the inferior domestic American produce an additional chance to get to the seaboard, and acted in reality as if, the already highly protective tariff had been doubled. The Baltic has not had a full supply of all it wanted. The scarcity of ships and the high rates of freights base contributed to this. Most of the ports have no stock, and a large siring demand may be looked for. The chemi- cal trade has in the aggregate taken full quantities. Mid- dlesborough and Fleetwood seem to prepare to enter actively into the arena of competition with our Cheshire salt fields.
THE WIDNES TEMPERANCE
ISSION.

On the evening of the 13th inst., the meetings in connec- tion with this mission were continued, a lecture being deliv- ered by Bro. M. Jones, of Liverpool, on " Keep to the right." The Rev. J. Tessyman presided.

The CHAIRMAN said he had been a teetotaller rather more than half his life, and still kept on in the good old way. (Cheers.) He did not know that he could be considered a good specimen of a teetotaller from a muscular point of view, but he believed that he was healthier than most men. He had never had a serious illness in his life, and during the whole time be had been in Widnes he had not missed a service through ill-health. The LECTURER said there were many topics to which the words " Keep to the right" might be applied, but it was his purpose to use them as a peg whereon to hang a few observa- tions on the great question of temperance. He was brought up in a drunkard's home, and could speak of the evils and horrors of the traffic from early experience. But that night he should like to call their attention to two points in particular in which the phrase "keep to the right" could be associated with the drink traffic. He should like to see them keep to the right nationally and individually. But were they as a nation keeping to the right? It was not right when they had in their midst public-houses and gin-places which, if placed in a line, would reach from Land's End to John O'Groat's. It was not keeping to the right when they had 600,000 drunkards in their midst. It was not-keeping to the right when they had 43,000 inmates in their lunatic asylums, and a million and a half of paupers. It was not keeping to the right when, in the city of Liverpool, they had 2,500 pnblichouses, and only 222 churches, or more than ten licensed houses to one houscof prayer! £58,000 was com- puted to be spent every week in strong drink. It wrought evil on every hand; it desolated many a happy home; it ruiled as a nation morally and financially. How was it that England was the last to go in for Sunday closing? Why because the English people loved their beer. He appealed to the young men and young women to put their shoulders

_ _ to the wheel and to work with heart and soul for the tem- perance cause. It was not keeping to the right when young men spent their evenings in public-houses. He next spoke of being in a Liverpool Police Court the other Monday, when there were 150 men and women of all grades of society brought up in custody—and for no other crime than strong drink. The speaker then dealt with individual drunkenness. Five years ago 94,903 persons were prosecuted in England in one year for drunkenness, and out of this number 22)560 were women. And the acts which a drunken woman would do were terrible to contemplate. Not long ago in Liverpool a woman took the corpse of her dead baby out of its coffin, and sold the coffin for strong drink. People said, "Oh this must be exaggeration. You should not make such statements as these." But they were facts, not creations of the imagination. It was difficult to exhaust the long tale of horrors connected with the traffic in strong drink. Passing on to speak of the week's mission which they had held at Widnes, he expressed a hope that it would prove the forerunner of a grand reformation as far as drink was concerned in that part of Lancashire. (Applause.) He did not doubt that in Widnes, as in Liverpool, they keenly felt the evils of strong drink. The latter town had sometimes been called the black spot on the Mersey, but he did not think it much worse than other places. He only knew one cure for the drink curse. That was total absti-

nence, and the adoption of this principle he urged upon all among them who wished to avoid the pitfalls in their path, and unswervingly "keep to the right." (Applause.)— After a few words from the Chairman, the meeting broke up.

The seventh and last of the meetings took place on Satur- day, when an address was given by Bro. Prescott, of Earles- town, Grand Scribe for the Order of the Sons of Temperance, Liverpool, D.G. Mr. J. Duxbury presided. The Star of Temperance brass band was in attendance, and gave a selec- tion of music during the evening. The CHAIRMAN dwelt upon the evils of drunkenness as they were to be seen in Widnes, and expressed his deter- mination to do his utmost to further the temperance cause. Bro. PRESCOTT then proceeded to deliver an interesting address, in the opening portion of which he gave several examples from his own experience of the widespread evil which accrued from indulgence in strong drink. He next went on to speak of the order NI ith which he was connected, the " Sons of Temperance," and of friendly societies generally. It was very important that the working man should have somewhere where he could safely invest his money; but he cautioned them against friendly societies which held their meetings in public-houses. If they attended their meetings they would find that they would have to spend something in drink for the good of the house. There was another ob- jection against joining societies which admitted drinkers to their ranks. The drink increased their liability. He instanced one composed of 120 members of hom 22 were abstainers. During one year .f.,07 was paid for sickness. Of this the abstainers' share should have been £l7 15s. Bd., but it was only £1 55., so that the drinkers had £l6 103. Bd. over and above their proper share. He thought they would see clearly from this that in a mixed society of drinkers and teetotallers, the latter, while paying an equal sum with the drinkers, did not get their fair share of the benefits. The temperance societies found out this, and the order of Rechabites was established. Shortly afterwards the order of the "Sons of Temperance," first founded in America, was introduced into this country, and it took root 28 years ago, and would now take its place among the temperance benefit societies of the land. He proceeded to quote a number of statistics, which showed that the average period of sickness among the temperance benefit societies during a year was only a third c‘f what it was among those societies which admitted drinkers. During six years the average death-rate ammz the teetotal benefit societies was 1 in 41, but in the otheri it was 1 in 44. He quoted the following recent statistics of the death-rate amongst various classes, which showed the inestimable boons which temperate habits bes- towed. The death-rate among publicans was 44 per 1,000; among the general public 23 per 1,000; among friendly societies all classed together 15 per 1,000; among the Sons of Temperance 8 per 1,000. He thought that these figures proved that in the temperance benefit societies the liabilities were only one-half of what they were in others, and he urged upon all temperance men to join them. If they were paying £5O in sick money elsewhere, in the -Temperance Society they would only pay £25, and instead of paying £3O in funeral money they would only pay £l5. After describing the success of the Temperance Benefit Society in Earlestown, he addressed himself to the young men in the room, and urged upon them the desirability of joining the order of the Sons of Temper- ance. What were the necessary qualifications? Well, they would have to be teetotallers or else they would not hf ye them. Addressing himself to the Good Templars present, he asked_ what were they doing outside the temperance friendly societies? Let them be staunch ;let, them be true; but above all le_t them be out and out abstainers. He pointed out the necessity of young men joining the society at once. After 45 years of age they did not admit them. As to pay- ments they had now adopted the sliding scale. Youths could join their society at 18 years of age, when they paid 51d. per week. In the case of sickness, for the first twelve months they were allowed 12s. per week, for the second twelve months 63. per week, and for the third 33. per week, with £lO at death. He was glad that their order had gained a footing in Widnes. He believed as they had prospered in the past they would succeed in the future. The fight against the monstrous evils of the drink traffic was a hard and uphill one, but he thought they would triumph at last.

For freedom's battle once begun. Bequeathed from bleeding sire t) son, Though often lost, is ever won. So it would be with them. (Applause.) A vote of thanks having been accorded to Bro. Prescott, who briefly responded, and to the Chairman, the proceedings erminated.

div.head: NEWTON AND -EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND -EARLESTOWN.

LECTURE AT EARLESTOWN.—The Rev. M. Jones, of Derby, delivered a'lecture at the Viaduct Institute, Earles- town, on Monday evening, his subject being "Thomas Carlyle." The Rev. M. Dickenson occupied the char. The lecturer briefly sketched the literary career of the "Sage of Chelsea," and gave a number of anecdotes illustrating the idiosyncracies and peculiarities of his grim but lofty char- acter. He also described some of the principal achievements of the great writer, dwelling upon the vivid pictures drawn by him in his "History of the French Revolution," upon the original if Utopian ideas enunciated in his "Latter-day Pamphlets," and of the many and varied qualities which made him one of our greatest original thinkers as well as one of the masters of English prose. The lecture was well attended and listened to with evident interest. The usual votes of thanks terminated the proceedings.

Lord Justice biker took his seat for the first time on Monday in the Appeal Court at Lincoln's Inn, the other judges being the Master of the Rolls and Lord Justice Brett. The court was crowded, amongst the spectators being Lady Holker. Three amateur detectives were remanded at Glasgow, on Monday, on the charge of housebreaking and stealing a gold watch. One of the " detectives " has been successful in arresting several criminals, and only recently he was com- plimented by one of the judges for his cleverness. Whist a passenger train from Liverpool for Manchester was standing in the tunnel near Teviot Dale Station, Stock- port, on the Cheshire line, on Sunday morning, a pilot engine ran into it. Several of the passengers were injured, two of them seriously. For the most part the injured were mem- bers of the Salvation Army on their way to take part in services in Stockport. _

The two Staffordshire farmers, Johnson and Clowes, sentenced some time ago to ten years' penal servitude for t 1;.; alleged mutilation of a farmer named Brooks, arrived at their hoiles on Saturday afternoon, having been. liberated by l order of the ti.tiale Secretary. The searching inquiries made during the past week have fully confirmed the truth of the dying confession of the man ElTOoks, on whose evidence the two unfortunate men were convicted. The meeting between the liberated prisoners and their relatives, after a two years' cruel separation, was of a most touching character. - T t is not known yet whether Johnson and Clowes will receive any compensation from the Government. Apart altogether from the mental torture they must have suffered in their condem- nation and weary imprisonment—" like cold death itself," as they describe it—the men are of course heavy pecuniary losers, and come out of gaol to commence life afresh as it were.

A FACT WOETIT KNOWING.—The recently published re- ports of medical officers of health show that the mild autumn weather and excessive rainfall have produced an unusual amount of scarlet and typhoid fevers throulhout the United Kingdom. There is also in many districts exce,sive mortality from measles and smallpox. Every cautious householder should use reliable preventive measures, and none arc bettee than washiiw with Wright's Coal Tar Soap, recommended alike by the entire mPdictl profession and the public. Let the soap be in every bed-room, bath-rcom, and nursery, and when you purchase, insist noon being supplied with Wright's. Refuse all imitatiens.-4drt.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

It is understood that the application of the tinplate forge. men of North Wales, who had memorialised the Association of Manufacturers, asking for an advance in wages equivalent to the reduction made last year. has been refused. A joint meeting of representatives of the South Wales coal owners and colliers was held at Cardiff on Wc lnesday to consider alterations of the sliding scale. As it was found during discussion that the house coal men came pledged to a certain programme, the masters would not proceed on this condition, and the meeting was adjourned to allow the heuse coal men to consult their constituents.

A correspondent at Oldham says the opinion gains ground that the demand of the operatives for an advance of wages will be postponed to some future time. The movement for the erection of cotton mills at Oldham does not meet with the support expected, and the balance of feeling seems to be against any extension of the spinning power of the district at the present time. A meeting of delegates from all the operative cotton spinners' associations of Lancashire was held in the Spinners' Institute, Blackburn, on Sunday, to consider the question of the wages of spinners of coarse yarns. It was resolved.that the result of the discussion should not be published at pres- ent, but it is to be laid before the different associations, and another representative meeting is to be held in a fortnight to receive reports as to the views of the general body of the operatives.

WAGES IN THE COTTON TRADE.—The committee of the Oldham Master Cotton Spinners' Association has forwarded a circular to its members asking them (Ist) whether they are prepared to give the five per cent, advance in wages asked by the operatives, and (2nd) whether, if it is refused, they are prepared to stop their mills if necessary. it is thought most of the firms will answer "No" to the first question. Many leading limited companies are strongly op- posed to the advaiice.—Recently the committee of the Black- burn Cotton Spinners and Manufacturers' Association re- fused to grant an application for the payment of the wages of absentee strippers and grinders, in full to those who do their work, instead of a deduction of a third being made as at present; they have since declined to receive another deputation for the discussion of the question. The Opera- tives' Association have consequently resolved that no mem- ber be allowed to do an absentee's work except full wages be paid.—A circular enamating from a representative meeting held at the Spinners' Institute, Blackburn, on Sunday, has been sent to each of the local committees of the cotton spinning districts in North and North-east Lmcashire for the purpose of ascertaining the feeling of the operatives in regard to two questions, namely (1) Whether the present state of trade warrants an application to the employers for an advance of wages; and (2) whether it would be advi, able to solicit the employers to pay by indicator or length of yarn spun, instead of weight as at present.
