div.p: L. AND N.-W. EMPLOYES' ANNUAL SUPPER AT WIDNES. This annual dinner was held on Thursday night, at the house of Mr. Gerrard, the Alexandra Hotel, Widnes. The chair was occu )iecl by Mr. Sansom, stationmaster to the company, and there was a goodly company present, consist- ing of representatives of the wagon, passenger, goods, and traffic departments. Inspector Larter tilled the vice-chair. The dinner was served in capital style. After the removal of the cloth, several loyal ard patriotic toasts were given by the vice. chairman. The CHAIRMAN, on rising to propose the health of the London and North-Western Railway Company, said, as he regarded the task which they had been good enough to assign to him that night, it presented no great difficulty,. Happily he had not to handle, as speakers sorlinies nau, matters encircled in doubt and uncertainia'. In speaking upon the topic which he purposed to touch, he should very caref ally avoid the probleint, and deal only with the facts, which were as hard in themselves as the steel which formed the roads over which their fleet engines flew, chasing the dollar across the land with a flight only surpassed by elec- tricity, thought, and the wind. (Applause.) He did not speak of a new floated building or insurance saciety, but of one requiring no persuasive rhetoric to win them to a con- viction of its stability—of the king of railways; and he should only be placing it in a moderate comparison with its rivals when he ascribed to it the figure of Saul among the Israelites. To make the illustration of present worth, he had but to announce that during the last year they had carried no less than 50,000,000 passengers and 35,060,000 tons of merchandise, in this small island, over 35,000,000 miles. Since the birth of the enormous child which came to add to the old world something new 90,000,000 had been expended in its development; and last year their receipts had amounted to more than £10,000,000 sterling. (Ap- plause.) But he had an infinitely greater achievement to tell them of, and he felt a pride in what he was about to say, which could be well understood—tb ey had not sasrificed a single life in a train collision through the entire year. (Loud applause.) This, they would be prepared to allow, was a most satisfactory circumstance, and a condition of things which spoke of a high state of efficiency which would well stand the application of the public gnage, especially if they joined the sentence he had 'just delivered with one of a like import he was able to use 12 months ago on a similar occasion. He could account in some measure for the success which appeared to dance attendance on the company, but which, in reality, was the outcome of strenuous efforts on the part of the employes and compre- hensive management on the part of the directors. He might pay a slight tribute to the high discipline they were under by using it as an argument. Bound hard and fast by the rules and conditions of their service, framed on the gathered wisdom and experience of half a century, they were very ' properly obliged to either act in accordance with them or literally die. No enterprise could get on without the pro- peller of which he spoke. It was an absolute essential, and without it nothing could be effected—it was in fact as indis- pensable to them as to an army before the enemy. No man had lived for four times seven years without being made subordinate to it. A healthy and a heaven born thing, it pervaded all the earth. (Applause.) But there was another agent always working equal in some degree, but in a sense excelling the power of which he had just spoken. A hive of industry was theirs where no man could afford to "case his reputation in his tent," so strong was the desire of the rearmost to come forward; and the ambition for place evinced by all grades in the service was another decided factor of success. They were aware the railway servant was a normal creature (laughter) who must take whatever humour he might be in himself. "Every man in his rumour." (Laughter.) It was their lot sometimes to listen to the complaints of those who talked an "infinite deal of nothing and knew scarcely any periods to their woes." (Renewed laughter.) While, on the other hand, they met occasienally among the travellers such as might be said to possess "a noble and a true conceit of God-like amity." (Applause.) Well, then they had servants with whom the public did not come into contact, and on their vigilance the public life in no small measure hung. He re- ferred now to the signalmen whose cabins of watch, fitted with electric alarums, dotted the land, and shed from their signals the safety lights which regulated the traffic through the live long night, "whilst half the world was in a lonely solemn darkness hung !" and the never ceasing wheels per- formed their ever onward evolutions. Now, a signal speaks; the trains approach; "be ready !" and away flies the intima- tion to the next sentinel. Then after a nearer advice that the coaches have passed the last box, we looked up, and the smoke from the engine, illumined by the blazing furnace, was seen, and the rush and the roar of wheels were heard. So from stage to stage the journey waking the caverned echoes, was pursued—driver, guard, signalman, all alive to the importance of the moment. They were the representa- tives of perpetual motion a feat so difficult of accomplish- ment that it was only effected by the daily sacrifice of life from among the ranks of the workers.— "Each new day, new widows groan. New orphans crop! New sorrows Strike heaven on the face 1" Those who complained against them without cause saw it not—the disinterested felt it not —and those of themselves who escaped, it hurt net them; but there remained the unalterAble circumstance that the myrtled wreathed sword—the peace for which they laboured—the facilities they gave to all to "mingle with the universe "—these objects were not unattended with grief. Their bereaved were acquainted with that—it was of so flood-gate and overbearing a nature that it acted like multiplication, and increased the long deep dirge of the world's woe. (Loud applause.) Nearly every ship that came over the ocean brought them more carrying work, while there were few outward bound vessels that had not amongst their cargo merchandise which had in some form or other passed through their hands. The people of all nations knew of their existence, or those who did not " argued themselves unknown." He urged them individually to per- severance, which had demcnstrated itself to the satisfaction of many to amount to genius itself, and had enabled men who possessed in their presence little or no food for the eye to carry their physical disaclv.ntages to the front ranks of the fight. Aelwith the servant sso with the masters, the motto was "Forward !" Their gigantic enterprise was like a sea for motion—a something that never indulged in abso- lute rest. Like it, they fluctuated while their plenitude of swells rang out the joy bells of the commercial world. By per- suasion they were the prmoters, aye the harbingers of gentle peace, and in times of national emergency they hurried to the seaports their plumed troops, from whence they were wafted to the seat of war. (Loud cheers.) The health of "The Donors" was given by Mr. ASIITON, chief booking-clerk, and acknowledged by Mr. GERRARD, the landlord. The VICE-CHAIRMAN proposed "The Town and Trade of Widnes," which was drunk with much heartiness. During the evening Mr. Lea, Mr. Joseph Howard, and other gentleman favoured the company w;th songs; and the Chairman, who is an elocutionist of the first order, delivered a long recitation from one of the classics in a style which held the company spellbound. The toast of The Press" was proposed by the CHAIR- -I.;' and responded to by Mr. CLomiii, the representative of The Examiner. The proceedings terminated with the toast of "The Host," and the singing of "Auld Lang Sync."

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT,
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT,
MoD.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell (chairman) and Mr. William Bankes. •

OBTAINING MONEY AND GOODS BY FALSE PRETE'SCES.— A young man named Patrick Whelan was charged with having, on the 30th ult., fraudulently obtained from Mary Ellison the sum of 35.; and, on the 10th inst., obtained from Sarah Ann Bolton 40 oysters by means of false pre- tences.—The evidence of Mrs. Mary Ann Ellison, fruiterer, of Church-street; her daughter-in-law, Mrs. Alice Ann Ellison, and Sarah Ann Parr, of Liverpool, showed that the prisoner had worked several years for the woman Parr, who visits Runcorn about three times a week to sell fish. On the 27th ult. she called at Mrs. Ellison's with 12 pounds of dried haddocks. The prisoner saw her leave them, and knew that she had not been paid for them. On the 31st ult. the prisoner called at Mrs. Ellison's shop, and asked for the money owing to Mrs. Parr. Mrs. Ellison gave him 35., and Mrs. Parr was called to prove she had not given him authority to receive the account.—ln the second case Sarah Ann Bolton, wife of William Bolton, oyster dealer, Bridge- street, said that on the previous Tuesday she asked Whelan to go to Mr. William Waterworth's (the Boathouse Inn) to see if he required any oysters. On his return the prisoner asked for a score, for which he paid 10d. He then said that Mrs. Waterworth required 40 more oysters, which were to be opened. She gave them to him, but a short time after- wards found that the oysters had not been ordered by Mrs. Waterworth. She went in search of the young man, and he handei her 10d towards the.ls 8d owing. Mrs. Waterworth was called, and stated that she did not give the prisoner any authority to order the oysters ; and P.C. Kelly said he took him m itocustody.—Prisoner, in reply to the Bench, admitted his guilt n both cases, and added that he did not know what be was doing at the time.—He was committed to the Knuts- ford Quarter Sessions for trial.

A KINGSLEY SON'S LOVE FOR HIS FATHER.—Peter Grice a man about 45 years of age, was summoned by the Run- corn Board of Guardians to show cause why he should not contribute to the support of his father, 'John Grice' of Kingsley, whom his three sons have allowed to become chargeable to the common fund of the union.—Mr. Thomas Houghton, collector to the Board, said the defendant's father had been allowed 3s 6d per week by the Guardians since the 27th November last. They wished defendant, who was one of three sons of the old man, to pay is per week towards the allowance.—Defendant waxed quite indignant at being called upon for such an enormous sum per week, on the ground that he had only 20s. per week coming in, which only allowed him 3s 6d for each member of his family's keep 'after he had paid the rent. He protested that if he were made to pay the is per week all his calamities would come upon him at once !—The Chairman said defendant was bound to support the old man, and an order would be made upon him to contribute Is per week. There were also 13s 6d costs owing, but in regard to these the magistrates would not make any order. STRONG REIVARICS EY THE CHAIRMAN.—Patrick Ford, chemical labourer, was charged with having been found drunk in the Nelson Inn, High-street, on the sth inst.—The case was proved by Inspector Hollingworth, Sergeant Mc- Michael, and P.C. Noden, who said that they had spoken to the waiter in the inn, who acknowledged having supplied defendant with a bettle of spirits, and warned him that he

ought to be more careful. The waiter said, in reply, that he did not notice the man's condition when he entered the house.—Defendant now loudly protested that be as not drunk.—The Chairman: You are one of those drunken ! ruffians that make the very name of an Irishman a by word and a reproach all over the world. There are several con- victions against you, and on this occasion you will be fined 103 and 12s 6d costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. DIURSDAY.—Before Messrs. R. M. Brooke (chairman) and John Brundrit.

STEALING A BASKET OF CLOTHES.—Peter Skelhorn, aged about 50 years, was charged with stealing, on the 18th inst., a basket containing six aprons, a pair of drawers, two shirts, six pinafores, and four handkerchiefs, value 55., the pro- perty of Wm. White, Trinity-street.—The evidence showed that on the previous afternoon the daughter of the prosecutor was taking the clothes to hang out in the open air, when she made a call at a neiolibour's. durinr, which the prisoner managed to steal the basket and its content& 1".. ;le ea en- lug, whilst the prisoner was in the house of Thos. Griffiths, the George Inn, Pool-lane, a man named Patrick Coffey, of. Back Mersey-street, entered and asked Skelhorn if he bad left a basket of clothes at his house that day. At first the I prisoner said he had not, but on Mrs. Griffiths telling him I that he ought to take them back if he had done so, he ac- knowledged the charge. It appeared from enquiries after- wards made that Sktlhorn had offered the clothes to Mrs. Coffey for threepence, who told him to take them to whom they belonged. She gave informatioth to the police, and I Inspector Hollingworth took the prisoner into custody. The fellow told several different stories as to how he bad ob- tained possession of the things, all of which appeared with- out any foundation.—The prisoner elected to be summarily dealt with, and slid that on the day of the offence be and a pensioner who had just been paid his allowance had been drinking whiskey "and everything they could get at."—He was sent to gaol 21 days, With hard labour. RIOTOUS CONDUCT IN LOO:I-STREET.—Sarah Ann Meakin and Mary Ann Wilson, who had been previously convicted, were each sent to prison one month for disorderly conduct in Loch-street, on the previous night.—P.C. Clarke. proved the case.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COUItT,
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COUItT,

MONDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkine_4ton (chairman), and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. BRUTAL ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE. Thomas Goulding, a labourer, Sutton's-lane, was charged, in custody, with committing a savage assault on Inspector Barnett, with a poker ; and also assaulting and obstructing P.C. Brvdges in the execution of his duty.—The Inspector, and P.C.'s Brydges and Murray gave evidence to the effect that on Saturday night the prisoner was found in the streets drunk and disorderly. Brydges took him into custody, on which a large crowd collected. Goulding became very violent, and kicked him in so savage a manner that he became insensible, and had to be carried home. Goulding escaped, with the help of the crowd, and between 11 and 12 at night, the Inspector and Murray went to the prisoner's house, with other constables. On trying to open the door, it was found fast, and on telling those inside that the police demanded admission, they replied that they had lost the key and could not let them in. Another more incautious inmate, said "The first man that comes in we will split his head with a poker." The police ultimately forced the door, on which the prisoner was seen standing in the centre of the floor with a poker in his hand. Goulding immediately rushed at the Inspector, and in the struggle which followed succeeded in hitting Barnett on the head with the poker several times, with great force. He lost a great quantity of blood, but at last succeeded in knocking the fellow down, I and he was taken to the station by some of the other officers. Policeman Murray had a very tough struggle with a man named Tobin, and they both fell to the floor. On the follow- ing morning, the Inspector, who found himself badly hurt, went to Dr. Cooper's surgery. The doctor was now called, and said that on the top of the Inspector's head was a wound about two inches long and one-eighth of an inch deep, and also a contused wound on the back of the head.—ln answer to the Bench, the prisoner said he was not the man who com- mitted the assault. It was stated that he had previously been before the magistrates for drunkenness and assaults.— He was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on both charges.—James Buckley was committed to gaol 14 days with hard labour, for assaulting P.C. Brydges.—The officer said he was taking another prisoner to the station, when Buckley, who was under the influence of liquor, tried to get him away. On proving unsuccessful in this, he hit Brydges violently in the face, and several times on the head; and was only I secured with the assistance of the inspector and other officers. —A recruit in the 3rd Lancashire militia, named Thomas Tobin, was charged with assaulting the inspector and B.C. Skinner, and also with being drunk and disorderly. The evidence was to the effect that the prisoner tried to rescue Goulding from P.C. Brydges and P.C. Skinner, and struck Skinner several times on the face and head, knocking him down. Prisoner then kicked him, and gave him a blow in I the mouth. On the inspector going to the house in Sutton's- lane (as described above), the prisoner was found there, and, before a word had been spoken to him, he gave Barnett a blow in the face with his fist.—Prisoner denied both the assaults, and added that he never saw the inspector on the I night referred to. Every statement that had been made was false.—The Chairman said the offence was a most serious one, and was aggravated by the prisoner wearing the I Queen's uniform. He would be sent to gaol six months, with hard labour.—John Newall was brought up in custody charged with assaulting P.C. Rogers, and doing damage to the extent of is. to his uniform. The officer said that while he was on duty in IVidnes-road on Saturday, night he heard that the prisoner, who lived in Midwood- street, was abasing hi 3 wife. He went to the prisoner's house and met him on the way. On arriving at Midwood- street he found the prisoner's son engaged in a disreputable brawl, and told him that he should report him. While he was talking to the son, the father, without provocation, came up behind and struck him several blows in quick succession on the head. He struggled with the prisoner and in the struggle his overcoat was torn. Police-Sergeant Clarkson subsequently came to his assistance and the prisoner was locked up.—The Bench sent the prisoner to gaol for 14 days with hard labour for the assault, and ordered him to pay Is. fine f9r damaging the coat, with is. damkre and 6s. 6d. costs. ALLEGED STABBING BY A LABOURER.—Martin Walsh, labourer, was charged with unlawfully wounding Mark Walsh, another labourer, by stabbing him with a knife. Complainant said he lived in Cromwell-street, and the prisoner had lodged with him for about seven weeks. About seven o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner was in his his house, and quarrelling with some other lodgers when he asked him several times to sit down and be quiet, but he would not. Prisoner struck a blow at him, hitting him on the left arm with a knife. He went to Mr. Pattison, Dr. Cooper's assistant, and had his wound dressed. Dr. Cooper saw him on the Sunday morning following. He gave the prisoner no provocation.—Dr. Cooper was called and said the wound was not a very serious one, and if taken care of would soon be well. He thought the complainant would be able to work in about three days.—P.C. Graham said be ap- prehended the prisoner who, in reply to the charge, said " Well, I can stand it."—ln reply to the Bench, the prisoner said "We were all in drink, and I don't know anything about it" Ile was committed for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions. A "MOST IMPUDENT BEGGAR.”—John Pembertcn, tleScribed by the inspector as "a most impudent beggar," was sent to gaol 14 days for following his arduous calling near the Catholic chapel in Lugsdale, on Sunday. A PENITENT THlEF.—Sarah Coleman (17) was charged with stealing a dress, value 55., the property of Elizabeth Glancey.—Prosecutrix, who is a single woman living with her parents in Lugsdale, hung the dress out to dry on the afternoon of the 25th ult., and it was stolen, but she did not know who had taken it until Saturday last, when the priso- ner came to her and confessed she was the guilty one. Coleman offered to restore the article if Glancey would agree not to prosecute, but she declined, and told the police. —lt was stated that the prisoner was an orphan, and that, though she had been previously convicted for a similar offence, the prosecutrix did not wish to press the case.— The magistrates said they would give the girl another chance of living honestly, and she would accordingly be discharged. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. H. S. Hall (chairman) and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT Worm—The following were each ordered to pay 55. on the prosecution of the Widnes School Board, who were represented by Mr. G. H. DanhY, their clerk, for not sending their children to school : Patrick Martin, George Hulme, Philip Harris, Andrew Truscott, and John Knockton. Mr. Danby- asked the magis- trates to commit a lad, named John Dwyer, to an industrial school. He was nine years of age, in the habit of taking long journeys without the permission of his parents, and, when at home, of sleeping out in Messrs. Gaskell and Deacon's works. His parents had been fined three times for not senoing him to school, and the Board were inclined to think they had done all that could be expected of them. The magistrates ordered the boy to be committed to an indust!ial school until he is 16 years of age. ALLEGED THEFT FROM A DRAPER'S SHOT. —James Spencer, a stranger, was charged, on remand, with stealing three pairs of stockings from the door of Mr. Richard Barker's shop, Victoria-road. On the hearing of the case at Monday's court, P.C. Murray stated that on Saturday night he was near the shop and saw the prisoner pick up the stockings and walk away. He followed him and took him into t ustody.—Superintendent Barker said Spencer had been previously convicted, and as the officer engaged in the case was in attendance at Liverpool County Sessions, the Bench remanded the prisoner until Wednesday next. A DANGEROUS WOMAN.—Catherine Matthews was charged with threatening to kill Mary Clarke, who is a witness in an important case, which has lately been sent to the Assizes for trial from Widnes. Complainant said that a few I mornings ago, the prisoner came to her house and attempted to force the door open, and on another day she ran her out porfeavpublic-house, ,isnaying she would take her life, and thus en evidence at the Liverpool trial. —Superintendent Barker said this was a case of very serious intimidation, and he requested the Bench to insist upon the prisoner finding very substantial bail. She had only just come out of gaol, where she had been serving three months for larceny, and she had been no fewer than 26 times before the magistrates.—The prisoner denied having threatened eomplainant.—The Chairman said the charge against the prisoner was a most serious one indeed, and she would have to find sureties to keep the peace six months, herself in £2O and two sureties in £lO, or, in default, be sent to prison two months.—Matthews said she could not find the sureties.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 21, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 21, 1882.
PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT WIDNES.

On Tuesday afternoon, a sale of work was held in the pretty scheol-chapel belonging to the Primitive Methodist denomination at Widnes. The building, which has been already described in our columns, together with the freehold site upon which it stands, and the land adjoining, on which it is intended in the future to erect a more pretentious

-- structure, cost a little over £l,OOO, and it is situate in Prin- cess-street. The edifice will accotnmodate 200 people, and there is a debt of about £BOO upon it, if we include the sum of about £4OO which was paid for the extensive freehold. The opening ceremony began at about half-past two, with devotional services, conducted by the Rev. J. Morton, who

presided. . The finiumese observed that he had a Very pleasant duty to perform in introducing to them their friend, Mr. Benjamin Brown, who had kindly consented to address them and de- clare the sale of work open. He (the speaker) was voi:y glad to find that as in order to have a sanctuary, or house of prayer, in whica to worship God, they were dependent upon persons taking certain positions in ceiorch life, to find that they had a class of individuals who were disposed to occupy those important offices. It was, for instance, eery hazardous to occupy the position of trustee but though this was the case, they had a number of people who were ready to come forward and say "Now, if you people will form a society, or coreeregatiou in connection with this house, or hired room, and you feel disposed to build a house for God, we will take the responsibility of trusteeship." He found that whenever a church arrived at that healthy position that they were dis- posed to provide a permanent place of worship, there were a number of individuals who were so inspired with sympathy towards Christ and His cause, and so distinguished by feel- ings of self abnegation, that they at once said, "I am pre- pared to take the responsibility of trusteeship in connection with the contemplated building." When he told them that for the last fifty years the Primitive Methodist denomina- tion had been building at the rate of three chapels per week, they would perceive that the class of individuals of whom he had spoken, andeupon whom they could fall back in such cases, must have been a large one. In this particular case they had £BOO of a debt which had to be borne by a feeble society, but, notwithstanding this, during the time he had been acquainted with the friends connected with the place, and especially with those who occupied the posi- tion of trusteeship, he had. never heard one single word of complaint. On the contrary, they said that they were prepared not only to take the responsibility, but to give to the extent of their ability, and they found that those who were associated with them in the struggling church, were disposed to co-operate and give them their hearty sympathy. Whenever their friends were desirous of making an effort of this kind, whether on a large or on a small scale, they always found, either amongst their own people or within some other section of the Church of Christ, some good friend who was prepared to say "Well, now, if you want my help, I will give it." As he passed along the high- way of life—and he was getting on pretty well now, having been 26 years in the ministry—he found that there was a vast amount of this sympathy on the part of individuals who were in a middle class position in life, and sometimes even in a still higher rank. The other day, they had a meeting at Latchford in connection with his own station, at which one of the speakers paid them the compliment of say- in, that the Primitive Methodists were trying to do a work which no other branch of the Church of Christ seemed to reach. The same gentleman, who was himself connected with the Establishment, remarked to him on the same occasion, that a certain archdeacon had told him that if he left the Church of England, he should join the Primitive Methodists. In conclusion, he might say that the motto emblazoned upon their banner as Primitive Methodists, was "The world for Christ, and Christ for the world." (Ap- plause.) Mr. BENJAMIN BROWN, after a brief reference to his unfit- ness for the task of delivering an appropriate speech upon such an important occasion, said the only reason which induced him to yield to the request of the friends that he would do so, was that he had a sincere desire to help them in their undertaking. (Applause.) They would remember that at the time when they first catne to the decision to erect that building, they offered him the honour of laying the foundation stone. At that date he could not see his way to accept their kind offer, but when they asked him if he would be present that day, he felt he should be very glad to do whatever he could to help them by his sympathy or presence. He deeply sympathised with them in the move- ment which they had started at that place, on the ground that Widnes had need of every effort which could be put forth by the various-denominations of the Church of. God, for the purpose of raising the moral and religious tone of the town. They, as Methodists, and believers in the noble principles of voluntaryism, bad not neglected the claims which Widnes had upon them, for apart from the work of the Established Church, there had been many men in that town whose hearts the Lord had touched, giving them that confidence to which Mr. Morton had referred, which had made them not afraid of taking responsibilities for Christ and for their brethrens' sake. (Hear, hear.) It might not be so well known that there were 13 Noncon- formist places in the town, and these provided for about 14.003 sittings. These centres of Christian influence perma- nently maintained six or seven ministers in the township, who time was entirelydevoted to the service of God ; and, in addition to these, there was a band of about forty local preachers, who, Sunday after Sunday, were doing God's work, not looking for pecuniary reward, but in the fear of the Lord and for the love of souls, giving themselves to their holy toil for the church and the world. (Hear, hear.) The result of this religious teaching, in conjunction with the labours of the Church of England, had been to provide ' sitting accommodation which was above that to be found in the majority of towns in the district—(hear, hear)—espe- cially if they would take into consideration the fact that there was a large Catholic population in Widnes, for which the seats in Protestant places of worship were, of course,not available. This gratifying result had not been reached without strenuous effort, and not by taking heed to the advice of some people that they ought not to begin the erection of a building until they were prepared to pay for it, as to do so was morally wrong, not setting a good ex- ample to the world. What would have been the state of this glorious country to-day if the Nonconformists, when some of them left, and others were turned out of the Church of England, had done nothing in the way of erecting any place of worship until they had had in their hands the necessary money with which to pay for it? Certainly, if such a course had been pursued, the moral tone of our country would not have been what it was. (Hear, hear.) When people said that religious men ought not to under- take responsibilities as to buildings without having the money in their hands to meet them, he asked them in what they supposed the persons they criticised believed. Had they really a strong conviction that the preaching of the word of God was able to save men and women? Did they believe that the establishing of a place of worship in a neighbourhood like that would tend to the development of an improved state of society ; to the benefit of the neigh- bours who attended it, as it would get hold of their hearts and affections, and cause them to do what they could for that cause which had done so much for them? If they were building public-houses, or houses which would spread misery and ruin, and bring mischief, sin; and riot into the habitations about the place, then they would not be justi- fied to ask the people surrounding the building to contribute to the debt which bad been incurred. They, however, knew that the preaching of God's word, and the operation of the Gospel, as shown its the work which voluntaryism had done, tended to cultivate the spirit of liberality and self help. With a just cause, a clear case, and a united people the Church of God had no right to fear taking responsibilities, within certain restrictions. (Applause.) He could quite coincide with the remarks made by the Chairman as to trustees. In connection with the Wesleyan Methodist denomination, he might say they were always successful in finding men who would take such responsibility upon themselves, and not with any expecta- tion of reaping reward through occupying the position of treasurer. It was generally the case that treasurers stood a very good chance of losing instead of gaining in such cases, as they were bound to account for all the money they received; and if they paid for anything and neglected to put it down, they had simply to lose the money. The Non- conformists of Widnes , had no need to be ashamed of the position they occupied, but he trusted that instead of being satisfied with the progress they had made they would make the position they had already attained a starting point for a. new departure. He trusted that the members of the deno- mination he saw before him would be united and pull together. The various branches of the Methodist family in the town were to him very much alike, at least in one thing, namely, that people did not see very many carriages at their chapel doors. It was said that so long as a man was poor he remained a Methodist, but as soon as he got more money, and more pride than religion, then hetwent to the Established Church. kLaughter and applausel They said Methodism was not suited to educated people, as it did not provide the sort ot service they required, and he did not know what beside. (Renewed laughter.) Hewes not really aware how this class of people felt, as he had not got to the point at which they had arrived. He might, however, say he generally found that when a man was anxious to 7et something to do and provide a living for his family, then Widnes would do for him ; hut as soon as he got MI in life the town did not quite suit his wife's health, and his chil- dren wanted more educational advantages ; and somehow they got away and left those who remained with the work, and the rates too. (Applause and laughter.) In conclusion, he had to thank them for the manner in which they had re- ceived him, and the honour they had conferred upon him. He had now to declare the sale of work open. (Applause.) —The CHAIRMAN said he bad been,very much pleased with the stirring and breezy remarks made by Mr. Brown. He did not think that alay of the "men of the cloth" could have done so well.—Mr. LEE moved, and Mr. Duorener seconded. a vote of thanks to Mr. Brown for the services he had rendered, which was passed amidst applause, and the public proceedings terminated. The Christmas tree, which had been presented by Mr. Lee, was ornamented with the usual pretty articles. There were also two stall % filled with a goodly assortment of useful and ornamental articles. The working committee, upon whom has devolved the labour of making the necs.ssary pre- parations for the sale, consisted of the ladies connected with the sewing class. The ladies who had charge of the stalls, including one devoted to refreshments, were Mesdames Lee, Wiles, Buckley, Hill, Drought, and the Misses Pinches, Sutton, Barker, Hudson, Wiles, and Jones.

On Wednesday evening a tea meeting was held in the same place of worship, to which about 150 people sat down. The tables were presided over by the following ladies :—The Misses Hudson, Jones, Wiles, Barker, Sutton, Pinches, and

Mrs. Mullard. Aftea tea the tables were removed, and the room cleared for holding a public meeting. Mr. Marshall occupied the chair, and there were also present the Rev. J. Morton, and Messrs. S. Dwught, T. Rollason, and String-

fellow. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the meeting, made a few brief remarks, and called upon the Rev. J. MORTON, who said he was proud to be associated with so (food an object. He regarded any matter standing, connected with the furtherance of Christ's kingdom as the . _

best object that could engage the mind of any man. (Hear, hear). They were associated with a movement which had for its object the aid of the Trust Fund of the building whose roof then covered them. It was utterly impossiblz

to carry on the good work in which they were engaged without sanctuaries. If they were 'w put forth any efforts to eise the masses, they must have houses of prayer —schools and chapels in which to gather the people. There had been a period in the history of the wo:id when the Primiti:,,e Methodist denomination had a comrneneefnent,

?..-dd when the sanctuary in which they worshipped did not require trustees, inasmuch as it was the earth's grand cathedral—the blue vault of heaven. rt was, however, soon found that as they made converts, they wanted, metaphori- cally speaking, cages for the birds which they caught—in other words, chapels were required to keep them together. Some of the circumstances under which these edifices had
ben built would surprise them. Some little more than 30 years ago there lived in Lancashire a good old pioneer of the Primitive Methodist cause. On one occasion he, ac-

companied by a band of his followers, were singing in the streets, and as the day was hot he took off his hat and closed his eyes. While he stood in this position, a passer-by, either by way of a juke or thinking he was blind, dropped a few ooppers into the hat. He quickly accepted them, re- marking that they would be something towards building a chapel. He and a number of others then commenced the. work; a plot of ground was obtained,:and the building was commenced; but when it rose to the height of a few yards 1 from the ground, work had to be suspended, as the funds were not forthcoming. The old pioneer of the scheme perambu- lated the country in order to get money to carry on the Work. In the course of his peregrinations he becamw acquainted with a farmer who promised him a sovereign. He accord- ingly went to the farmer's house, but invariably found him away. One day, however, as he was walking up a hill, he saw the farmer and hastened towards him, when, to his sur-

prise, on reaching the top of the hill the farmer was nowhere to be seen. On examining the vicinity, however, he found him hiding in a large open drain. On being caught the farmer paid him the sovereign, and with the help of that and many others, a place of worship was subsequently built. He (the speaker) thought that was proceeding under difficulties. The work commenced then had been steadily progressing, until at the present day there was scarcely a village in Eng- land where no Priniltive Methodist chapel existed. (Ap- plause.) Another instance of the peculiar circumstances under which some of the chapels were built was in the case of a little village in Lincolnshire. The parson and the squire happened to have a quarrel, and the squire, in a tit of revenge, gave the Primitive Methodists, who had previously only held meetings in cottages, a piece of land on which to erect a chapel. It was built, and he had preached in it many times. The motto which had floated on the banners of the pioneers of the movement was a glorious one. "Christ for the world, and the world for Christ." They knew that the world was in need of Christ, and they considered it their duty to tell their less fortunate brethren about Him. It was a very pleasing that the motto had not yet gone out of exis- tence ; it was still on their banners, and they were now as strong as ever in their determination to win the world for Christ. Some people thought that the old-fashioned way of preaching the Gospel would not accomplish its object. Roman Catholicism was rife in their midst, and scepticism appeared to be on the increase. They were inclined to fear that those pictures of the world bowing down to the name of Christ were all myths, but he had no doubt in the matter, as the decree had gone forth that the uttermost parts of the earth should be the inheritance of the Son. He was sorry to make the statement that the chapel or school was £BOO in debt, but he had no fear about its removal if every one would do his or her best, and he hoped every one present would undertake to do this. The CHAIRMAN remarked that he hoped with a little patience and perseverance the debt would soon be removed. Some time ago a debt of £9OO rested on the chapel at Hutchinson-street, but with a little energetic work this huge incubus was removed in about five years. and the chapel now stood upon freehold land, free from debt. (Hear, hear.) He had not the shadow of a doubt aboutthe removal of the debt if they would be men and pull together. Mr. T. ROLLS SON said it was very encouraging to the active workers to see so many present who sympathised with them. It had been hinted to him that the debt resting -on the chapel was too large, after what had been given to the fund in subscriptions, but it must be understood that the amount was originally £1,200. They had raised £4OO, and now the £BOO was what remained. The building they oc- cupied was only intended for a Sunday school, and not for a chapel. They had sufficient land at the front of the school to build a very commodious place of worship, and that was their intention as soon as it was practicable. He urged all to do their utmost, as their work could not be accomplished by a few. They could not all labour in the same way, but if they were all willing there was always something for them to do. Mr. S. DROUGHT, in the course of a few observations, said he was happy to state that the Sunday school was pro- gressing, they having gathered around them a considerable ! number of children from the vicinity. The object with which it was held were their intellectual advancement and spiritual good. lie thought it was a great acquisition to a neighbourhood to have a place of worship in it, for he could not think of anything more gratifying to the eye or pleasing to the senses than to see the house of God in their midst. The opportunity of coming together for the pur- pose of singing the praises of God, and listening to the words of Divine truth, was also a great boon. A cause which had for its aim the gratification of the wants of the , soul was one well worthy of support, and he sincerely hoped that all present would see fit to help in it. The CHAIRMAN said that the sale of work, together with ! the proceeds of tea party, had realised £3O for which he ' desired to thank all who had helped in the matter. The usual vote: of thanks were then accorded, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) and the Ex-Mavor (Councillor Fairclough.)
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) and the Ex-Mavor (Councillor Fairclough.)

THE SWEET' WHO PULLED HIS WIFE OUT OF BED.— John Cartledge was charged with having, on the 12th and 13th instants, assaulted and beaten his wife, Mary Cartledge. —Prosecutrix said on Wednesday night prisoner came home drunk, about half-past ten o'clock. She put his supper on the table, and sent one of the children for a pint of ale. Prisoner commenced calling her "all sorts of names," and continued to do so until about two o'clock on Thursday morning, when he caught hold of her legs and pulled her out of bed.—The Ex-Mayor: Did not you think he had had enough when he came in drunk withnut sending for more 2 Prosecutrix : He said what he would do if I did not send for drink.—Prisoner complained that his wife was always on to him "when he went into the house, and that she last week "slat his machine" into the street. He also com- plained that there were too many sweeps in the town, and Mr. Hunt promised to look after some of them.—Prisoner was fined 40s. and costs. UsING OtscENg LANGUAGE. Three youths named Maguire, Kilroy, and Curley were summoned for having, on the 11th instant, made use of obscene language in Bridge- street.—P.C. Bruen proved the case, and said the language used by the defendants was most filthy.—The Chief- Constable said the police tried as far as they could to sup- press this bad language, but they had now and again to bring the offenders before the magistrates to show them that they could bc dealt with.—Major Cartwright: The only way to Stop it is by conviction.—The Mayor remembered that seven or eight years ago a similar ,thing took place in the town, and the magistrates inflicted penalties which stopped it.—The Chief-Constable : We have never had such youths as these here before.—The defendants were each fined is. and costs, or seven days.' STREET OBSTRUCTIONS.—Peter Baguley was charged with obstructing the thoroughfare in Golden-square, on the 17th instant, by allowing his horse and cart to stand there an un- reasonable time.—P.C. Hollingwerth proved the case.—Mr. Hunt said the defendant had not been before the Bench since 1878. He had been in Zululand since that time, and had been invalided home.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs.—A boy named Critchley was fined is. 6d. including costs, for obstructing the footpath in Winwick-street by wheeling a barrow laden with coal thereon. KEEPING AN UNREGISTERED LODGING—HOUSE.—Bridget Fleming was summoned for keeping lodgers, on the 9th instant, without being registered.—lnspector Church proved the case, and the Bench imposed a fine of ss. and costs, or, in default, seven days' imprisonment. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE PROSECUTIONS.—SeveraI persons were summoned by Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, for neglecting to send their children to school, and were dealt with as follows :—John Wilcock, Atherton-street, case adjourned; Joseph Ashurst, Twiss-yard, fined 55.; John Duffey, Bakehouse-yard. 28. Gd. in three cases ; George Ashurst, Old-road, 58.; Wm. Evans, Old-road, 55.; Wm. Blanchard, Bank Quay, ss. in three cases; Mary Ann Gee, Glasshouse-row, 23. 6d. TuEsim.y.—Before Major Cartwight, Alderman Davies, and Councillor Monks.

INDECENT BEITAIIIOUR.—Annie McCarty was charged with being guilty of indecent behaviour in Golborne-street, on Monday evening—On the evidence of P.C. 29 (Hennessy), the prisoner was committed for one month's imprisonment with hard labour. " Jusm OUT FOR A WALK."—George Dutton was charged with being a suspicious character, and loitering in Bewsey- road, at a quarter past three o'clock that morning, with intent to commit a felony.—P.C. Monaghan observed the prisoner loitering about Bewsey-road at the time stated, and on speaking to him he said he had "just come out fora walk." He reported the circumstance to Inspector Proffit, who ordered him to lock the prisoner up.—Mr. Hunt : He lives on beer chiefly.—Alderman Davies: Is not this Tatney ?—Major Cartwright : No, this is a rather better , looking man than Tatney.—Mr. Hunt: He is often taken for Tatuey, and gets many glasses of ale in consequence.— Alderman Davies (ironically) : It is a great shame. I think we ought to send him to prison for getting beer on false pretences.—Major Cartwright (to prisoner): Don't you think we should be doing you a good turn by sending you for three months.—Prisoner : Bless you, it would kill me ! I promise you faithfully I'll be better.-Major Cart- wright : We will forgive you this time.—Prisoner : Thank you, sir. God bless you.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOTAL ABSTINENCE SOCIE tY.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOTAL ABSTINENCE SOCIE tY.

ANNUAL MEETING. Although well advertised, the announcement of the annual meeting of the above society brought together only a moderate audience at the Public Hall, on Wednesday evening. Mr. John Naylor preside.l, and there were also. present :—Mr. Thomas Whittaker (ex-mayor of Scarboro'), Mr. Wm. Neild (Reading), Mr. Thomas Hardy (Manchester), Messrs. B. Garnett, D. Garnett, W. Darbyshire, T. Birchall,
J. Toft, Thomas Prince, Thomas flail, Edward Twiss, John

Greening, C. Plinston, The CHAIRMAN said he would not take up the time by making a speech, as they had several gentlemen present who had come specially to address them. He, however, alluded to the report, which would be read by the secretary, and said

- - he was under the impression they might have done more, and he hoped in the coming year they would be able to do more than they had in the past. As a temperance society they found their operations very much nullified by the increased number of houses opened for the sale of intoxi- cating drink. They were not at all a political society, and he hoped they would not think he was a strong party man, but he must say that that Bill of Mr. Gladstone's that had practically converted every available corner shop into a house for the sale of intoxicating drink had increased the vastness of the trade, and had done a deal of harm to the country. It had affected the operations of their society to a very great extent, inasmuch as it affected the women and children. It struck them a blow in a very tender part; and one of their resolutions that night was, he believed, that they send a message to Mr. Gladstone stating that they were . .

quite tired of this sort of thing, and that they must have a change of the law either by him or some one else. (Applause.) Ihe SECRETARY then read the annual report, which was as follows :—lu placing their 47th annual report before the public, after another twelve months' work, the committee are compelled to ask themselves the questions: Have we carried out the power placed in our hands in a satisfactory manner? and What success has attended our efforts? We are deeply sensible • that we have been found wanting in many respects, and that had greater diligence been given to the work, a larger measure of success would have been ours We congratulate the friends of temperance that we have passed the time when such associations as curs were looked upon with derision and dis- trust. It is now beyond the age of conjecture and experiment and is established as an institution, which occupies a dis- tinguished place in active Christian philanthropliy, as the handmaid to religion and the honoured instrument whereby thousands are preserved in the path of virtue and sobriety. This society has helped to bring about this shange of opinion to the best a its ability in the town and neighbourhoal. We have been encouraged in our undertakings by the marked success which has attended them, and by a steady increase in our operations, indicating the growth of popular opinion, and a wider and more earnest appreciation of the movement in the churches and Sabbath schools of the town. We have during the year had fairly successful meetings, several of which deserve special notice. The series of meetings held on the 11th of April, commenced with a conference of ladies in the afternoon, which was thoroughly appreciated, and will long be remembered by the ladies of Warrington, for the earnestness of the addresses of the deputation from the British Women's Tem- perance Association. The tea meeting following, proved to be more largely attended and successful than any for several years past. The addresses after tea, by Mrs. Parker, Mrs. Lucas, and Mrs. Sauthworth were listened to with great interest and profit. The United Band of Hope entertainments, two of which were given in the Public Hall, were declared on all sides to be a success, and were heartily enjoyed by the children of the various Bands of Hope in the the town and district, 16 of whom took part in the proceeedings. As a result of these meetings, each society has been aroused to a greater activity and earnestness, and societies have been established at other schools an exemplification of which may be found in the Parish Church Mission and the St, Paul's Bands of Hope. The choir, led by Mr. Thornton, sang with creditable precision and efficiency, and added greatly to the interest of the meetings. The Alliance meeting of the 9th November, was presided over by Mr. P. Rylands M.P., and ably addressed by the Rev. Canon Barker, J. H. Raper' Esq., and Wm. Hoyle, Esq., as deputation from the Central Office, and also by several local ministers and gentlemen. We have also had several open air meetings, addressed by Mr. C. H. Murray and Mr. Goad, which have been appreciated. The number of pledges taken has been at public meetings, 1513; British Workman Public House, Horsemarket-street, 132; Bridge-street, 73; other books, 63 ; total, 424. We tender our very sincere thanks to all who have given us assistance either financially or otherwise, and in conclusion express our gratitude to the Giver of all good for:the success which has thus far attended our efforts, and we would earnestly commend our work to the prayerful, sympathy, and co-operation of all Christians. The safeguard offered by such societies cannot be doubted. The temptations sur- rounding us are numerous and ensnaring, and the adoption of the pledge of abstinence arms us with a most powerful weapon of defence against the foe. In the past God has greatly blessed the enterprise, much success has been achieved; but there yet remains hard persevering effort before victory is obtained, and England's curse driven from our midst. Until that time the committee desires to zeal- ously labour on believing that the Lord of Hosts is with us, "the God of Jacob is our refuge," and that with His blessing the remainder of the work will soon be accom- plished, and we shall be able to turn from the horrid and awful past to the pure, peaceful, and happy future "When drink no more shall blight and ruin spread, Nor the nation mourn for sons to slaughter led."

And see the springs of life and feeling, and intelligence renewed on every hand, health, industry, and prosperity glowing around us. Mr. R. GARNETT said he had listened somewhat atten- tively to the result of the labour done during the past 12 months, and he confessed the only weak point in the report seemed to be the absolute result which had been achieved by the labour put forth. He did not think they had much in the shape of labour in temperance work—he meant that which used to distinguish the cause 20 or 30 years ago. One reason why they had so little, or rather less, was the fact that there were more people temp,rately inclined, and the result was they did not meet with that opposition which was so , healthy years ago in stimulating effort. He thought it would be one of the best things that could happen if they had a little mere of it. The whole question had assumed during the last quarter of a century a very different position to that which it occupied 25 years ago. It must be patent to all that those who ridiculed the question 25 years ago spoke favourably of it to-day, and in many cases accepted it. That was one of the risks they ran; they wanted opposition. But they were pleased to see that the question was being taken up, and that it was no longer a very creditable thing for a man to be able to drink eb, three, or four bottles of wine at a sitting. (Laughter.) He had heard of such a thing, al- thoughhe had never seen it done. But the previous night he met with a remark by a very successful physician who said it was impossible in the present day for a man to take two bottles. He accounted for that by the increased culture of the intellect. It was not good for the brain, and throughout the length and breadth of the land men were not physically capable of taking so much as they used to do. A great deal had been done to promote antipathy to liquor by the posi- tion which the medical men themselves had taken; and it was a very gratifying thing that to-day, throughout the length and breadth of the lap.d, intoxicating drink was not recommended as a medicine to such a large extent as it used to be. In conclusion he moved the adoption of the report. (Applause.) Mr. E. DVSS seconded the adoption of the report. He said although, as Mr. Garnett had said, the labour might not be so energetic at present, yet a degrie of satisfaction arose to his mind, and to that of many of the friends who had been engaged in the work that had been carried on during the year, in the fact that the labour had not been un- productive. Though the number of recruits was not s ery large still that number in the past history of the movement would have been very significant. It was perhaps gratify- ing in some respects that they had not got the opposition spoken of ; and in other respects it might serve the purpose of stimulating friends of the movement were there more oppo- sition. But there was a degree of confidence in the minds of the people generally that those who had adopted absti- nence principles had quietly maintained their position, and were satisfied with the progress of the efforts put forth. He felt pretty well assured that there never was a period in the history of this great movement when so much work was being accomplished. Public opinion in favour of the move- ment was progressing, he was happy to think, more rapidly than it had done at. any past period. (Applause.) He felt pleasure in seconding the adoption of the report, and said though the product of their labour might not be so large, he was pleased to think it had not been lost, and that there were some who would be gladdened by it during the remainder of their lives. (Applause.) The report was adopted. Mr. TRO/sfAS HARDY, who appeared as the representative Of the United Kingdom Alliance, then addressed the meeting. He supposed that most if not all of them would be aware that that orgaliisation differed very much from the organi- sation whose anniversary they were met that evening to cele- brate. It differed from that organisation inasmuch as it was not necessary for persons becoming members of the United Kingdom Alliance to take the total abstinence pledge, though a 'very large number of those who were associated with the movement, those who constituted the backbone, were persons who had taken the pledge of total abstinence. He thought that a very wise step, and if all reformers only took the trouble to apply the broom to their own door step first they might depend upon it that reform would be much more easily and much more speedily accom- plished. (Applause.) He had been a total abstainer for more than 36 years. (Applause.) The circumstances associated with the movement were very different indeect when he took it up. There was more novelty associated with meetings of this kind, and consequently greater crowds came to look at them, and to hear what they had got to say for themselves, and what they had got to say on behalf of their subject. That novelty had now passed away. They had filtered down to sober facts, and the people connected with the movement had become satisfied as to the ground which they occupied, and people outside the movement conceded the whole of their argument, and so it was. perhaps, they had the indifference which they otherwise would not be well able to account for. After pointing :out that the object of the Alliance was to make a demand upon the Government that houses that were said to be public houses should not be planted, as they had too long been, without the public sane-

Mr. T. BIRCHALL briefly seconded the motion, Mr. W. DARBiSHIRE rose to propose the following tees.o- carried, the meeting terminated lution :—"That it is desirable to give legislative effect to the I just and reasonable principle embodied in the Lc-cal Option Resolution, passed on June 18th, 1880, by conferring upon local communitiea the power to protect themselves from the operation of the liquor traffic; and that copies of this reso- lution be sent to the Premier and the Home Secretary." He which Was said he had a map of the township of Texteth Park, Liver- pool, which contained some of the most important informa- tion that he reinembered, showing the reason why the Legislature should pass a bill during the next session, to reduce the number of public houses if the people in the district • wished them to be reduced. The map was drawn up through the instrumentality of several members of the Board of Guirdians in Toxteth Park, Liverpool, because those gentlemen had from time to time attended to give reliet to the persons who applied for relief, and they found out that year after year nearly all the paupers came from a certain part of the Union. They could not tell at first how it was, and they instituted an inquiry as to the number of public-houses in that locality. They found in the one part, with a population of 25,000, the number of public-houses was 100, and the number of paupers who applied for relief was 011, or one pauper for every 28 of the population. In another part there was a population of 45,000, the number of public-houses was the same as in the first case, 100, and the number of paupers applying for relief was 542, or one for every 80 of the population. In the third part there were no public-houses at all, and in that district there were 50,000 inhabitants and only 45 paupers, or one for every 1,000 of the population. (Applause.) That showed to everyone that where the temptation did not exist there was comparative sobriety. He wished the Government could see its way to remove the temptation, and then he thought there would be very little drunkenness. He then referred to what took place at the Warrington Board of Guardians a fcm weeks ago. A discussion arose as to whether the inmates of the Workhouse should have beer at the ratepayers' expense or not. It was decided that they should have beer to dinner on Christmas Day, although some two years ago the Board passed a resolution that no alcoholic drink should be given to any inmate of the house, except the medigal officer recommended it in case of sick- ness. But although there was no sickness in the Workhouse at Christmas, they broke through the resolution and gave beer at the expense of tie ratepayers. He was opposed to the inmates having beer, because of the resolution the Board had passed. But he was opposed, ridiculed, and buffetted by one of the oldest mem- bers of the Board, who, in a sarcastic, ridiculing manner said, "Oh, I hear my friend Derbyshire goes on the stump I now. (Laughter.) I often read his speeches in the news- papers, but it took me some time before I could understand that he was the man who made them." (Laughter.) Not only did the ordinary members of the Board laugh at him— and he sat:there as simple as a lamb brought to the slaughter— (laughter)—but ministers of the Church of England laughed at him. He was a laughing-stock. He did not know whether Mr. Garnett called that opposition or not—(laughter) —but he felt it to be opposition. He felt it so now. time wention, and at the next meeting the same member was not satisfied. There was a discussien about the quantity of liquor consumed. He (Mr. Derbyshire) made some remarks, and at that meeting the member he had spoken of said, "Oh, aye, Derbyshire goes on stump. Derbyshire quotes epitaphs. I wonder where be gets them from." He felt that was opposition, too. He wondered what the Board of Guardians had to do with Derbyshire, whether he was on the stump or whether he was off the stump. (Laughter.) It was no business of the Board of Guardians, but the chair- man, instead of calling the member to order, laughed and chuckled, and thought it was a tit-bit. (Laughter.) The words he had quoted were the words of one of the oldest members of the Boarct of Guardians, the words of a gentle- man who once filled the position of chief magistrate of the borough of Warrington, the words of a gentle- man who no w sat occasionally at the Borough Court and fined ss. and costs poor fallen humanity for getting drunk, and who buffetted and ridiculed him for try- ing to persuade people not to get drunk. (" Shame.") But as Mr. Garnett and one of the previous speakers had said, a little opposition might do good. He did not think he would have been there that night if it had not been for that. little opposition. (Applause.) He felt stimulated by that little opposition. (Hear, hear.) It had made him more enthusi- astic than "ever in the cause—(hear, hear)—and he hoped those present would not cease to use every exertion to pro- mote the cause of temperance in every way. He was sure they had Christianity on their side, they had goodness on their side, they had contentment on their side, and they had the Scriptures on their side, for they would remember it said, "Blessed are ye when men shall revile and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven." (Applause.) 'Mr. WILLIAM NEILD, who met with a cordial reception, seconded the resolution. He said it was rather a fortunate accident, so far as he was individually concerned, that he had an opportunity of once more daying that his interest still continued in the temperance Cause. (Applause.) It was some years now since he left Warrington, and it was purely an accident that he was present that night. He found their annual meeting was being held, and he could not resist the temptation of coming to look at them. (Applause.) They had heard that night a good deal of what ought to be done in regard to the removal of this sad business, the multi- plication of public-houses, where he suppose nine out of every ten ought not to be. If a majority was to decide what the laws of the countiy ought to be, surely it was quite time some decision was taken as to whether they would or would not have public-houses in their midst. (Applause.) They all knew that where there were so many public-houses drunkenness was almost sure to abound. In regard to the opposition which Mr. Derbyshire had described, he thought opposition of that kind was very good. It stimulated one to do what one would otherwise not do. He remembered the time when opposition was a very much more common element in the temperance movement than it was now. He had seen in that hall much larger audiences than the one that night, but he was not at all discouraged, and thought the report was encouraging than otherwise. He dared say a good many of them were aware he had been resident in a town which stood more prominently forward in the tem- perance movement than any other town in the kingdom. He referred to Reading, where there were many gentlemen who spent time and money in the cause, and consequently they were able to do a great deal more than they were in War- rington. But he would not have them to be discouraged, because whilst there a great many discouraging elements there were also a great many encouraging elements. They saw the question was being taken up by individuals who held high positions in society, and by that means giving countenance to the movement which until recently had not been the case. That was a very encouraging- element, and they had to look forward to it as being the promoter of a great deal of the success of the cause. He had pleasure in seconding the resolution, and it afforded him great pleasure to meet many of his old friends. (Applause.) The resolution was unanimously carried. Mr. THOMAS WHITTAKER gave a highly amusing address descriptive of the opposition to the temperance cause when he was a temperance advocate, and exhibited the rattle with which, in the streets of Warrington, in 1836, he called his own meeting. He adverted to the Sunday Closing Bills that had been passed, and to to the temperance agitation that was going on, and main- tained-that this showed they bad net laboured for nought. There was now a very different sentiment and practice in this country on the temperance question, and it was grow- ing every day. Might God help them to work until the last drunkard was re-claimed and the last public-house closed. (Applause.) The Rev. THOMAS Rirrox moved a vote of thanks to the chairman and the speakers. He remarked that he was proud his name was that night to be associated with the name of Thomas Whittaker, whom he regarded as the prince of ad- vocates of tempeeance principles. As the only minister of religion present, he rose simply to show his colours. (Ap- plause.) He rejoiced as a Christian minister that the doctors of the land were taking their tight stand on this question. The Anglican Church was taking a right stand. It had a splendid organisation, with the Queen herself as patron, and the whole bench of bishops as presidents. When he remembered that under the dome of St. Paul's Canon Wil- berforce, and in the Old Abbey Canon Farrar, eloquently proclaim • ed temperance, should he not gratefully say that night thank God for the Church of England Temperance Society. (Applause.) He was glad the Roman Catholics in this country had their crusade with Cardinal Manning and Father Nugent leading. The Nonconformists were not lagging behind. At the two Wesleyan training institutions at Headingley, near Leeds, and Didsbury, Manchester, they had 83 students, 80 of whom were total abstainers. (Ap- plause.) They had 1,000 ministers, and upwards of half of that number were total abstainers. (Applause.) They had also 2,033 Bands of Hope, with 202,516 members. He thought this was a fair sign of the times. He knew there was a time when even for a Methodist preacher to have spoken on this subject would have brought down showers of abuse, and although Wesley. was one of the greatest refor- mers, it was not until Charles Garrett spoke out on the sub- ject that others stood by him, and to-day, thank God, he did not stand alone. (Applause.) Warrington people mugi stand by the flag of temperance. lie had seen something since he came to that town, which if he had not been con- vinced before he came that total abstinence was the thing to respect would have convinced him, and had made him doubly so a sworn foe of the drink traffic.
